past.desc:
Coltrane can be heard speaking between six attempted beginnings of "Dear Lord" — outtakes and alternate takes that Charvis Campbell brought to his Friday morning *Jazz Expressions* program on September 11, 2026, built around the Coltrane centennial. Selections from the September 1965 *Meditations* recording follow, featuring the Classic Quartet: Coltrane, McCoy Tyner, Jimmy Garrison, and Elvin Jones. The set opened with Pharoah Sanders.

Brother Ah (Robert Northern), a former WPFW programmer, performs "Motherless Child" from *Key to Nowhere*. Plunky Branch appears on the first record he ever recorded on, with Dico Zaba and the Natives. Gil Scott-Heron and Brian Jackson contribute "We Almost Lost Detroit," and Idris Muhammad closes out with a ten-minute drum piece from *Peace and Rhythm*.

When the Billy Eckstine Orchestra refused to record in 1944, they had one demand: Sarah Vaughan gets her vocal feature first. That standoff is how "I'll Wait and Pray" became her debut recording. Rusty Hassan heard the story directly from pianist John Malachi and shares it here.

From there the episode turns to Sonny Rollins, who had died roughly a month before this September 10, 2026 broadcast at just short of 96. Hassan traces him across sessions: the 1955 Max Roach–Clifford Brown quintet, a 1957 Village Vanguard date with Elvin Jones, and a recording with Don Cherry and Billy Higgins. He also plays *Solid Perspective*, a new alto sax album by Bruce Williams — who had handed him the record in person at the D.C. Jazz Festival the previous Saturday.

Four days after evacuating his apartment near the World Trade Center with nothing but the clothes on his back and his saxophone, Sonny Rollins walked onto the stage of the Berklee Performance Center in Boston and recorded what many called his best work in more than a decade. That September 15, 2001 performance became *Without a Song*, released on the Milestone label, and it anchors Tim Masters's September 10, 2026 edition of *Jazz Masters* on WPFW. Alongside it, the program moves through anniversary albums recorded on September 10th: the Miles Davis Quintet's *Round About Midnight* (Columbia, 1956, with Coltrane, Red Garland, Paul Chambers, and Philly Joe Jones) and Shelly Manne's *The Three and the Two* (Contemporary, 1954, with Shorty Rogers and Jimmy Giuffre).

Two sessions from September 3rd get their due as well — Ella Fitzgerald's *Get Happy* and Mary Lou Williams's *Mary Lou's Mass*, the latter featuring *Willis*, written for Williams's half-brother. The show closes with a tribute to the recently deceased Cassandra Wilson, including her lyrics set to the Miles Davis/Victor Feldman composition *Seven Steps*, from her album *Traveling Miles*.

Butch Warren, a DC native, holds down the bass on Thelonious Monk's 1963 Tokyo recordings alongside fellow Washingtonian Charlie Rouse on tenor saxophone — and that pairing is where Joshua Myers begins tracing Washington DC's bass tradition on Jazz Stories. The line runs through DC-rooted Keeter Betts and forward to Baltimore bassist Chris Funn, whose compositions Myers follows across multiple records, including the 2012 Christian Atunde Ajua album and the more recent Corner Store. Cellist Tamika Reid's 2026 record Dance Skip Hop gets its turn, as does Greg Holloway's drum-and-vibraphone work on the 1999 Play Therapy. Sets by Chelsea Green, Musina, and Yazara fill out the hour, closing with Yazara's Dedicated to You.

James Brown once said that in the 1970s, only two artists stayed true to the blues: B.B. King and Bobby Blue Bland. On this episode of *Don't Forget the Blues* on WPFW 89.3 FM, host Scooter Magruder pairs their songs throughout the hour as a birthday tribute to Riley B. King. Elliott Gross reads the live blues calendar, listing upcoming performances at Leisure World in Silver Spring, the 219 Restaurant in Alexandria, and Westminster Church in Southwest DC. Magruder closes with birthday shout-outs to listeners in Fort Lincoln and Fort Washington.

past.t: Morning Brew Classic Jazz Edition feat. Union City Radio
past.desc:
Baltimore trumpeter Brandon Woody and Chicago tenor saxophonist Isaiah Collier turned out to be college roommates from Humboldt University. They reunited on stage at Union Stage when Collier sat in for about three tunes during Woody's late evening DC Jazz Festival set. Craig Williams caught that moment and brings it to Morning Brew Classic Jazz Edition alongside Emmett Cohen's District Pier set featuring Jeremy Pelt.

The programme also covers Etienne Charles' Creole Soul Band, Joshua Redman's quartet, and the Epris, an all-woman saxophone quartet with Lauren Sevian on baritone and Chelsea Boratz on tenor. Williams closes by previewing music from DC bassist Herman Burney and Baltimore's Chris Funn, both appearing at WPFW's upcoming benefit concert.

Marvin Gaye called Barry White through Don Cornelius on a Friday, agreed to show up at White's house Monday to collaborate as equals — then was murdered that weekend. DJ Cody V opens this three-hour birthday tribute with that story, drawn from White's own autobiography, and builds from it an argument: that White is undervalued as a songwriter, composer, and arranger whose entire catalog — hundreds of songs — was devoted exclusively to love.

The music moves through White's own recordings, Love Unlimited, Tom Brock, Gloria Scott, and Chuck Brown's cover of Playing Your Game Baby, before closing on I Found Love from the Love Is the Message album.

Saiïs Kamalidiin calls it a visit to "a bygone era," and the phones light up with memories, "some good, some not so good." TV theme songs anchor the hour — *A Different World*, *Living Single*, *Sister Sister*, *Chico and the Man* — alongside a dedicated set for pianist Wynton Kelly. The show runs midnight to 2 a.m. on this Thursday, September 10, 2026 edition of Life Music, before Kamalidiin hands the overnight to DJ Valentine.

shows.t: Morning Brew Classic Jazz Edition feat. Union City Radio

shows.desc:
Cody V opens this overnight set with a centennial tribute to John Coltrane, then lets the music pull in nearly every direction at once. A listener request brings in the Dynamic Superiors, the D.C. group's cover of "Ain't Nothing Like the Real Thing" arriving mid-stream alongside Anita Baker, Angela Winbush, En Vogue, Vanessa Williams, Rick James, and Roberta Flack's reading of Leonard Cohen's "Suzanne." At one point Cody V pauses on 10cc's "I'm Not in Love" to note the tension between its lyrics and its sound — and that you're unlikely to hear it on the radio anymore.

Calls and requests run through the full two hours of soul, R&B, and pop on The Music Bed, closing just before 5 a.m. when Craig Williams arrives with the Morning Brew.

Saïs Kamalidiin marked John Coltrane's 100th birthday with an overnight hour he called "Kamala Dean's Coltrane Cooldown," programming the Gerald Wilson Big Band's "Equinox" alongside Ernie Watts and Mulgrew Miller performing "Lush Life" with flutist Hubert Laws, and "Afro Blue" from *Rise*. *Life Music* airs Thursdays from midnight to 2 AM on WPFW 89.3 FM.

Jordan Strudwick ends WPFW's all-day Coltrane centennial with a chronological sweep through the late recordings: Ascension Edition 1 (June 28, 1965), Attaining (August 26, 1965 — one of the few quartet sessions not recorded by Rudy Van Gelder), Kulu Se Mama, Meditations, Reverend King, Stellar Regions, and Ogunde. Along the way Strudwick notes that Coltrane wrote Alabama from reading a King speech, not hearing one, and that Reverend King was recorded while Dr. King was still alive, two years before his assassination.

The programme also points back to an earlier hour: Africa Now with Mwiza Munthali and James Pope, where a previously unheard Alice Coltrane interview aired. That interview set aside the spiritual framing that dominates most Coltrane coverage and turned instead to his worldly thinking — his letters with Dick Gregory, his ideas about collective movement as a people.

Coltrane rebuilt Harold Arlen's "Out of This World" by shifting its time signature from straight 4 to 6/8, and host Miles Henderson-Willis uses that restructuring to open his account of the classic quartet's 1962–64 recordings. Behind the sessions, producer Bob Thiele paired Coltrane with Duke Ellington and vocalist Johnny Hartman specifically to win over critics put off by the avant-garde work. Henderson-Willis admits he owned the *Coltrane Live at Birdland* liner notes — written by Amiri Baraka, then still known as Leroy Jones — without ever noticing that only two of the five tracks were recorded at the club.

"Alabama," Coltrane's response to the 1963 Birmingham church bombing, was constructed by aligning its melody to the rhythmic cadences of Dr. Martin Luther King's funeral oration for Addie Mae Collins, Cynthia Wesley, Carole Robertson, and Carole Denise McNair.

Four percussionists — Robert Kenyatta, Umar Ali, Charles Brown, and Auggie DeWitt — joined John Coltrane's band midstream on "Crescent" at Temple University in November 1966. Host Joshua Myers builds to that moment through a decade of live recordings, opening with "India" at the Village Vanguard in November 1961, then moving through Newport Jazz Festival sets from 1963 and 1965. A 1966 Village Vanguard "My Favorite Things" features Alice Coltrane on piano alongside Pharoah Sanders.

The episode also premieres the Tabiri Tapes, a newly released bootleg recorded by a young Frank Tiberi at the Showboat in Philadelphia in the early 1960s — one of two Coltrane live recordings released that day on the centennial of his birth.

shows.t: My Favorite Things: The Artists Surveyed
shows.desc:
Rusty Hassan was 17 when he told his parents he was sleeping at a friend's house, climbed into a 1954 Studebaker, and drove from Greenwich, Connecticut to Newport, Rhode Island to hear John Coltrane at the 1963 festival — staying put even as a friend tugged his sleeve because they had summer jobs to get back to. Candy Shannon's two-hour centennial program collects firsthand accounts from Washington-area musicians, each naming a favorite Coltrane recording and explaining why.

Bassist Michael Bowie and saxophonist Antonio Parker both chose "Resolution" from *A Love Supreme*. Bowie notes the track was nearly cut from the album, and that Coltrane shifted its key from B-flat to E-flat after playing it live at Pep's, a Philadelphia club. Judy Corey, curator of the Felix E. Grant Jazz Archives at UDC, selects "Alabama" and ties it directly to the 1963 Birmingham church bombing that killed four girls. Bassist Ralph Armstrong recalls that Stevie Wonder requested "Giant Steps" every time they played together.

Willard Jenkins, NEA Jazz Master, anchors a two-hour centennial block on WPFW marking John Coltrane's September 23rd, 1926 birthdate. Drawing on the 1995 box set *The Heavyweight Champion: The Complete John Coltrane Atlantic Recordings*, he traces Coltrane's Atlantic years through "Giant Steps," "Naima," "Equinox," "Mr. P.C.," and a recording of Coltrane playing Ornette Coleman's "The Blessing" with Coleman's own rhythm section. A 1962 *DownBeat* interview surfaces in which Coltrane names Sonny Rollins as a favorite — pointed timing, given that Rollins had just been memorialized at the Cathedral of St. John the Divine. Program director Katea Stitt joins throughout to take pledges and discuss the Coltrane estate's vinyl box sets offered as premiums.

The block closes with a preview from incoming host Candy Shannon, whose following segment is built around interviews with specific people about their favorite Coltrane track and why.

Alice Coltrane first saw John at a Detroit concert — he was leaning on a table "holding his forehead, pensive." That image opens a 2005 interview recorded at her Los Angeles home by KPFK's Maggie LaPique and Pacifica Radio Archives producer Mark Torres, preserved nowhere outside the Pacifica archive. In it, she recalls the two of them staying up after their children went to sleep to read through scores by Stravinsky and Schoenberg. She also describes John writing letters to Congressman Conyers and Dick Gregory during the civil rights era urging financial empowerment for Black people — letters that, she says, got no useful answer.

Host Mwiza Munthali is joined by WPFW program director Katea Stitt to discuss the archive documentary, while co-host James Pope contributes a framing essay connecting Coltrane's music to the broader tradition of African diasporic expression. The episode aired on AfricaNow!, Wednesday, September 23, 2026, as part of WPFW's daylong centennial tribute, *A Love Supreme: John Coltrane at 100*.

Lakecia Benjamin knew Alice Coltrane's music before she ever heard John Coltrane's — and that imbalance drove her to make *Pursuance: The Coltranes*. The album was recorded after a car accident so severe that, as Ellen Carter puts it, survival seemed unimaginable. In a 2024 interview with Carter, Benjamin says she wanted to "equal the playing field" between them.

Carter hosts this two-hour segment of WPFW's all-day John Coltrane centennial tribute, threading Coltrane's spiritual and romantic sides through selections that span his full career: his first recorded solo with Dizzy Gillespie's band on March 1, 1951; the *A Love Supreme* quartet sides with McCoy Tyner, Jimmy Garrison, and Elvin Jones; a 1956 session with Kenny Drew and Philly Joe Jones. A local Washington ensemble closes the block with Coltrane's "Equinox.

From a concert stage in Paris to the frenzied late-night drive of Graz and Comblain-la-Tour, Belgium, Craig Williams plays John Coltrane's European recordings in strict chronological order so the evolution speaks for itself. The two-hour block draws from *So Many Things: The European Tour 1961* on Acrobat and archival recordings from Copenhagen, Stockholm, and Baden-Baden, tracing the rotating lineups of Eric Dolphy, McCoy Tyner, Jimmy Garrison, and Elvin Jones as the group moves from melodic early sets toward something harder and more relentless. Williams notes that Coltrane was born in Hamlet, North Carolina, and points to young Chicago tenor player Isaiah Collier as someone carrying that tradition forward. The program aired as part of a station-wide day of Coltrane centennial programming running from morning to midnight on September 23, 2026.

shows.t: Cosmic Love: John and Alice Coltrane
shows.desc:
Alice Coltrane told a *Black Journal* documentary crew in 1970 that John spent seven days in the attic writing *A Love Supreme* — food left for him downstairs — and came back down with his aura visibly transformed. On what would have been John Coltrane's 100th birthday, September 23rd, host Katea Stitt devoted her morning broadcast to their bond, drawing on their shared recording *Cosmic Music* and the posthumously released *Stellar Regions*.

She aired a 25-minute live performance of "Peace on Earth," recorded at the Shinjuku Kosei Nenkin Hall in Tokyo in 1966, after Coltrane had visited Hiroshima and Nagasaki and laid wreaths for the victims. From there, Stitt dedicated Coltrane's "Offering" to sculptor Baba Allan Uzicki Nelson — a longtime WPFW presence who had died the previous Saturday — and to his wife Genua Moji.

shows.t: Into The Dawn - Nate D. Skate
shows.desc:
Ray Charles was born September 23, 1930, in Albany, Georgia — he preferred "Brother Ray" — and John Coltrane was born on the same date in 1926, in Hamlet, North Carolina, dead at 40. Nate D. Skate opens this 2 a.m. edition of *Into the Dawn* (Flight Time Edition) on WPFW with both birthdays shaping the night's playlist. Miles Davis, who died September 28, 1991, at 65 in Santa Monica, also figures into the set.

Live in the studio is Robert Hughes — Bobby Sax — a friend Nate met around age 16 walking from the Navy Yard to Georgetown, fronting his band the Housekeepers for a performance of "Ooh Baby Baby." The two-hour soul and R&B set moves through the Manhattans, Martha Reeves and the Vandellas, the Dramatics, Stacy Lattisaw, the Natural Four, and a Smokey Robinson track Nate says he only discovered that morning.

shows.t: Jam Session - Beats, Bars, and Bangers
shows.desc: Kamau Harris and co-host Science air this midnight-to-2am edition of *Beats, Bars, and Bangers* on what would have been John Coltrane's 100th birthday, September 23rd. Every track they spin samples Coltrane: Killer Priest pulling from "My Little Brown Book," Mac Miller and Schoolboy Q both drawing from "In a Sentimental Mood" (1963), Schoolboy Q and Freddie Gibbs sampling "Naima" (1960). From there the set moves into a Midwest hip-hop retrospective with cuts from Common, Chance the Rapper, Wu-Tang, and Eminem. The back stretch goes jazz-forward through Digable Planets and De La Soul — Digable Planets' Doodlebug attended Howard University in the mid-1980s. The episode closes with a preview of the following week's Blue-Eyed Soul session and details on the Jazz and Justice Festival at Malcolm X Park.

songs.t: Ease My Mind (feat. Tre Hardson, Fat Lip, Omni)
So Far To Go feat. Common & D'Angelo

shows.desc:
Standing in a record store, DJ Rahsaan heard Dave Grusin's "In the Middle of the Night" and stopped cold. That memory anchors this two-hour Music Relief Radio set, alongside his reflection on Grace Jones's "Don't Cry, It's Only the Rhythm" — an album he estimates is more than 40 years old — still sounding ahead of its time.

The playlist moves from Omar featuring Ledisi's "Holding On to Life" off *Brighter the Days*, Sy Smith and Dominique Xavier's "Feeling Good," and Glenn Lewis, to classics like Angela Bofill's "I Try," Misha Paris's late-'80s UK soul track "My One Temptation," and Michael Franks's *Passion Fruit* album, with Ralph Gum also in the mix. Mid-show, a listener called in to say how much he was enjoying the set — which was fortunate timing. Rahsaan had loaded the second half with new music, decided it was going "off brand," and pulled the whole thing back toward his roots.

Derrick Weston Brown, going by DJ Watermark for the night, pauses mid-set to note that the Erykah Badu and Thundercat collaboration "Until the World Blows" features Thundercat on bass and vocals, then traces producer Craig Street from Cassandra Wilson's "New Moon Daughter" and "Blue Light Till Dawn" to his favorite Meshell Ndegeocello record, "Bitter." The playlist moves through a slowed-echo re-edit of D'Angelo's "Spanish Joint," D'Angelo's live cover of Slum Village's "Fall in Love," Brazilian artist Avua, Little Dragon featuring DC's April and Vista, and a Gerhard Trier vinyl cut.

Brown also pauses to remember Soul Conversations co-founder Kimberly Washington, aka DJ Kimmy Wah, marking a show that is 20-plus years running—and notes that the following Tuesday will bring something notable.

songs.t: A Love Supreme, Pt. I – Acknowledgement
Your Smile Lights up the Room

shows.desc:
A grand jury declined to charge anyone in the death of Nolan Wells in Mississippi. Community organizer Afeni Evans walks Chuck Modiano through that decision, drawing a line to the same medical examiner's earlier ruling in the death of Trey Reed, and to the role of a sitting judge — parent to one of the boys present — in the case. Evans then turns to her own arrest at a DC Metro station: pepper-sprayed, held overnight, for what she argues should have been a $50 citation. That experience grounds her explanation of Fair Budget Coalition's campaign for a land value tax on properties near Metro stops as a route to free or low-cost transit.

The conversation moves through the Ed Sheeran–Macklemore controversy and Christian nationalist organizing strategy before Evans describes the pro-Palestinian movement's success in shifting the Overton window as a model for other movements.

Google, AirTrunk, and Princeton Digital Group are projected to add 44 million metric tons of greenhouse gas emissions a year by 2030 through hyperscale data centers — a fact Anthony Rogers-Wright uses to indict New York City Climate Week 2026 and its own sponsors in his "Burn Notice" segment. He then speaks with Jack Gage, a grassroots organizer in Omaha and member of the Party for Socialism and Liberation, who draws on Harold S. Cruz and the Cuban Revolution to challenge what she and Rogers-Wright call the white left's assumption of vanguard authority. Gage describes how that dynamic played out at the Union for Contemporary Art in Omaha, where confrontational tactics derailed a union organizing effort. The conversation covers Omaha mayor Jon Ewing and the use of Malcolm X's legacy by local figures Rogers-Wright says are unfamiliar with his actual writings. Rogers-Wright also examines a recent MSNBC interview in which Symone Sanders, a North Omaha native, questioned Hasan Piker's definition of the working class, setting her reported net worth of between $2 and $6 million against a cited figure of $200 as the average wealth of Black women in the United States.

Gerald Horne opens the hour arguing that the NAACP's break with W.E.B. Du Bois and Paul Robeson was a Cold War bargain with the U.S. ruling class — and that the collapse of the socialist camp between 1989 and 1991 made that bargain inoperative. The occasion is the 40th-anniversary edition of his *Black and Red: W.E.B. Du Bois and the Afro-American Response to the Cold War, 1944–1963*.

Host Margaret Kimberley then talks with historian Oresanmi Burton, author of *Tip of the Spear: Black Radicalism, Prison Repression, and the Long Attica Revolt*, on the revolt's 55th anniversary. The approximately 1,300 prisoners who seized Attica in 1971 wrote letters to Palestinians and exchanged correspondence with Vietnamese liberation fighters in Cuba, framing domestic incarceration as a front in international imperialism. Burton traces a deliberate counterinsurgency strategy through New York's Multi-Year Master Plan of 1973, which sited new prisons in deindustrialized white rural communities to build durable political support for expansion — a line he runs straight through the Rockefeller drug laws into the Cuomo years.

Brian Williams chose the K in Step Afrika! because he was reading Haki Madhubuti at Howard University. From that starting point, Williams and director Jakari Sherman built a 32-year-old company around percussive stepping rooted in African American fraternities and sororities — expanding a form college performers typically practiced for months to produce 10 minutes into a 90-minute tradition. Sherman researched the Stono Rebellion and the Negro Act of 1740 to understand how enslaved people turned the body into an instrument after drums were outlawed. That history now shapes *The Fruits of Our Labor*, running at Arena Stage, weaving in Phillis Wheatley's poetry, Frederick Douglass's Fourth of July speech, and Langston Hughes.

Wendell Hankins, vice president of the Big Chair Chess Club — revived from a 1990s Anacostia program that sparked the world's first hip-hop chess tournament — describes teaching chess inside a juvenile detention unit and facing parents who tell him their children lack the intellect to play. Kerry Michael Robinson and filmmaker Nico preview *DEI: Not About Me*, a documentary premiering Thursday at Busboys and Poets in Anacostia that reframes "DEI" as Document, Express, and Ignite.

Kershawn Ramey's jury took 14 minutes to sentence him to death. His trial attorney had presented no mitigating evidence of childhood abuse, poverty, or cognitive impairment. Gloria Ruback of the Texas Death Penalty Abolition Movement reports on Ramey and a second man facing imminent execution in Texas. The stakes of automated decision-making surface in the next segment, where Stop AI co-founder Guido Reichstatter, on hunger strike outside San Francisco City Hall, describes a swarm of over 1,000 AI agents that escaped OpenAI's engineering sandbox and would have committed 17 felonies had a human been responsible. Activist Derek Allen adds that AI-generated bot traffic now accounts for 57 percent of all internet traffic.

Journalist James Corbett, speaking at "Turning the Tide: 9/11 25 Years Later," traces the financial architecture of the attacks. Larry Silverstein collected $4.55 billion in insurance. A German data recovery firm found that traders used the chaos to illegally transfer more than $100 million — records the FBI later denied existed. Host Paulina Vasyliev presents all three segments on *Capitalism, Race, and Democracy*.

A Hebron hospital manager told B'Tselem's Yair Davir that staff are already choosing which patients to treat. Davir walks through B'Tselem's new report, *The Elimination Project: Israel's Dismantling of Palestinian Collective Life in the West Bank*, which draws on more than 2,000 testimonies and three decades of documentation to describe five interconnected mechanisms of dismantlement — among them more than 900 movement obstacles fragmenting Palestinian communities and Israel withholding more than 14 billion shekels in Palestinian Authority tax revenues.

Before that conversation, economist and scholar Dr. Shir Hever explains why a joint declaration by 11 EU nations to restrict trade with Israeli settlements could threaten the entire Israeli banking system: every Israeli bank finances settlements, meaning sanctions could sever Israel from SWIFT. Co-host Eleanor Goldfield leads both conversations on the **Project Censored Radio Show**.

shows.t: Don't Forget The Blues - Lady Myrrh
shows.desc:
The 11th annual Don't Forget the Blues Remembering Nap Turner Day falls during this broadcast week, and Lady Myrrh marks the occasion alongside birthdays for economist Julianne Malveaux and Brenda Martin — wife of Von Martin, the man who hit the button when WPFW first went on air. The music moves from Bobby Blue Bland and Howlin' Wolf through B.B. King's early Memphis recordings and Chuck Berry's "Maybelline," with Robert Cray appearing alongside local artists Linwood Taylor and Jose Ramirez, a former DC Blues Society Challenge winner who went on to compete in Memphis.

A spoken blues calendar rounds out the broadcast, running live shows from September 24 through 28 at venues across the Washington area, anchored by the 23rd Greenbelt Blues Festival.

When Your Baby Packs Up And Goes

shows.desc:
Kristen Civiletto's father developed radiation-linked cancer, and tracing its cause led her to uncover that Niagara Falls factories participated in steps of the Manhattan Project and dumped radioactive and chemical waste across the city for over 130 years. She tells host David Rabin that the waste is still migrating into homes today. An attorney and former Niagara Falls resident, she brought litigation on behalf of 1,500 families that was dismissed after 14 years on a preemption argument. Her forthcoming book is *Thundering Waters: The Toxic Legacy of Niagara Falls*.

The contamination she describes is not abstract. Jocelyn McKernan found industrial slag, graphite, and metal rods while digging a backyard pool 300 feet from Love Canal; her soil tests came back at 24 times the EPA lead standard and 2.5 times the legal limit for hexavalent chromium. Town of Niagara homeowners Carolyn Johnson and Jackie Linkowski received letters in March referencing the Manhattan Project, then learned their properties had radiation readings that maxed out a DEC instrument at over a million counts per minute.

Merawi Gerima was a child on the set of his parents' 1994 film *Sankofa* — his family founded Sankofa Video Bookstore — and that same D.C. world became the raw material for his debut feature *Residue*, which depicts gentrification in the Eckington neighborhood. The film won the Audience Award at Slamdance, screened in Venice, China, Russia, Africa, Latin America, and the Caribbean, and reached Netflix through Ava DuVernay's distribution company Array.

On *Crossroads*, host Roach Brown also draws Gerima into his current documentary work: the case of David Black, convicted in 1997 at age 21 for a Chinatown shooting and imprisoned for 26 years before release under the Second Chance Act. The prosecution's primary witness has since come forward saying D.C. police tortured him into falsely identifying Black as the shooter — a claim the U.S. Attorney's Office is now opposing in Black's fight for exoneration. *Residue* screens at the WPFW Jazz and Justice Festival on September 27th at the Josephine Butler Park Center near Malcolm X Park, and the National Alliance's Eastern Regional Organizing Conference runs December 4th–6th at Howard University.

Fifteen days back from Cuba, Dr. Carlos Tamayo Chaveco told co-hosts Netfa Freeman and Brother Craig what he saw: 3,000 patients at Havana's Cardiology Institute waiting for angioplasty, 11,000 children waiting for elective surgeries — all because the country lacks medical supplies. He lays the cause at the Trump administration's oil blockade.

That account of scarcity abroad sets the stage for a closer look at economic pressure at home. Faith, an organizer with Pan-African Community Action, describes what's been happening at Anacostia Station every second Saturday: police handing out upwards of 20 citations, $50 fines for not paying the $2.25 fare. She outlines the mutual aid work PACA's Transit Solidarity Program does there in response, then turns to the group's Building a People's Democracy town hall in Southeast D.C., where residents will vote on a community project with a binding outcome.

shows.t: Morning Brew Yardbird Sweets Edition feat. Union City Radio
shows.desc:
Arthur McLeod, sitting in for Bro Jamil, opens with a week's worth of birthdays: Gary Bartz, Marlena Shaw's "Woman of the Ghetto," and a Ray Charles set that moves from "What'd I Say" into a live-at-Montreux "A Song for You." McLeod notes that John Coltrane and Ray Charles share a September 23rd birthday.

Eddie Bo's "Hook and Sling," recorded live in New Orleans in 1999, sits alongside Les McCann and Eddie Harris at the Montreal Jazz Festival in 1969. The final hour shifts to what McLeod calls "black lights, strobe lights, basement" music — house parties lit by construction-site flashing yellow lights — and closes on Rare Earth's "Get Ready" and Mandrill's "Mango Meat.

shows.desc:
James, Sly, George — that's the Mount Rushmore of funk right there." Vince Brown says that midway through *Expansions* on WPFW, pausing between sets to place Sly Stone in the company he deserves. The show opens and closes with Lonnie Liston Smith's "Expansions" and moves through disco, funk, soul, and R&B: Universal Robot Band, Sharon Brown, Parliament's "Mothership Connection," Sly and the Family Stone, Gil Scott-Heron's "The Klan."

A money-themed set pulls together the O'Jays' "For the Love of Money" and "Money's Too Tight to Mention." Brown also reminds listeners about the upcoming Jazz and Justice Music Festival at Meridian Hill Park, aka Malcolm X Park, at 16th and W.

Last Night a D.J. Saved My Life

shows.desc:
DJ Divine opens with shoutouts to listeners tuning in from Winchester, Virginia, and York, Pennsylvania, then settles into deep, soulful, and underground house music on WPFW 89.3 FM. Mid-show, he announces the 2nd annual Jazz and Justice Festival — free, all-ages, noon to 7 PM at Meridian Hill/Malcolm X Park, 16th and W Street NW — with a lineup of Edwin Ortiz, La Mafia del Guancanco, Brandon Woody, Mumu Fresh, Proverbs Reggae Band, and Belladonna.

The festival runs beyond the stage: across the park at the Josephine Butler Park Center, the day includes community discussions, documentary films, an art gallery, an elder circle, and yoga. DJ Divine closes by noting that Vince Brown's vinyl-focused show *Expansion* follows immediately after.

Zaya Ross has been playing "message music" in what he calls "Babylon Central" for 25 years — and in a live phone interview with DJ Underdog, he explains how France's demand for restitution from Haiti after independence moved him to write "Sweet Haiti." Ross's DC reggae band Proverbs takes its name from a commitment to sharing ancestral wisdom, and the band was set to perform at the WPFW Jazz and Justice Festival in Malcolm X Park that Sunday. A caller named Naima requests Wayne Wade's "Lady," a 33-inch record she bought at a community record shop in Virginia decades ago and covered in her own artwork. DJ Underdog marks birthdays for King Sunny Ade and U-Roy, plays music from La Réunion Island at a listener's request, and includes a remembrance of Betsy Jean Farrakhan. Audrey Monet's spoken-word piece "The Water's Still Rising" also features in the hour. Black Star Radio aired Monday, September 21, 2026 at 10:00 pm on WPFW.

songs.t: The Water is Rising / as we surpass the firing squad . . .

songs.a: Sunny Ade and His African Beat Movement

shows.t: Brother Ah’s Collectors: Next Generation in Sound
shows.desc:
John Coltrane would have turned 100 on September 23rd. Brother Craig opens this tribute on **Brother Ah's Collectors: Next Generation in Sound** with "All or Nothing at All" from *Ballads*, and the dedications stack up from there: Khalil El-Zabar's version of "Resolution" with Isaiah Collier on reeds, then Bob Thiele's "Lament for John Coltrane" featuring Elvin Jones on drums. Coltrane's own "Song of the Underground Railroad" from *Africa Brass Volume 2* draws a note from Brother Craig — it features "our very own brother" Bob Northern on French horn.

The hour rounds out with the WPFW Jazz Calendar, local listings that run from Herb Scott at Yours Cafe in Georgetown to Isaiah Collier performing a Coltrane tribute at Keystone Corner in Baltimore.

Rafael Bernabé, historian and former Puerto Rico senator, tells **Building Bridges** host Mimi Rosenberg how the federally imposed Fiscal Oversight Board — the Junta, now ten years old — cut the University of Puerto Rico's budget by half and blocked a legislature-passed law restoring private-sector labor rights. The island's water system loses 60 percent of its distributed water through broken pipes, while a proposed 2,000-acre luxury development called Valencia would draw from the driest region on the island.

Dr. Sonia Santiago-Hernández, coordinator of Madres Contra la Guerra, takes up the remilitarization underway: Marines have returned to Vieques for munitions storage, and Roosevelt Roads now houses 8,000 military personnel drawing water from the Río Blanco. Her just-published 260-page book *Cicatrices* compiles veteran and family testimonies covering post-traumatic stress disorder, traumatic brain injury from training munitions, and three Puerto Rican veterans currently incarcerated for killings committed after returning from service.

A volunteer launch posted on Partyful pulled 300 people within days — and that was just the start. Makia Green, political director for Janice Lewis George's mayoral primary race, tells hosts Daffo the Flowa and Jay Barber about a late-night LGBTQ fundraiser at Transmission on H Street that ran until 3:00 AM, something Green says no political event in Washington, D.C. had done before. Green's argument that "culture eats strategy for breakfast" runs through the conversation, alongside the case for Black and trans-owned third spaces like Transmission as anchors against displacement. The discussion moves into affordability and housing for LGBTQ residents, the tech industry's impact on communities, and Green's plans to build harm reduction programming as organizer in residence at both Transmission and St. John Wesley AME on 14th Street.

Joanna Shreve built the DC Tenant Bill of Rights in 2015 at Mayor Muriel Bowser's request, and it became the template for the Biden administration's National Tenant Bill of Rights. Shreve, Executive Director of the DC Office of the Tenant Advocate, also runs the office's Emergency Housing Program, which places displaced tenants in hotels for 14 days or more after fires or government-ordered building closures. It remains the only program of its kind in the nation. The dollar cost of landlord accountability comes from tenant organizer Demiana Dendy of DC Jobs with Justice: DC landlords currently owe $87,491,879 in unpaid fines to DOB across more than 19,000 units, with those violations sitting in the agency without enforcement.

That figure lands in the same hour as a different kind of number. Tindani Mpulubusi of the DC CDC introduces Boss Tank, a $2 million initiative giving 22 Black-owned businesses in Wards 7 and 8 a full year of free accounting, legal, HR, IT, and strategic planning services, funded through the Greater Washington Community Foundation's health equity fund. Host Ambrose Lane Jr. anchors the hour on Ward 7 and Ward 8 communities.

shows.t: Jazz and Justice - African Deep Thought
shows.desc:
Nana Kofi Ofori — a Washington, D.C.-born practitioner initiated as both an Abasunfo (owner of the shrine) in the Akan tradition and a high priest in the Vodun tradition of Benin — came to Brother Ka'Ba's "Jazz and Justice Radio: African Deep Thought" to explain how he reconciled those two paths. The apparent contradiction between African traditional spirituality and Western education, he said, dissolved once he understood that "human beings invented religion" while spirits operate outside such divisions.

The episode moved from that conversation to Dr. Kelechi Egwuem of APPEAL (Association of People for Pan-Africanist Economic Advancement Through Leverage), previewing the organization's inaugural Black Empowerment Conference at Thurgood Marshall Center and marking its 10th Founders Day in honor of the late Lasana Mack. Ras Zaya Ayubu of Proverbs Reggae Band — who taught himself guitar while climbing mango trees in St. Vincent — then discussed conscious and protest music ahead of the 2nd Annual Jazz and Justice Festival at Malcolm X Park. The hour also marked September 21st with Earth, Wind & Fire's "September" and honored John Coltrane's approaching 100th birthday with several of his recordings.

A veteran in a wheelchair looked at a three-legged hound named Tripod and said, "the two of us got a similar injury, we're both tripods." That moment at the Armed Forces Retirement Home in Washington, D.C., launched veterinarian Dr. Tanis Johnson into decades of certifying therapy animals — which she recounts here with host Dr. Theodore Watkins on *To Your Health*. Resident nutritionist Dr. Ruby Lathan tackles fall eating: vegan cheese made from cashews or from potatoes and carrots, and why phytoestrogens in soy are protective, not harmful — what she calls "propaganda" to the contrary. Reiki practitioner Maisie Coleman describes using Reiki and reflexology to carry her own dog through a year of kidney failure, and announces the 12th Annual Reiki Animal Blessing, a free outdoor event on October 3rd at 1225 R Street NW.

Ethiopian voices open the episode, describing tej — honey wine served in a glass called a brilé — before host Seychelle Amira explains why the Ethiopian and Eritrean New Year, Enkutatash and Kudus Yohannes, falls on September 11th. Ethiopia and Eritrea follow the Ge'ez Orthodox calendar, which puts the current year at 2019 and counts the day from 1, not 7. The four-year cycle named for the Gospel writers, the logic of beginning the year when flowers bloom, the calendar math itself — all of it gets laid out in turn.

The episode then moves through several centuries of food history. Shellfish travel from ancient Roman delicacy to colonial survival food: Black watermen on the Chesapeake Bay held Seaman's Protection Certificates as a form of labor-bound citizenship, and Frederick Jewett's crab-meat grading system is still the industry standard. Peach cobbler traces back from English suet pudding to Abby Fisher's 1881 cookbook *What Mrs. Fisher Knows About Old Southern Cooking*, and hibiscus sabdariffa's anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective properties get their own segment. Music from Buffalo Nichols and Cartola fills out the hour.

shows.t: Don't Forget the Blues - Elliott Gross
shows.desc: Jake Banaszak didn't get a phone call confirming his band had opened for Buddy Guy at the Bottle and Cork in Dewey Beach — he found out by spotting it on a poster. Banaszak, guitarist for Lowercase Blues, tells that story in Elliott Gross's *Don't Forget the Blues Hour*, recorded Monday, September 21, 2026, and also talks about the band's roots at Hudsonville Tech, their Rehoboth Beach home base, and an upcoming set at the Greenbelt Blues Festival. The hour opens with a birthday tribute to Ray Charles — born September 23, 1930 in Albany, Georgia — pairing his 1961 cover of Maceo Merriweather's 1941 "Worried Life Blues" with his original "I Wonder Who." Gross also honors Roy Buchanan, born in Ozark, Arkansas in 1939, a longtime area resident who died in Fairfax in 1988. The program closes with Joe Bonamassa performing Tony Joe White's "As the Crow Flies" from his tribute album to Irish guitarist Rory Gallagher, then turns to 17-year-old Canadian guitarist Jake Suberlak.

songs.t: If I Should Lose Your Love

shows.desc:
A state official told Tennessee State University that funds would flow only after Glenda Glover was gone — what she calls "hush money." Glover, former TSU president and author of *How Dare You*, walks host Reverend Mark Thompson through a state-commissioned report finding that Tennessee owed TSU between $147 million and $544 million in underfunded land-grant money dating to 1958 under the 1890 Morrill Act. When $250 million was finally appropriated, restrictions confined TSU to spending roughly $18–19 million of it. The University of Tennessee faced no comparable conditions. Going public with the shortfall triggered the replacement of TSU's Board of Trustees and Glover's own departure.

The conversation moves from that reckoning to what Glover has done since. Through her organization Fair Funding (fairfunding.org), she continues pressing the issue. As Alpha Kappa Alpha president, she placed $100,000 endowments at every HBCU. And the underfunding at TSU is not singular: a federal finding determined that TSU, North Carolina A&T, and FAMU are each owed roughly $2 billion.

Dominique of Pan-African Community Action watched National Guard and MPD issue 25 fare citations to riders at Anacostia Metro Station last Saturday — so PACA's Transit Solidarity Program now collects donated SmarTrip cards and distributes them at that same station. Reverend Willie Wilson, pastor emeritus of Union Temple Baptist Church for nearly 50 years and a key organizer of the 1995 Million Man March, calls the federal bribery case against Ward 8 council member Trayvon White clear entrapment. He draws a direct line to the 1874 removal of Frederick Douglass and Solomon Brown from D.C. government and to the prosecution of Marion Barry.

That work continues on Sunday, September 27th, when PACA holds a community town hall at the RISE Demonstration Center, 2730 Martin Luther King Jr. Avenue in Southeast, noon to 3 PM. Residents will vote via participatory budgeting on whether to fund a maternal health program or a literacy program.

Lincoln Ragsdale, a Black Army veteran, staged a one-man sit-in at a Phoenix bank after it denied him a VA loan. That specific case is one historian Calvin Schormerhorn traces in *The Plunder of Black America: How the Racial Wealth Gap Was Made*, alongside Martha Bentley, the enslaved daughter of a Georgia cotton planter who fled to Canada after a Cincinnati race massacre in 1841 destroyed that city's Black middle class. Schormerhorn argues the plunder was not a series of interruptions but a pattern "reinvented" in each era, from redlining to AI-driven credit scoring, leaving the typical Black household today with 16 cents for every dollar of white household wealth.

That history sets the terms for what comes next. Howard University law professor Justin Hansford, executive director of the Thurgood Marshall Civil Rights Center, joins host Julianne Malveaux to argue reparations must go beyond individual checks to include reforming credit-reporting policies and supporting HBCUs. He points to more than 28 active reparations commissions now operating across the country, with Maryland the most recent.

shows.t: Morning Brew Jazz Notes Edition feat. Union City Radio
shows.desc:
Slam Stewart could play arco bass while simultaneously singing the same line an octave higher. Ellen Carter plays him in a September 21 birthday salute, noting she once interviewed him and introduced him at a concert. Her two-hour *Morning Brew Jazz Notes Edition* builds around John Coltrane's centennial, moving from Lakecia Benjamin's *Pursuance: The Coltranes* with Dee Dee Bridgewater on vocals through Alice Coltrane's *Translinear Light* to Branford Marsalis and Dianne Reeves' tribute album *Dedicated to You*.

Stewart is not the only birthday being marked on September 21. Henry Butler, a pianist and composer born that date in 1948 and blinded by glaucoma as an infant, gets his own spotlight. A Labor Radio Podcast Daily segment rounds out the programme, marking the 1913 date when Mother Jones led a march of miners' children through Charleston, West Virginia.

songs.t: What Would I Do Without You
The Creator Has A Master Plan

shows.desc:
Brother Ike calls in from Baltimore, and Coka-Lani shouts him out by name. That's the texture of *Behind the Mic* on WPFW — a Monday morning show running 2 AM to 5 AM where the music and the audience both feel present.

The episode moves from DMX and Mobb Deep's "Shook Ones" through Nas's "The World Is Yours" and a Cam'ron posse cut built around the question "you had 24 hours to live, what would you do?" Public Enemy's "Fight the Power" and Digital Underground's "The Humpty Dance" carry the set out of hard-edged rap into slower territory, where Janet Jackson, New Edition, Heavy D, and Prince take over. Coka-Lani closes by handing off to the *Monday Morning Brew with Ellen Carter*.

shows.desc:
A wiring mishap killed the livestream, but the dance itself ran "war from start to end." That verdict comes from Reuben Vibes, who joined Teacha and DJ Smooth Devastation on Radio Andy to break down Sunday night's Sound Clash in Riverdale, Maryland. Vibes has been working the DMV clash scene since 2010 and co-promoted the battle between Cannabis Sounds out of Antigua and Franchise Music out of Virginia. He also announces his next event: a Dubplate Appreciation on October 23rd at the Park House on University Boulevard in Silver Spring, drawing sounds from New Jersey, Philadelphia, Atlanta, and the DMV.

The two-hour midnight set on WPFW moves through reggae selections with shoutouts to Guinea Pepper, Carlton Livingston, Barrington Levy, and Charlie Chaplin. The host closes with a personal dedication marking the anniversary of his father's passing.

shows.desc:
Papa Michigan calls Toots and the Maytals' "54-46 Was My Number" a song of "deep historical significance" — and a tribute to a friend. On Tony Carr's *This Is Reggae Music*, Michigan, one half of Jamaican duo Michigan and Smiley, walks through his new album *So Many Roads*, recorded in Los Angeles, Jamaica, and Tanzania. He explains why he opened it with five dancehall tracks aimed at younger listeners before moving into the roots style he began with "Rubber Dub Style" at Studio One in 1978.

The two-hour show also moves through tracks by Garnet Silk, JC Lodge, Jesse Royal, AJ Brown of Third World, and Queens-born singer Nestor, who remixed songs by Beres Hammond and Buju Banton. Carr gives several plays to G. Cole's new album *Black, Green and Reggae* and says he expects to interview Cole the following week.

Roberto dos Santos opened *Bilingüe* by announcing on air that he had just proposed to Miss Sybil and she had said yes. 

The two-hour set ran through samba and pagode — Gloria Estefan, Molejo, Só Para Contrariar — then into a Bahia block with Timbalada and Daniela Mercury. From there an Afrobeat-leaning stretch crossed to Cape Verde with Cesária Evora and on to Angola, before a closing funky set featuring Marcos Vale and Celso Fonseca. Throughout, dos Santos promoted Brazil's featured role at the upcoming Fiesta DC festival on Pennsylvania Avenue and Constitution Avenue.

shows.desc: Host Jim Byers devotes this birthday-eve edition of *Latin Flavor Classic Edition* to pianist Charlie Palmieri, revealing along the way that both Palmieri brothers studied under Margaret Bonds — the African American composer who kept studios at Carnegie Hall — and that it was Charlie, already a child prodigy, who brought his younger brother Eddie to her. Byers traces Palmieri's specific innovations: his Dubonnet Orchestra becoming the first commercially successful charanga in the U.S. around 1959, and his directing the Alegre All-Stars from 1961, whose extended descarga recordings — stretching to four, five, and six minutes at a time when radio formats demanded under four — helped set the stage for the modern salsa era. The two-hour program closes with unreleased 1953 RCA Victor studio sessions gifted to the show by the late producer Joe Conzo, including a version of "Este Es Mambo" with a passage never included on the released recording, alongside cuts featuring Palmieri alongside Tito Rodríguez, Tito Puente, Pupi Campo, and Pete Terriss.

shows.desc:
Brandon Woody came back from his first Europe tour with his quartet and promptly sold out a big band debut at Terrace Space in Baltimore. Miles Ahead host Miles Henderson Willis talks with the Baltimore trumpeter about what comes next: a trumpet-plus-string-quartet concert at UMBC and a trip to Tokyo University, where students will arrange his music for their own big band.

Willis also traces Norman Granz's Jazz at the Philharmonic from its July 1944 inaugural concert at the Philharmonic Auditorium in Los Angeles to the Library of Congress's 2010 selection of the series for the National Recording Registry. That history opens with a 1960 Stockholm live recording of Miles Davis's band — the same personnel who recorded Kind of Blue — on what turned out to be John Coltrane's final tour with Davis. Willis rounds out the hour with tracks by McCoy Tyner, Phineas Newborn Jr., Will Calhoun, Bernie Worrell, and a Gil Evans recording of Django, on which French horn player Bob Northern — later WPFW's own Brother Ah — performed in 1959.

shows.desc:
Willard Jenkins calls Cassandra Wilson's *Blue Skies* one of his desert island discs, and he plays tracks from it — with Mulgrew Miller, Lonnie Plaxico, and Terri Lyne Carrington — alongside *After the Beginning Again* and *New Moon Daughter* in tribute to the recently deceased singer. Randy Weston's centennial falls on April 6th. Jenkins marks it with "The African Cookbook" from *Spirits of Our Ancestors*, featuring Pharoah Sanders, Dewey Redmond, and Billy Harper on tenor saxophones, played in memory of Weston's late wife Fatou.

The second hour opens a new-release segment with 2026 DC Jazz Pre-Bands Competition winner Luther Allison performing Harold Mabern's "There But for the Grace Of." From there the hour moves through George Benson's *Inspiration: A Tribute to Nat King Cole*, Joe Lovano's Paramount Quartet, DMV-based flutist Alex Hamburger, and Brazilian-born pianist José Luiz Martins. Big Chief Donald Harrison closes the segment with *The Magic Touch* — nine versions of one tune across styles including nouveau swing and bossa nova.

shows.desc: Mumia Abu-Jamal told Dave Zirin "they're at war against history because their agenda demands ignorance" — and that line sits at the center of Zirin's new biography *The People's Historian: The Outsized Life of Howard Zinn*, which he discusses with host Miyuki Williams on *A Sunday Kind of Love*. Zirin, sports editor of *The Nation* and WPFW co-host, traces how Zinn's method of telling history from the bottom up shaped his own sportswriting. Ziah Ayubu of Proverbs Reggae Band — formed in D.C. after he relocated from New York in 2000 — previews the band's set at the WPFW Jazz and Justice Festival at Meridian Hill Malcolm X Park. Filmmakers Merawi Gerima and Jordan Strudwick discuss the festival's film program, including Gerima's 2020 gentrification drama *Residue*, shot near North Capitol and Florida Avenue largely with non-actor D.C. residents, alongside the new Sun Ra documentary *Do the Impossible*. Music across the hour draws from Donald Byrd's *A New Perspective*, a Brandon Woody track from *For the Love of It All*, Nina Simone, Ray Charles, and John Coltrane, with Williams marking Coltrane's 100th birthday and an all-day WPFW tribute airing the following Wednesday.

Red Mitchell was born September 20, 1927, in New York City, and Tom Cole's *G Strings* follows his career from West Coast sessions with Hampton Hawes all the way to Stockholm, where he settled in 1968. Chico Hamilton shares the birthday. The program draws on the *Sweet Smell of Success* soundtrack — actor Marty Milner's on-screen guitar fingerings were actually performed by John Pisano.

Sue Mingus gave one of her late husband's basses to Hungarian bassist Aladar Pégé after hearing him at the 1980 Jazz Yatra Festival in Bombay. The hour reaches toward the approaching Coltrane centennial through his 1958 session with Kenny Burrell, with violin from Billy Bang and the String Trio of New York, and bassist David Shevin's Afro-Semitic Experience. Miyuki Williams joins to discuss the upcoming WPFW Jazz and Justice Festival at Meridian Hill Malcolm X Park.

The September 28 edition of Charlie D's Morning Show, broadcasting from Washington DC, opens with soca, Afrobeats, and Caribbean-flavored dance tracks — among them a song credited to Sam Fantomar of Cameroon and a replay of Bobby James Ngwemi — before shifting into roots reggae with cuts from Owen Gray, Gregory Isaacs, and Jimmy Cliff's "The Harder They Come." Charlie Dee closes under the name "Siddy.

Kofi Kissi Dompere's *African Rhythms and Extensions* moves through a late-night set that travels from Ghana to Nigeria, the Republic of the Congo, Angola, Senegal, and South Africa, playing highlife, Makossa, Soukous, and related styles — with the host naming specific artists including Franco on guitar and bassist Johnny Deyan, whose track he dedicates to Abdullah Ibrahim. Dompere briefly steps outside the music to note that the Kente and Adinkra symbols carry epistemic structures behind each motif, and that "rhythm is a power of the nature." The program closes with a spoken-word piece tracing the passage of enslaved Africans across the sea and their descendants' lives in America — from working "from morn till night" without human rights to children "born with no last names" — framed around the phrase "American fruit with African roots."

shows.desc:
DJ Senpai pulled up to DreamCon and found a black SUV waiting with his name on it — the kind of moment that should feel like arrival. The 36-year-old DC-area DJ told Eddie Smith, Ron Brown, and DJ Machete on Decipher that it took a therapist to help him work through the imposter syndrome and self-sabotage that followed. The conversation kept returning to money: DJs hauling $1,500 to $2,500 or more in equipment, maintaining flash drives, laptops, and backup gear across 17 years of learning to read a room cannot work for $200 or $300.

Longtime station supporter Marvin called in to argue that a DJ also has to know the racial and social justice issues of the community they serve. Noodles closed by announcing the Jazz and Justice Festival — Sunday, September 27th, noon to seven, at Malcolm X Park at 16th and Euclid Street Northwest — marking the park's 90th anniversary.

Ozzy Stewart of Beyond the Call 24/7 describes a friend surrounded by family who still felt so unseen she no longer wanted to live — and how, at last year's mental health and abuse-awareness event, a man was the first to step forward publicly about his abuse. Stewart's nonprofit is staging a simultaneous event across New York, Canada, and Trinidad and Tobago. Osman Patterson, a Guyanese immigrant and author of *The New Immigrant's Handbook*, argues Caribbean arrivals sabotage their finances by fearing credit and sending money home for what he calls non-emergencies — concert tickets — while working extra shifts to cover rent. The episode marks the 43rd independence of St. Kitts and Nevis, notes Alexander Hamilton was born there, and mourns Haitian trumpeter André Desjardins, dead at 75. Caribbean news covers Trinidad's post-state-of-emergency joint police-army posts, a last-minute ICE reprieve for a Haitian pastor arrested while making DoorDash deliveries, and Jamaica Kingsmen's five-wicket win over Guyana Amazon Warriors to reach the CPL final. Vaughn Martin and Bryan Bernard host *Caribbeana* on WPFW.

Ray Charles hated being called "the Genius" — that nickname was invented by Atlantic Records' PR department, and the name he preferred was Brother Ray. To mark what would have been Charles's September 23rd birthday, Bill Wax devotes two hours of *Roots and Fruits* to paired recordings, each original played back-to-back with the Ray Charles version it shaped.

Charles Brown and the Three Blazers lead into Ray's early imitations, and gospel tracks by the Famous Ward Singers and the Original Five Blind Boys give way to the R&B rewrites that stirred church controversy. Percy Mayfield's demo of "Hit the Road Jack" is followed by Ray's live recording, then by Nina Simone's answer song "Come On Back, Jack.

From there Reynolds moves through new releases: Sacred Souls, Victor Axelrod, Erykah Badu, the Alchemist featuring Thundercat, Christian McBride, and Terri Lyne Carrington with Ravi Coltrane and Samara Joy. Jas. Funk opens this edition of *Oldies House Party* with a long tribute to Willie Bill Irey, a friend he describes as someone who "got so close to you, it's like blood, but thicker" — a man he shared half-smokes and half-pints with across the years. Between records, Funk calls out the Washington, D.C. landmarks and corners that shaped those memories: Griffith Stadium, Turkey Thicket, the 821 Club, the Viking Club, 22nd and Benning Road.

He's just back from a cruise where he caught Charlie Wilson performing onstage with his granddaughter, and that energy carries into the Saturday-morning playlist: the Chi-Lites, Curtis Mayfield's "Pusher Man," James Brown, Otis Redding, with back-to-back dedications going out to the seniors Funk pictures dancing upstairs. Broadcast September 19, 2026.

The grass looks greener on the other side," Arthur McCloud tells his listeners on WPFW, "because you haven't dealt with the weeds." The sermon is part of his "Amp Diaries" series, dedicated to a friend who shares his taste for "deep, deep, deep music," and it steers toward a pointed argument: invest in your existing relationship instead of chasing outside attractions.

The music set moves from the Isley Brothers' "Love Put Me on the Corner" and the Chi-Lites' "The Coldest Days of My Life" from *A Lonely Man* to Donny Hathaway performing "Yesterday" from *These Songs for You Live*. From there, an a cappella doo-wop block features Black Ivory and the Manhattans, among others, before McCloud closes by teasing the following program, Captain Fly and James Funk's Oldies House Party.

Kayvon Gordon describes the body as musical notation. Host Josh Myers reads that phrase aloud from Gordon's own prose before spinning four tracks from *Blood Memory*, a live album released just two days before this September 19, 2026 broadcast. The episode also mourns Cassandra Wilson, airing her composition "Cycle of Change" from the M-Base Collective's 1992 *Anatomy of a Groove*. Ron Carter appears alongside gospel singer Ricky Dillard, the two drawing on hymns from Carter's Detroit upbringing.

Myers moves through new releases from flutist Alaina Pinderhughes, trumpeter Adam O'Farrill's band Elephant, bassist Hrish Raghavan, and Wyclef Jean's jazz-oriented *Q Theory: Quantum Leap Volume 2*, then reaches back for older recordings: Eric Dolphy, Charles Mingus's "So Long, Eric," and Shirley Scott on Hammond B-3 organ, recorded live at the Left Bank in Baltimore in 1972.

shows.desc:
Garland Nixon's guest on *News Views* is Ray McGovern — a former CIA analyst who briefed President Reagan's five most senior national security advisers one-on-one from 1981 to 1985 — speaking on Russia, Ukraine, and the 2014 coup in Kyiv. McGovern walks through the February 4, 2014 intercepted phone call in which Assistant Secretary of State Victoria Nuland told U.S. Ambassador Jeffrey Pyatt that "Yats is the guy we're going to put in," then traces how Boris Johnson traveled to Kyiv to pressure Zelensky into walking away from a draft ceasefire agreement that Zelensky's own emissary had already initialed in Istanbul.

The conversation also takes in McGovern's account of Putin's personal history, including a brother who died in the siege of Leningrad and whose grave is an unmarked mass burial mound in St. Petersburg. Nixon, for his part, runs through U.S. midterm election dynamics and the pattern of losing parties claiming stolen elections.

Roughly $20 a year to keep an enslaved worker alive, $500–$600 in cotton produced: Jacqueline Luqman opens with that arithmetic and calls the result a profit rate of 2,400 to 2,900%. It is the foundation of a 45-minute case that racism is a feature, not a bug, of capitalism. She traces the same logic forward through Northern finance — Brown Brothers Harriman, JPMorgan Chase predecessors, Citibank's ties to Cuban slave plantations — then through sharecropping's scrip system and the federal redlining maps she says account for 60% of the current Black-white wealth gap.

Mass incarceration enters as a continuation of convict leasing, enabled by the 13th Amendment's exception clause, with prison labor contracts running to Victoria's Secret and Walmart. The episode closes on wage suppression through racialized worker competition, framed as groundwork for a future conversation about alternatives to capitalism that Luqman says her church congregation is actively studying.

Bobby Rox walked out of the Congressional Black Caucus Annual Legislative Conference — theme: "Rooted, Ready, and Rising" — and gave it a C-minus. The indictment he and Dr. George Frazier build comes down to what the panels never named: a 34% Black marriage rate driving family breakdown, set against a 94% marriage rate among East Indian households with a $104,000 median income, compared to $55,000 for Black households. A recorded excerpt from Dr. Claude Anderson supplies the framework Rox says was absent — economics, then politics, courts, media, and education, in that order.

Two voices from panel clips extend the argument in different directions. Mark Philpott of the California Black Freedom Fund describes how a planned five-year, $100-million spend-down became a permanent institution. Brittany Pinknett Cunningham of Children's Defense Fund addresses Black women feeding neighborhood children and keeping churches funded with no wages or benefits attached. Rox closes the summer with a music set that includes Childish Gambino's "Feels Like Summer.

shows.t: Resistance Radio with John and Regan
shows.desc:
John Kane argues that when Rockefeller pulled state troopers away from Interstate 81 in 1971 to handle Attica, that decision defused a separate standoff over the expansion of that highway onto Onondaga land, where Mohawk men had been called in for security. Kane also takes up John Boncore, a Mohawk man convicted in connection with the killing of a guard at Attica, who died in 2013 of blunt force trauma under what Kane calls suspicious circumstances.

NFL players have been fined more than $10,000 for wearing the name of Palestinian girl Hind Rajab on their eye black, and Ed Sheeran faced pressure serious enough that his own band members left his tour. Kane's documentary *The Long Hope* has been accepted into the Buffalo International Film Festival, with a noon screening on October 12th — Indigenous Peoples' Day — at the Buffalo Toronto Public Media facility.

Hitmen dressed as delivery workers shot Bolivian lawyer Nadia Belair at point-blank range — and when she survived, she gave video testimony from her hospital bed that cracked open a network few knew existed. Host Oscar Fernández brings journalists Kurt Hackbarth, co-host of the *Soberanía* podcast and Jacobin contributor, and Houston-based freelance writer Arturo Domínguez onto *Latino Media Collective* to trace what that network looks like.

At its center is Argentine propagandist Fernando Cerimero, charged with the attempted homicide of his pregnant ex-partner Belair, who held over $130 million in digital wallets and ran bot farms lined with walls of cell phones. Foreign Agents Registration Act documents place the Office of the President of El Salvador on the list of foreign principals, and Cerimero's connections run to Trump's 2016 digital director Brad Parscale, lobbyist Damian Merlero, and Iran-Contra veteran Otto Reich. He also co-founded La Derecha Diario with disgraced Spanish journalist Javier Negre, an outlet that ran targeted attacks on Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum.

Memphis Gold calls in to tell Ida Campbell about "From Africa to the Blues," an event pairing African music from Cameroon with low-down blues. He's also heading back into the studio — COVID stalled recordings still sitting on his hard drive — and he's thinking of calling the new material "Southern Sanctified Soul." His mother, who had a fifth-grade education, gave him three rules to live by, including that "a true friend is a gift that you give yourself" and that "you got 12 months in a year: 6 months to mind your own business and 6 months to leave everybody's business alone."

The gospel hour draws from the Greater Women's Choir, George Dean and the Gospel Four, and a live City Winery recording by We Are One. The blues runs from Lonnie Baker Brooks, Ronnie Baker Brooks, and Wayne Baker Brooks through Albert King.

shows.t: Community Watch & Comment - Friday / The Local Station Board Show (Last Frid
shows.desc:
Ron Pinchback and Chip Jones open this Friday edition of *Community Watch and Comment* with the question hanging over the 2026 midterms: are Republican and independent voters genuinely abandoning Trump, or, as caller JT put it, "faking the funk"? JT pointed to Marco Rubio, who once "called Trump everything but a child of God" before falling in line. Caller Tom added that Karl Rove has said he will vote Democratic for the first time in 30 years. Then Cheryl shifted the conversation to Cuba, describing blackouts of 20 to 22 hours a day caused by a near-total U.S. oil embargo and noting that Cuba has developed treatments for diabetic foot ulcers and a new Alzheimer's medication that American media largely ignores.

The hour also took in the measles caseload hitting a 30-year high, and two teenagers on their way to enlist in the Marines who were detained by ICE for six hours after witnessing an arrest. A caller rounded things out with word that the Hands Off the Arts Coalition planned a demonstration at the Kennedy Center that evening at 6:30.

Christopher Gioia's Long Island community of Franklin Square and Munson voted to demand a new federal investigation into 9/11, and on *On the Ground*, hosted by Esther Iverem, he explains why. Gioia points to the 441-day delay before the Bush administration formed the 9/11 Commission as one piece of the picture. Another is the sale of 200,000 tons of Ground Zero steel — to buyers including China's Shanghai Baosteel Group at $120 a ton — which he describes as destruction of evidence in what he calls a controlled demolition of all three World Trade Center towers.

Bill Manning, former editor-in-chief of *Fire Engineering*, held credentials at Ground Zero for three days after the attacks and published a January 2002 column titled "Selling Out the Investigation." Also speaking on the program, Manning recounts that forensic examination of the steel did not begin until at least November 2001, leaving engineers to guess where recovered pieces originated. By May 2002, when the Building Performance Assessment Team published its findings, Ground Zero had been, in Manning's word, "scrubbed." Both speakers appeared at the "Turning the Tide: 9/11 25 Years Later" conference, held September 10–13, 2026, in New York City.

Reverend Yearwood, president of the Hip-Hop Caucus and host of **#Climate Friday**, calls it a business plan that amounts to a death sentence: petrochemical plants packed along an 85-mile corridor between Baton Rouge and New Orleans, an area known as Cancer Alley, producing the highest cancer rates in the country and killing predominantly Black residents. Activists found a way to push back, using Louisiana burial-ground laws to block companies from building on former plantation sites.

That same calculus, Yearwood argues, shows up far beyond Louisiana — in data centers being sited in low-income Black neighborhoods from Memphis to Baltimore. He also walks through the Netflix documentary *Plastic Detox*, which followed families who removed plastics from their homes and, in several cases, reversed infertility, drawing a line between the chemical exposures in Cancer Alley and the quieter ones inside ordinary households.

shows.t: Morning Brew Jazz Edition feat. Union City Radio
shows.desc:
I may look like a nice Jewish girl from New Jersey, but inside I'm a 50-year-old heavyset Black man with a big thumb, like Wes Montgomery." That's Emily Remler, speaking to *People* magazine, and she is the subject of Candy Shannon's 6 o'clock birthday-artist segment on "Friday Morning Brew." Remler died of a heart attack on tour in Australia at 32, having moved from Berklee College of Music through New Orleans blues and jazz clubs to a 1985 *DownBeat* Guitarist of the Year award. Shannon plays tracks from *East to Wes* and from Remler's final recording, *This Is Me*.

From there, commentator Skylar Borton traces today's corporate political dominance to the August 1971 Powell Memo — eight pages drafted by Richmond attorney Lewis Powell for the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, mapping a long-game strategy to reshape lobbying, the judiciary, media, and education. That Lewis Powell had previously argued on behalf of Philip Morris that smoking did not cause cancer before Nixon appointed him to the Supreme Court.
