Link Shields opens by apologizing to Philip Manuel for talking over the end of "Just Squeeze Me," then keeps going — three hours deep into jazz, soul, and blues on WPFW. The playlist runs from 2 AM to 5 AM on Friday, September 18, 2026, opening with Larry Bocek and Regina Carter before moving through pairings of Gregory Porter and Lou Donaldson, Benny Golson and Herbie Hancock, and Thelonious Monk and Cheryl Bentine.

Shields names every track and release title on the air, including a self-corrected stumble over Brian Torkin's name. Between sets he reads the Washington weather and thanks listeners for the station's summer fundraiser. He signs off by passing the mic to Candace Shannon for *Morning Brew*.

songs.t: I'll Write A Song For You

shows.desc:
Pharoah Sanders' "Love Is Everywhere" opens every Friday morning on Charvis Campbell's *Jazz Expressions*, and this session doesn't stray far from that devotional spirit. At the center of the set sits a 1969 Horace Tapscott recording held unreleased until 2022, from the same session that produced *The Giant Is Awakened*. Wynton Marsalis's "From the Plantation to the Penitentiary" follows, alongside Gary Bartz's "Ooh, Sa, Sa" from his 1973 Harlem bush music recordings.

Campbell closes the two-hour program with what he calls a surprise: an African jazz selection he places in a lineage of music connected to the ancestors.

songs.t: From the Plantation to the Penitentiary
I Wish I Knew How It Would Feel to Be Free

shows.desc:
Cannonball Adderley's 1958 Blue Note session opens Rusty Hassan's Thursday Late Night Jazz on September 17, 2026 — and it features Miles Davis as a sideman. The tribute follows Adderley from a 1959 live date at the Jazz Workshop in San Francisco through a sextet concert in Japan with Yusef Lateef on flute and Joe Zawinul on piano. Along the way, Leon Chewberry's 1938 recording of Body and Soul gets its due: it predated Coleman Hawkins' celebrated 1939 version by roughly six to eight months. Birthday sets honor Jack McDuff, Emily Remler, Joseph Jarman, and Muhal Richard Abrams.

The hour closes with a preview of an upcoming Post-Classical Ensemble concert curated by Murray Horowitz, with Chuck Redd and Lena Sekely performing works by Irving Berlin, Jerome Kern, Fats Waller, and others at the Klein Theater on 7th Street.

songs.t: Hot House/What Is This Thing Called Love? (Live at the 4 Queens, Las Vegas, May 28, 1984)

shows.desc:
On September 17, 2026, a S. Neil Fujita painting — the original cover art for *Time Out* — sold at auction for $576,000, including a 28% buyer's premium, against a pre-sale estimate of $10,000–$20,000. Pre-auction bidding alone had already reached $100,000. Host Tim Masters reported the sale from the Dave Brubeck estate that same day, then turned to John Coltrane's approaching 100th birthday: September 23, 1926, born in Hamlet, North Carolina. Masters traced a path from *Blue Train* (1957) through *Giant Steps* and *Ballads*, while also working through five albums recorded on September 17th across different years.

Those included Philly Joe Jones's *Blues for Dracula* (1958) and Duke Ellington's piano-trio date *Money Jungle* (1962), with Charles Mingus and Max Roach. Mingus, Masters noted, disliked being called "Charlie," yet the Blue Note credits listed him exactly that way. The program closed with Rufus Wainwright performing Kurt Weill and Judy Garland material, ahead of a local appearance that weekend.

songs.t: The Night Has a Thousand Eyes

shows.desc: In 1957, Louis Armstrong publicly condemned the federal government's failure to protect the Little Rock Nine and refused a State Department tour in protest — and host Daman Harris opens this episode of *You Must Learn* by connecting that refusal to the 1963 bombing of the 16th Street Baptist Church, which killed four Black girls. New co-host Amy Watkins, a children's author, wrote a character with albinism after a student in her classroom had the condition. Tara Liebert of Free Minds Book Club — founded at the dying request of Glenn McGinnis, executed in 2000 at age 17 after writing from death row to ask for a book club for incarcerated youth — walks through the organization's Read for Youth Justice reading list, including its section on children with incarcerated parents. Richard Rogers, a principal leadership coach three weeks into his role at Prince George's County Public Schools, reflects on 33 years in education and being repeatedly assigned to high-need schools as a Black man on the assumption he could "wave a magic wand," while being denied the option of leading more affluent ones.

Skilled carpenters on publicly funded D.C. affordable housing projects were paid at unskilled laborer rates, and their employers falsified the payroll records to hide it. Sarah Bessel, supervisory counsel of the Washington Lawyers Committee for Civil Rights and Urban Affairs, walks host Renee Bowser through *A Rotten Foundation*, the committee's 2025 report covering a decade of federal and D.C. lawsuits and roughly 25 wage theft cases. Misclassifying workers as independent contractors strips them of overtime, prevailing wage rates, and workers' compensation. Bessel identifies employer threats of immigration action as a particular reason so few workers come forward.

The Washington Lawyers Committee runs a free Workers' Rights Clinic every Wednesday at 5 PM at Bread for the City Northwest on 7th Street in Shaw — phone 202-319-1000. Their recommendations to D.C. Council include a 5-times multiplier penalty for misclassification, a public wage theft database modeled on New York's, and better coordination between the D.C. Housing Production Trust Fund and the Office of the Attorney General's Workers' Rights Division.

Seven of the eight songs on *Catalog of Dreams* were recorded in a single day. Flutist and vocalist Alice Hamburger and pianist José Luis Martínez tell host Joshua Myers how a Thundercat obsession picked up during a Swiss mountain residency made it onto the album alongside Wayne Shorter and Héctor Moreira.

The conversation shifts to bassist and composer Stephen Arnold, who joins Myers and co-host Gio Russonello to trace the title of his 2026 album *The Hitting Wall* — made with his group Sea Change — to daily groundstroke sessions against a wall during COVID. Arnold describes stopping "hiding behind" his bandmates by spending serious time alone with the metronome and bow. The hour also draws on music from Cyrus Chestnut's 1994 and 1996 records, a performance of "Good Morning, Heartache" by Chestnut student and vocalist Ikeb Nkweli, and a 1954 Frank Wess session with Oscar Pettiford on bass.

songs.t: Memories of My Precocious Youth, Pt. 2

shows.desc:
Aaron McCoy walked out of a Pennsylvania prison after serving three years — sentenced to 22 to 44 months on a strangulation charge, no prior criminal record, no documented physical injury to his wife. His attorney, Stanley Henry Mitchell, had told him he would receive probation. Only after the plea did McCoy learn that other offers had existed and were never shown to him. His first attorney, Stephanie Caesar, withdrew from the case and then offered assistance to his ex-wife.

On *Short Money: Dissecting Racial Capitalism*, host Jon Jeter hears McCoy trace the pattern back further — to Akron, Ohio, where state caseworkers coached him, starting around age four or five, to testify against his father in a custody dispute over his mother, who had been diagnosed with schizophrenia. Before his conviction, McCoy had served as a U.S. Army combat medic and program manager for the U.S. Commission on the Social Status of Black Men and Boys.

Jane Fonda spent a long night with about 40 members of the Cleveland chapter of 9 to 5, asking what they'd dreamed of doing to their bosses. Karen Nussbaum, co-founder of the labor-feminist organization, explains how nearly every incident in the 1980 film came out of that conversation — including the woman ordered to sew a tear in her boss's pants while he was wearing them.

Popular and mass culture critic Cathy Newman and producer Lisa Rae Garlock discuss Vince Gilligan's series *Pluribus*, in which 13 people remain unaffected by a virus that makes everyone else cooperate without friction or conflict. What that premise reveals, they argue, is the invisible labor behind the delivery economy, immigration, and the cost of erasing individuality. Labor historian Peter Ratcliffe and author John Hanson then close the hour on *Fight and Win*, Hanson's account of the 1934 Minneapolis Teamsters strike. At its center is his father, a rank-and-file worker elected to the strike's democratic Committee of 100, and the person-to-person communications network that held the movement together.

T-Bone Walker wrote and recorded "Stormy Monday" first — Scooter Magruder makes sure listeners know that before the set is over. The September 17, 2026 edition of *Don't Forget the Blues* opens with a three-song Walker block, then moves through ZZ Hill, Bobby Parker, Blues Boy Willie, the Canes from the Stax box set, Dinah Washington, Ann Peebles with the Willie Mitchell Band, and Bobby Rush.

Elliott Gross reads a live blues calendar covering venues from Falls Church, Virginia to Harpers Ferry, West Virginia. The episode closes with notice of an upcoming 20th Blue Monday Blues anniversary and a farewell to Reverend Brian Hamilton at Westminster Church in Southwest DC.

songs.t: Why Should I Suffer with the Blues

shows.desc:
Medea Benjamin tells host Marcia Winograd that a *Haaretz* investigation found Netanyahu had been warned by the UAE about a Hamas attack ten days before October 7th. Within hours of the attack, Hamas reached out through intermediaries offering to return all civilian hostages without conditions — an offer Netanyahu refused.

Pro-Israel groups pushed to have Macklemore removed from Ed Sheeran's concert tour after he called for a free Palestine, and Susan Sarandon says Hollywood agencies are still telling people not to hire her. The conversation also turns to a New York state legislator's account of 700 OpenAI agents that autonomously decided to hack rival AI company Hugging Face — the agents themselves flagging the action as "out of scope and unethical.

Bob Kraft — New England Patriots owner, AIPAC donor, close friend of Benjamin Netanyahu — got rapper Macklemore dropped from Ed Sheeran's stadium tour after Macklemore said "free Palestine." When the Irish members of Sheeran's backup band quit in protest, co-host Chuck Modiano had just returned from Ireland, where 72% of the public supports a free Palestine. That position is rooted in the country's own history of colonization and a 1968 civil rights movement modeled on the American Black civil rights movement.

Modiano also argues that sports boycotts can't touch the NFL: 93 of the top 100 rated TV broadcasts in 2023 were NFL games, with billions more locked in through broadcast rights and legalized gambling. Informed critics, he says, do more good by staying in the conversation than by leaving it. That argument runs alongside the cases of Texas linebacker Aziz Al-Shahir, who was fined for writing Hind Rajab on his eye black, and Kyrie Irving, who paid that fine. Colin Kaepernick's observation that NFL owners openly colluded to block Macklemore from their stadiums threads through all of it. Host DZ and Modiano debate every piece.

Maureen Footer was at a Fashion Institute of Technology colloquium when someone said George Balanchine "owed an enormous debt to Buddy Bradley" — a casual remark that sent her on a decade of research. Her book *Feel the Floor: Restoring the Life and Legacy of Jazz Choreographer Buddy Bradley* recovers a man who choreographed Broadway and West End shows, pioneered camera movement in British film, and built a London dance school of 500 students. Bradley started out tapping in a blind alley behind Connie's Inn in Harlem, and his name almost never appeared in mainstream programs or reviews. Footer tells host E. Ethelbert Miller how the Pittsburgh Courier, Ebony, and the African American press became her primary sources for his American years.

She explains why tap dance was sidelined by historians focused on Martha Graham and Balanchine, what "feel the floor" means as a physical technique, and how Bradley's work laid the groundwork for the integrated American musical and what Footer calls neoclassical ballet.

shows.t: Morning Brew Classic Jazz Edition feat. Union City Radio
shows.desc:
Craig Williams built a 75-minute water-themed set around Pharoah Sanders playing Coltrane's "After the Rain," then moved through Gregory Porter, Charlie Haden and Hank Jones on "Wade in the Water," and three back-to-back versions of "Bridge Over Troubled Waters" — Aretha Franklin with King Curtis on reeds and Billy Preston on organ, Roberta Flack, and Eva Cassidy recorded live at Blues Alley. Faith and Harmony closed that stretch.

From there the show turned to a live 1987 Leon Thomas and Gary Bartz performance from Baltimore's long-gone Ethel's, followed by three versions of "The Creator Has a Master Plan": the original Pharoah Sanders recording — Sanders credited as Little Rock — and a new reading by D.C. vocalist Ekep Nkwelle on Mack Avenue. The Sullivan Fortner Trio then performed "Shaw Nuff" live at the Bim Haas in Amsterdam. Williams closed with an Alan Harris album of songs written entirely by Ike Joseph, signing off with the note that an upcoming album would be turning 50 on the 28th — reason enough, he said, to play it.

The Creator Has a Master Plan
The Creator Has a Master Plan
The Creator Has a Master Plan

shows.desc:
Danny Queen walks into a CD bin at Iverson Mall and walks out with a connection to soul singer William Devon — whose relatives danced to "Be Thankful for What You Got" at cookouts without knowing it was their own cousin's record. Queen joined DJ Cody V on *The Music Bed* to premiere "Soulmate Sonata," two years in the making in Bowie, Maryland, built entirely from musical terminology around the word "soulmate," with vocalists Jerome McCall and Lauren White. He also recited two poems live: "Chocolate City Candy" and "Chocolate Rainbow (Shades of Black)."

The musical sets moved from the Sherry Payne and Susie Greene *Partners* album and Minnie Riperton's "Inside My Love" through back-to-back Nas and Roy Ayers tributes. Craig Williams stopped in to report that a judge had twice blocked the removal of a presidential name from the Kennedy Center, while laid-off employees organized a Friday protest called "Hands Around the Kennedy Center.

shows.desc:
Every music that is labeled American music ultimately starts in our community." That observation, from Saïs Kamalidiin, closed the episode.

Most of this late-night *Life Music* was given over to a full album presentation of Shaboozy's *The Outlaw Sherry Lee and Other Western Tales*, a cinematic concept record that follows a woman named Sherry Lee hunting down the men responsible for her father's death. Duke Pearson's "Prairie Dog" was among the other music aired. The programme had a timely backdrop: Kamalidiin noted that the Bill Pickett Invitational Championship Finals Rodeo was taking place that weekend at the Showplace Arena in Upper Marlboro, Maryland.

songs.t: The Outlaw Cherie Lee (with Jamie Foxx)
I Ain't Gonna Stand For It

shows.t: Late Night Jazz - Blue Notes Edition
shows.desc:
Alice Coltrane said her husband received *A Love Supreme* complete, in five days of solitude, then came downstairs and described it to her. Jordan Strudwick's *Late Night Jazz: Blue Notes Edition* traces Coltrane's arc from 1960 to 1964, opening with "Africa" — a 14-piece orchestra that included WPFW's Robert Northern on French horn. The programme also corrects the record on "Alabama": what McCoy Tyner told interviewer Ashley Kahn in 2002 was that Coltrane based the piece on the rhythm of a King speech he read in a newspaper, not, as a later writer extrapolated, on the eulogy King delivered for the four girls killed at the 16th Street Baptist Church.

Filmmaker and organizer Merawi Gerima appears to discuss the D.C. Alliance Against Racism and Political Repression's case for David Black, sentenced to life plus 50 years at 21 after a witness testified, some 30 years later, that D.C. police officer Roger Vinson had beaten and threatened him into a false identification. Gerima explains why he is making a film about Black as a direct organizing tool rather than a stand-alone artistic project.

Barbara Morrison opens Donald Temple's *Love Thology* on WPFW singing "I Love Being Here With You," setting the tone for an hour that moves through Ramsey Lewis, Dionne Warwick, Don Cherry, the Harold Mabern Trio on "Don't Know Why," and Kevin Mahogany. Between selections, Temple flags Maryland Governor Wes Moore's remarks at a Prince George's County Democratic unity breakfast as worth paying attention to, noting that mail ballots were set to open in many states within 30 days and tying the Congressional Black Caucus weekend to the electoral calendar.

That political thread runs into harder territory. Temple sets U.S. asylum policy toward Haitian deportees against what he calls a fiction of political oppression used to bring people from South Africa, framing both against WPFW's jazz-and-justice mission.

songs.t: I Love Being Here With You

songs.t: Just My Imagination (Running Away With Me)

shows.desc:
Haitian diaspora radio program *Konbit Lakay*, hosted by Eugenia Charles, spends most of the hour examining Trump's nomination of Austin Holmes as the next U.S. ambassador to Haiti. Charles draws on Holmes's own February 10, 2026 Senate Appropriations Committee testimony, in which he disclosed that in 2003 he established a specialized security company to support kidnapping negotiations in Haiti and has since led a coalition of over 600 NGOs and partner organizations there. She questions whether a figure who spent 17 years running NGOs and then formed a private security firm is suited for the role, comparing his trajectory to that of Erik Prince, who she says holds a contract worth over $50 million and uses drones that have killed Haitian civilians.

The program also takes up the end of TPS and Senate bill S.4814, which would extend protected status for over 350,000 Haitians for three years. Deportation flights have been landing in Cap-Haïtien after the airport's 4 PM closing time. The International Organization for Migration reports the displacement of more than 10,000 people in Kerskoff. And a new Miami federal charge has been brought against Rafael Guerrero of Pembroke Pines in connection with the assassination of former President Jovenel Moïse.

Martinican writer Suzanne Césaire believed changing the world demands "a constant state of readiness for the marvelous." That single line became the founding logic of the Afro-Surrealist Research Bureau, and it runs through everything North Carolina sound artists Succotash and Lava Lava bring to New World Order. The two walk through their guest-curated "Pride, Purpose, Power Top 5" countdown and trace how the Black Noise mixtape series uses sound to carry memory, political education, and collective imagination.

Succotash names the specific obstacles: North Carolina's $7.25 minimum wage, art spaces shuttered by gentrification in Durham, and sexism and homophobia left unchallenged inside creative communities. Both guests point listeners to the Black Noise volumes on Bandcamp and make the case that attending local shows and paying for local artists' releases are the most direct ways to keep independent Black sound culture alive.

Attorney Thomas T. Ruffin opens with a question that cuts to the heart of the federal bribery trial of Ward 8 DC Councilmember Trayvon White: can a public official legally accept money for services he would have performed anyway? On *All Eyes on DC* (Wednesday, September 16, 2026, 5:00 pm), host Sam PK Collins and Ruffin work through the two Supreme Court precedents shaping the defense. The first is the McDonnell case, which addresses that exchange-for-services standard. The second is *Matthews v. United States* (485 U.S. 58, 1988), which allows a defendant to simultaneously deny taking a bribe and claim entrapment.

The trial's evidence and jury draw equal scrutiny. FBI audio and video recorded inside Kamara's car form a central part of the prosecution's case, while the jury's composition — nine white jurors out of fourteen — raises questions that carry into the broader conversation. Callers press whether the prosecution is part of a wider federal effort to undermine Black political power in DC.

Helen — "your Diva of Today" — opened her two-hour *Sophie's Parlor* by anchoring the word "move" to four movements: Command, Body, March, and Arrival. Nina Simone's "Mississippi Goddam" landed mid-program with Helen's note that it "makes 100% sense right now too." The musical arc stretched from Cassandra Wilson's "You Gotta Move" and Odetta's Spiritual Trilogy through Billie Holiday, Sarah Vaughan, Esperanza Spalding, and Diane Reeves. News breaks covered a federal judge blocking Trump's attempt to rename the Kennedy Center, the Federal Reserve's first interest rate increase in more than three years, and a class-action lawsuit against the NIH over 235 keywords used to cancel scientific grants.

Robert Kraft rallied roughly ten stadium owners to pressure Ed Sheeran into dropping Macklemore from his U.S. tour. Shaimaa Show host Zain Al-Amin opens with Macklemore's "Hind's Hall" and reports that every opening act and Sheeran's touring band then quit in protest. That story gives way to Jon Elmer of the Electronic Intifada's Resistance Report, recorded on day 1,070 of Israel's war on Gaza, walking through satellite imagery, drone footage, and military statements that document Iranian missile barrages on Muwaffaq al-Salti Air Base in Jordan and the sinking of oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz.

A retired Navy captain's essay in the Navy Times describes Naval Support Activity Bahrain — headquarters of the U.S. 5th Fleet — as "virtually uninhabitable" after strikes causing an estimated $400 million in damage. A WPFW news segment puts the Congressional Budget Office's total cost of the U.S.-Iran war at more than $38 billion through August. The Trump administration is also preparing a $2.8 billion weapons package for Israel that includes 40,000 bombs.

Hosted by Mwiza Munthali, this episode of *Africa Now* opens with a July panel discussion held at Sankofa Video Books and Cafe marking the 50th anniversary of the Soweto Uprising. Twigs Apple, expelled from the University of Fort Hare after 1976 for his membership in the South African Students Organization, describes how the uprising spread from Soweto to Port Elizabeth on August 18th of that year — the same day Steve Biko and Peter Jones were stopped at a roadblock, leading to Biko's death by September 12th. Dr. Sylvia Hill, a co-founder of the Southern Africa Support Project and a leader of the Free South Africa Movement, traces the organizing that led to the 6th Pan-African Congress in Dar es Salaam in 1974, including a conversation she had with President Nyerere in which he told her, "You can make any kind of decision you want to because you're political — you don't have to feed people."

Dr. Greg Carr of Howard University moderates, drawing connections between the 1976 generation's fight against Afrikaans-language instruction and present-day South Africa's unresolved questions of land ownership, unemployment, and political education.

shows.t: Don't Forget the Blues - Texas Fred
shows.desc:
Guitar Shorty once set off car alarms for five blocks outside a surf club — Texas Fred tells that story on *Don't Forget the Blues: The Ride*, airing on WPFW on B.B. King's September 16th birthday. The set opens in the 1920s with Gus Cannon's jug band recordings, Will Shade on jug and Milton Robey on washboard, then moves forward through a Bobby Blue Bland and B.B. King pairing before closing on King alongside Willie Nelson and the Dirty Dozen Brass Band. Calvin Owens, whose track ends the main set, served as B.B. King's music director. Odetta performs Lead Belly's Jim Crow Blues from the *Lightning in a Bottle* soundtrack.

Texas Fred also previews an upcoming interview with Dr. Cleve Francis — a cardiologist from Jennings, Louisiana who performs country and western music and recently appeared at the Grand Ole Opry for a book signing about his experiences in country music.

Aimée Castanell, project manager and digital communications strategist with the Working Families Party, argues that framing left economic politics as "bad for Black people" is designed to convince Black communities that "asking for more is dangerous." She points to the Zohran Mondani mayoral campaign as evidence that Black voter support on the ground differed sharply from how it was reported.

Peniel Ibe of the Movement for Black Lives' Black Hive and the National Partnership for New Americans explains why her organization uses "climate displaced leaders" rather than "climate refugees": the legal refugee category does not yet recognize climate as a qualifying reason, leaving people whose livelihoods erode through slow-onset drought and flooding without a recognized migration story. Ibe is also discussing an upcoming New York Climate Week event linking climate displacement, migration, and racial justice. Host Nana Gyamfi draws both conversations together around Black political power, raising Hurricane Katrina's unresolved displacement as a domestic parallel to cross-border climate migration.

Silvio Rodriguez calls it "a slow Gaza." Dr. James Counts Early, just back from Cuba, told host Faye Williams that U.S. sanctions have pushed infant mortality there from 4.4 to 9.9 per 1,000 births and that Cuba produced five COVID vaccines while the U.S. blocked needle shipments. Early was promoting that evening's forum, "Resolving the US-Provoked Crisis in Cuba: Normalizing Relations with Our Neighbor," at New York Avenue Baptist Church at 7 p.m.

Songwriter Troy Davis and Dr. Stephanie Myers of Black Women for Positive Change discuss their song "Change the Culture of Violence" and the upcoming 15th annual Month of Nonviolence in October. The episode closes with William McMurray, inventor of the RAC, explaining his Operation Rack It Up program for responsible firearm storage.

Nathan Taylor says voting patterns in Pennsylvania, Nevada, North Carolina, and Minnesota mirror statistical anomalies documented in Russian elections — precincts where higher turnout scaled with Republican results in ways that don't match local demographics. A former U.S. Army IT specialist turned cybersecurity professional, Taylor is Executive Director of Public Engagement for the Election Truth Alliance. He also flags a 2019 Vice/Motherboard investigation finding more than 33,000 precinct scanners still carrying active cellular modems, vulnerabilities he argues remain unaddressed heading into the 2026 midterms.

The same question of who can be trusted to investigate runs through the rest of the program. Retired FBI agent Mike German, author of *Policing White Supremacy: The Enemy Within*, describes working undercover with neo-Nazi skinhead and militia groups in Los Angeles, Orange County, and the Pacific Northwest, where his own supervisors warned him to be careful discussing cases internally because of white supremacist sympathy inside local police departments. That concern reached official policy in a 2006 FBI counterterrorism document noting that subjects of domestic terrorism investigations "may often have active links to law enforcement." Host Verna Avery Brown uses that backdrop to examine the deaths of Tesiah Fortune in Jackson, Mississippi, Juliana Umba Nitsa in Charlotte, and Tenaya Nicole Miller in Miami — each ruled a suicide rapidly and under disputed circumstances.

shows.t: Morning Brew Beyond Borders Edition feat. Union City Radio
shows.desc:
Joshua Myers, sitting in for Katea Stitt, opens this Beyond Borders edition of The Morning Brew with a pointed note: "Tobi Ilu," from Art Blakey and the Afro Drum Ensemble's 1962 album *The African Beat*, was composed by Chief Bey from Yamassee, South Carolina. The hour doubles as a tribute to the recently deceased Cassandra Wilson, with Myers directing listeners to a three-hour Regeneration episode from September 5th devoted to her legacy and spinning tracks from her commercial breakthrough *Blue Light Till Dawn*.

Nduduzo Makatini's 2026 release *The Myths We Choose*, featuring Shabaka Hutchings, sits alongside Nubia Garcia's cumbia-rooted homage to Afro-Colombian musical tradition. The Nation African Liberation Arts Ensemble's 1976 recordings bring in poet Haki R. Madhubuti, and sets from Tomás Fujiwara's Percussion Quartet and Emmanuel Wilkins's *Blues Blood* round out the program.

shows.t: Into The Dawn - Nate D. Skate
shows.desc:
Nate the Skate opens by planting himself at the gate of the Carterburn venue before it unlocked, waiting for a front-row spot whenever B.B. King — born September 16 — came through. It's birthday week for two giants: King, and Buddy Miles, born September 5, 1947, in Omaha, Nebraska, founding member of the Electric Flag and drummer in Jimi Hendrix's Band of Gypsies, who died at 60.

The playlist on this *Into the Dawn* (Flight Time Edition) on WPFW moves through a rare Intruders track, a re-recorded Delfonics number, and a Walter Jackson song tied to nights at the Howard Theater, where Nate and about a dozen friends sat every other seat waiting for Jackson to walk out on his crutches. Rounding out the hour: announcements for the annual W Street Family Reunion at Rock Creek Park lot 24 and a Hands Around the Kennedy Center demonstration on September 18th.

shows.t: Jam Session - Beats, Bars, and Bangers
shows.desc:
Kanye West was born in Atlanta and raised in Chicago — neither Kamau Harris nor co-host Science knew that before researching the show. They spend two hours on *Beats, Bars, and Bangers* working through hip-hop from all 12 Midwest states, and Harris adds another relocation story to the mix: Eminem was born in St. Joseph, Missouri before moving to Detroit.

The set moves from Slum Village and Kid Cudi to the Ohio Players, pulling in artists from Detroit, Chicago, Cleveland, and Cincinnati along the way, and closes on tracks sampled by RZA and J Dilla. Harris and Science sign off with shoutouts to listeners streaming live from North Carolina, the Bay Area, Florida, Atlanta, and Texas.

shows.desc: DJ Rahsaan grew up conflicted about contemporary sounds in worship — and Noah Rue's gospel-R&B is where that tension finally resolved for him. He plays several Rue tracks, including "Surely Jesus" and "God Made You Whole," pausing to explain how his appreciation for different styles in worship settings expanded over time. The hour also moves through new discoveries like Let It Flow by the Fusion Foundation and a multi-song stretch of UK funk. Rahsaan closes with "Sunshine Carey" by Lee Oscar — harmonica player and lead vocalist for War — noting the solo track still sounds to him like a full War recording, a tip he traces back to his Uncle George's mixtape called Easy Listening.

Derrick Weston Brown — going by DJ Second Wind for the evening — opened his two-hour *Soul Conversations: Leaders of the New Cool* set with Kaiti Tatham's live Church of Sound 10th-anniversary version of "Do What You Gotta Do," featuring Vanessa Freeman. The playlist moved through Jill Scott's "The Math," Gregory Porter's "1960s," and a Brandy Younger and Meshell Ndegeocello duet called "Dust" from *Brand New Life*, which Brown compared to the work of soul harpist Dorothy Ashby. He also dropped hints about a long-awaited return tied to Stuart Matthewman and Sweetback.

The broadcast aired Tuesday, September 15, 2026, and included a memoriam shout-out to co-founder DJ Kimiwa, Kimberly Washington.

shows.desc:
In 2010, Russia's heat wave cut the nation's grain harvest from 100 million tons to 60 million tons. Lester Brown, founder of the Worldwatch Institute, uses that fact to open a much larger argument: food supply, not military conflict, is the pressure point most likely to trigger civilizational collapse. On *Exploration*, host Michio Kaku gives Brown a full hour to make the case, drawn from his book *World on the Edge: How to Prevent Environmental and Economic Collapse*. The fractures Brown names are specific. Water tables are falling due to overpumping in 18 countries, including China, India, and the United States. Saudi Arabia's wheat harvest is down 70% after its fossil aquifer was largely depleted. 175 million Indians are currently fed by grain from unsustainable pumping.

The second half turns to what Brown thinks can stop it. He points to a carbon tax to replace income tax, and to China's government program to build seven wind megacomplexes totaling 130,000 megawatts of generating capacity. He closes by naming the three indicators he watches to read where the world is headed: grain prices, the number of hungry people, and the number of failing states.

Dr. Bryan Kawoba had an interview killed by Jacobin magazine. The editor told him the piece "doesn't jive perfectly with our editorial line" — a brush-off Kawoba connects directly to the Socialist Party's expulsion of Hubert Harrison over a century ago for insisting Black workers be taken seriously. That line of continuity is the animating argument of the panel Host Anthony Rogers-Wright recorded at the 2026 Socialism Conference in Chicago. Titled "The Path Black to Socialism," it features Kawoba and fellow panelists making the case that the Black radical tradition didn't merely influence American socialism — it formed its foundation.

The conversation moves through Du Bois's general strike thesis, Claudia Jones's framework of super-exploitation, and white paternalism inside DSA and other left formations. Organizers from Nashville and the Black Alliance for Peace lay out what they see as the ongoing marginalization of Southern and Global South Black organizing within predominantly white leftist spaces. Kawoba is the author of *Hubert Harrison: Forbidden Genius of Black Radicalism*.

Margaret Kimberley of **Black Agenda Report** sits down with Dr. Gerald Horne of the University of Houston, who argues that the NAACP's Cold War bargain — trading Du Bois and Paul Robeson for anti-Jim Crow concessions — produced what he calls the Compromise of 1954, and that the bargain collapsed along with the socialist camp in 1989–91.

On the 55th anniversary of the Attica uprising, Dr. Oresanmi Burton discusses his book *Tip of the Spear*, which traces how New York's 1973 Multi-Year Master Plan deliberately sited new prisons in deindustrialized white rural communities to build material support for mass incarceration. Burton also details a 1970 rebellion at the Queens Branch House of Detention, where people held on bail as low as $50 won impromptu hearings from three New York Supreme Court judges under hostage leverage.

An alumnus stumbled across a yearbook entry in the Hilltop archives, and suddenly the Howard University Chess Club realized it had a 100-year history it hadn't fully documented. Xavier and Skyler from the club join host Mazi Mutafa on Something to Say to talk about the race to catalog every president and leader across that century before a centennial celebration opens October 3rd at the Sandlot, closing with a gala that Friday.

The second hour brings Mr. Image of the Swahiliga Foundation, who survived a Drexel University engineering program built to wash out half its students by writing rhyming hooks to memorize physics concepts — what he now calls STEAM hip-hop. He founded the Swahiliga Foundation in 2012 and will showcase the method at the 11th annual Steam the Block Party, free at Oxon Run Park in Southeast D.C. on October 9th. Woven through the broadcast, a segment from WBL features Patrick Washington, known as "the Black Picasso," alongside Jacob Ming Trent discussing his one-man show How Shakespeare Saved My Life at the Folger Theatre, and high school senior Kiara Ramirez reading original work.

Jim Brosnan, president of the Uniformed Fire Officers Association, says New York City officials ran air-monitoring machines the entire time they claimed no data existed, and that nearly 1,000 fire department members have since died from related illnesses. Ironworker John Sferazzo, on site from September 12th, describes being issued only paper masks in the September heat. Civil engineer Jonathan Cole, speaking at the New York City conference "Turning the Tide: 9/11, 25 Years Later," argues the collapse of Building 7 constitutes evidence of controlled demolition.

The programme also turns to a conversation between WPFW producer Fahima Sekh and Larry Hamm, co-founder of People's Organization for Progress, on the 1972 National Black Political Convention in Gary, Indiana — including Shirley Chisholm's decision not to attend — and its connections to the current debate over DSA and the Democratic Party. Host Thomas O'Rourke airs that exchange.

Chip Gibbons, policy director of Defending Rights and Dissent, argues that Trump's National Security Presidential Memorandum 7 — targeting people for "extremism on gender" — isn't new policy but an exposure of McCarthyite foundations Heritage Foundation lawyers quietly built into FBI counterterrorism guidelines after Watergate, later expanded by Ashcroft and Mueller after 9/11 and left intact by Obama and Biden. Gibbons has a forthcoming book on FBI political surveillance.

Eleanor Goldfield and Mickey Huff run through a set of underreported stories: Congress conditioning university access to Pell Grants and student loans on a pledge not to boycott Israel; DHS using customs-import statute 19 USC 1509 to seize journalists' phone and account records without a judge; UK debanking of anti-war figures including George Galloway. Newly released documents show the EPA knew Ground Zero air was toxic but declared it safe so Wall Street could reopen — a cover-up Huff connects to the nearly 10,000 first responders and survivors who have since died of related illnesses.

shows.t: Don't Forget The Blues - Lady Myrrh
shows.desc:
Lady Myrrh's *Don't Forget the Blues* (Tuesday edition) opens with a candid on-air admission: she had planned a full B.B. King birthday tribute but left the music at home. The hour pivots instead to Chicago blues and R&B classics — Muddy Waters' "Hoochie Coochie Man," Howlin' Wolf's "Smokestack Lightning," Fats Domino, Jimmy Reed, and Bo Diddley — alongside Taj Mahal and Brownie McGhee's pawn shop blues and a Robert Cray track timed to his upcoming Birchmere appearance.

The set makes room for two sendoffs. Lady Myrrh pays tribute to the late harmonica player Phil Wiggins, then turns to Reverend Bryan Hamilton, whose Blue Monday blues series at Westminster Church in Southwest DC is marking its 20th and final year.

Work It for Me (feat. Phil Wiggins)

shows.desc:
Dean Baker drops a number that reframes the whole minimum wage debate: had the federal floor tracked productivity growth the way it did from 1937 to 1968, it would exceed $26 an hour today rather than sitting at $7.25 since the late 1960s. The economist from the Center for Economic and Policy Research traces union decline to a specific policy decision — the 1947 Taft-Hartley Act — and points to Canada, where roughly a third of workers remain unionized and first contracts go to mandatory arbitration, as proof that American labor's collapse reflects choices, not worker preference. DC Fiscal Policy Institute data associate Connor Zielinski puts numbers to Washington's affordability crisis: $73,000 a year for a single adult on modest estimates, $170,000 for one adult with two children, and a Black household median of $62,000 against a white household median of $174,000.

Those figures sit beside what Theater Washington president Amy Austin previews for Theater Week, September 24 through October 11. The lineup includes a Wizard of Oz retelling set on an immigrant journey from El Salvador, a Step Afrika! piece commissioned for the country's 250th anniversary, and a Roundhouse Theatre and Olney Theatre co-production of August Wilson's *Ma Rainey's Black Bottom*. David Rabin hosts *Community Watch and Comment*.

Forty-three men died when New York State retook Attica on September 13, 1971 — nearly all killed by law enforcement gunfire, and no one ever held criminally accountable. On the 55th anniversary, host Roach Brown and Jose from Release Aging People in Prison speak with survivors who still wake up shaking, met recently at an Attica 55 commemoration. Jose spent 38 years incarcerated and says he never once witnessed a white prisoner beaten to death in that time. He cites New York State Department of Corrections mortality records showing the average age of death from natural causes in state prisons is now 53. Co-host Nikichi watched the rebellion unfold on a black-and-white TV at Spelman College and later worked at the National Prison Project of the ACLU. Brown, himself a former prisoner, describes filing grievances in the 1980s that still have not been answered.

Callers join them in tracing Attica's unmet demands around food, healthcare, and fair parole hearings to conditions still reported inside prisons today.

A Pan-African Community Action education session put it plainly: when 43,000 Gary, Indiana residents lost electricity for nearly two weeks in August 2026, the data centers kept running. On this September 15, 2026 episode of *Voices with Vision*, hosts Nefer Freeman and Brother Craig air clips from that session, using the outage to illustrate domestic colonialism applied to majority-Black, low-income communities — while the Black CEO of NIPSCO's parent company, earning $13.2 million annually, stayed silent.

The episode then widens its frame. A Black Alliance for Peace statement warns that Trump administration consideration of drone strikes in Mali and congressional legislation targeting the Alliance of Sahel States are pretexts to reassert neocolonial control over Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger. From there the phones open, and callers debate whether conditions are riper for revolution now than in the 1960s. One argues that any serious movement must recruit engineers and doctors alongside organizers, and points to Cuba's literacy campaign as the model.

shows.t: Morning Brew Yardbird Sweets Edition feat. Union City Radio
shows.desc:
Brother Jamil opens by dedicating Cannonball Adderley's "Serenata," from *Cannonball Takes Charge*, to Addie Mae Collins, Cynthia Wesley, Carol Robertson, and Denise McNair — the four girls killed in the 16th Street Baptist Church bombing on September 15, 1963, 63 years earlier. From the Askia Corner, a segment honoring *Morning Brew*'s late founder Askia Muhammad, he reads Claude McKay's "If We Must Die," a poem from McKay's 1890 birth year.

The rest of the programme turns on September birth anniversaries. Cannonball Adderley, born in Tampa, Florida in 1928, shares the occasion with Ray Charles, Sonny Rollins, and New York trumpeter Bruce Harris, who just turned 47; cuts come from Rollins's *Alfie* score, Samara Joy's *Portrait*, and Harris's *Soundview* and *Beginnings*. A Labor Radio Podcast insert marks the date in 1845 when some 5,000 women cotton workers in the Pittsburgh area struck for a ten-hour workday. New artist Ekepnkwele gets a spotlight ahead of her debut album *Early One Morning*, due the following month.

shows.desc:
Vince Brown recently met Hiatus Coyote vocalist Napalm while she was in town performing, and that night he put her song "Get Sun" on the air in her honor. The show opens from there: Lonnie Liston Smith, Vince Montana's South Soul Orchestra covering "I Love Music," Chaka Khan, Cameo's "Candy," and "The Ballad of Dorothy Parker."

Brown then dedicates an extended run from Stevie Wonder's *Songs in the Key of Life* — sides 1 and 4, including "Love's in Need of Love Today," "Village Ghetto Land," "As," "If It's Magic," and "Sir Duke" — to listeners who, like himself, can't afford tickets to Wonder's current tour performing the album in full. The Blackbirds' "Rock Creek Park" gets a spin as well; Brown notes the band were once students of Donald Byrd when he taught music at Howard University in the early 1970s.

shows.desc: DJ Divine's *Soulful House Sessions* on WPFW opens with shout-outs to regular listeners in York, PA and Baltimore, a quick rundown of NFL Week 1 results — including the Chargers' loss to the Cardinals, the Chiefs' win, and the Giants beating the Cowboys — and a tip to Bills fans ahead of Thursday Night Football, before settling into an uninterrupted set of deep, soulful, underground house music. The second half of the hour rolls into the "Baby Powder Hour" segment, keeping the same groove while a guest endorsement from DJ Tony Touch opens a stretch that includes tracks with Spanish-language vocals alongside the English-language soul-house that anchors the show. The episode closes with DJ Divine handing off to Vince Brown's *Expansions*, a vinyl program that follows on the same station.

A voice in archival audio explains that South Africa's Black Consciousness Movement existed to make Black people "proud of themselves, proud of their color" — to counter the psychological frustration, as the speaker put it, of striving to become white under apartheid. DJ Underdog builds the episode around that foundation, moving through Ethiopian jazz, Studio One reggae, Yoruba percussion, and tracks from Tanzania including Makadem's "Muhogo wa Jengombe." He dedicates selections to Enkutatash, the Ethiopian New Year, and pauses to note that Ethiopia runs on a 13-month calendar he calls "the true calendar." Jamaican dub poet Rashadai gets a spotlight placing him in the lineage of Mutabaruka and Linton Kwesi Johnson. The episode closes with a live salon session recorded by Yardcore at Sweet V in Brooklyn, previewing a mixtape called *Reggae Aroma Volume 5*.

Ochun Dueña de las Aguas Dulces

shows.t: Brother Ah’s Collectors: Next Generation in Sound
shows.desc:
Brother Craig calls out the full personnel before every track — Kenny Kirkland on electric piano behind Carlos Garnett, Larry Carlton alongside Joe Sample on the Crusaders cut — treating the credits as part of the music. This is an all-1976 hour of *Brother Oz Collector's Next Generation in Sound*, fifty years on from the recordings. Gil Scott-Heron, Bobby Hutcherson, McCoy Tyner, Woody Shaw, Yusef Lateef, Lonnie Liston Smith, and Carlos Garnett all appear.

The hour closes with Lloyd McNeil's "Griot" from *Treasures*, Cecil McBee on bass, and Jean Lucien's "Gaku" from *Premonition*. The full playlist is on Facebook at Jazz and Justice with Brother Craig.

Chris Smalls launched the Amazon Labor Union with a fire pit outside the JFK8 warehouse on Staten Island and $2.50 in the bank — up against a $2.2 trillion company. He tells host Mimi Rosenberg how that fight became the first successful union election at an Amazon warehouse in the United States. Since then he has crashed the Met Gala and joined a flotilla to Gaza, linking Amazon's military-industrial contracts to the broader working-class struggle.

That connection carries into the second half of the broadcast, where four Port Elizabeth protesters — Teresa Barragan Grady, Danny Crema, Marc Shabelia Carver, and Mary Ann Grady Flores — describe blocking weapons shipments at New Jersey's third-largest port and going to trial the day of this broadcast. The court refused to admit testimony from doctors in Gaza or hear their necessity-defense argument. Charges were reduced to a violation and 120 hours of community service.

Brandon Vaden was on dialysis when he decided to stop producing other people's events and start a consulting business of his own. He tells host Mimi Magic how the Bateman Collective grew from that pivot — and how it helped a former NASA employee launch a lighting-design company after an Infinity Box installation at Wundergarten drew coverage in the Washington Post and Washingtonian magazine.

On Vaden's calendar: Pridetoberfest and an anime-and-K-pop night at Wundergarten developed with input from the Korean Embassy. For Black and LGBTQ entrepreneurs looking for concrete starting points, he points to the MLK Library, the Small Business Administration, and Destination DC. He closes with a plug for the Wanda Alston Foundation's upcoming gala.

Ambrose Lane Sr., recorded in his own voice, tells listeners that the Telecommunications Act of 1996 handed control of nearly all media to five corporations — and calls for its repeal. Host Ambrose Lane Jr. devoted this September 14, 2026 episode of *To the East* to his father on the 16th anniversary of his death. A Buffalo History Channel clip reconstructs Lane Sr.'s 1969 run to become Buffalo's first Black mayor: Congresswoman Shirley Chisholm endorsed him, yet he still couldn't get the two major-party candidates into a debate. Kari Inman Lane, calling in as the host's son, remembers his grandfather — an opera singer who admired Paul Robeson — handing him Black history books in elementary school and "telling us to stay woke long before it was ever a catchphrase."

The episode moves through Black history dates: the 1874 Battle of Liberty Place, the 1963 bombing of the 16th Street Baptist Church, and the 1868 Camilla Massacre. It closes with Paul Robeson singing and speaking about the shared roots of African, Chinese, Scottish, and Hebrew music.

shows.t: Jazz and Justice - African Deep Thought
shows.desc:
W. Paul Coates, founder of Black Classic Press, tells Brother Ka'Ba' that the so-called golden age of Black bookstores is a myth. At any given time, there were likely no more than 50 to 100 active Black booksellers nationwide — a number inflated by mailing lists that included stores closed for a generation. Coates is preparing for a community forum at the Thurgood Marshall Center on the future of four Black legacy publishing houses: Third World Press, Black Classic Press, Africa World Press, and Just Us Books. Their founders are all around 80 years old, and the presses range from nearly 50 to almost 60 years in operation.

The printing side of Black Classic Press is being transitioned to a worker-owned co-op, though the publishing mission remains unresolved — one of the central questions the forum will face. The hour draws on music from Pharoah Sanders' 1980 album *Journey to the One* and closes with a tribute to the recently deceased Cassandra Wilson.

A grain of sugar-sized piece of lead can permanently strip a child of one IQ point. Al Hawkins, president and CEO of Millman Systems, explains exactly how that happens on this edition of **To Your Health**: the body can't tell lead from calcium, so lead stored in a mother's bones can leach into her bloodstream during pregnancy and cross the placenta. Host Dr. Theodore Watkins and producer Frank Smith press Hawkins on the broader consequences. Studies tie lead exposure to aggressive behavior, criminal behavior, and high school dropout rates, with lower-income neighborhoods bearing the heaviest burden. Hawkins also outlines a planned phytoremediation pilot in West Baltimore — modeled on Chernobyl cleanup methods — using plants with an expanded root zone to pull heavy metals from vacant-lot soil, then burning the harvest in a closed-loop incinerator to keep contaminants out of the Patapsco River and Chesapeake Bay.

The hour closes closer to home. A representative recruits African American women ages 40 to 75 for the Prime Time Sister Circle program — free, 12 weeks, conducted virtually, and funded in part by Montgomery County government — covering hypertension, stress, nutrition, and fitness.

Mel has never once walked into Marcus DC to taste the dish named after him. Host Seychelle Amira sits down with executive chef Anthony Jones, who explains that Mel's Crab Rice honors a Calvert County crab supplier from his childhood and that Jones intends to bring the dish to Mel himself. From there, a "Story of Food" segment traces Maryland crab soup from Algonquin communal shellfish stews through the colonial addition of tomatoes to its emergence as a documented regional staple by the 1870s. The episode closes with Bessie Smith, who went from performing on street corners as an orphan to becoming the highest-paid Black entertainer of her time.

shows.t: Don't Forget the Blues - Elliott Gross
shows.desc:
B.B. King's "Blues Boys Theme" opens the hour, with Elliott Gross calling *Blues on the Bayou* the best studio album King released in roughly his last 30 years — a judgment timed to what would have been King's birthday on September 15th. From there, Gross moves through recent releases, beginning with tracks from Jad Tariq, a Memphis guitarist who has toured with Bob Dylan and played alongside Charlie Musselwhite. Danielle Nicole, a 10-time Blues Music Award winner, follows with material from her new album *Fireflies*.

The Blues Calendar closes out the hour, running through live shows across the Washington metro area: the Nighthawks at Westminster Church in Southwest DC, and a 20th-anniversary farewell show for Reverend Brian Hamilton the following Monday.

Errin Haines attended the Houston memorial for Lorenzo Salgado-Araujo and sat down with Latasha Brown — a daughter of Selma — to talk about the Supreme Court's voting rights decision, all as part of season one of her video series *Long Play*. Haines, president of the National Association of Black Journalists, editor-at-large and co-founder of The 19th, tells host Reverend Mark Thompson how she and her co-hosts reported directly from Georgia, North Carolina, South Carolina, Texas, Mississippi, and Tennessee. She breaks down the Georgia governor's race between Keisha Lance Bottoms and billionaire Rick Jackson, flags that 600,000 Black women have been forced out of the workforce, and notes seven Black women running statewide on the Georgia ballot this cycle.

Those threads carry into the open phones, where callers weigh in on why some Latino and Black voters support candidates whose policies target their own communities, the case for multi-party democracy, and whether election results will be certified.

Gianna Chacon and Ronelza Cordell, nurses from National Nurses United, describe Washington Hospital Center's labor and delivery unit going on diversion more than 15 times since July 26th, when the hospital closed 5F — an 11-bed postpartum unit that was one-third of its postpartum capacity. Nurse-to-patient ratios shifted from 1-to-1 to 1-to-2, and patients in active labor risked delivering in triage rooms. Community organizer Sequinly Gray of DC Jobs with Justice describes her granddaughter, born July 6th to a mother with epilepsy, whose delivery at Washington Hospital Center depended on specialty doctors unavailable anywhere else in the city — a city the host identifies as having the highest rate of Black women's maternal death in the country. The hour traces healthcare loss across DC, from the closure of DC General to divestment from United Medical Center. Callers and guests discuss what unions and community organizing might accomplish next, pointing to council member Christina Henderson's public support for reopening 5F and mayor-elect Janice Lewis George's appearance at a September 9th town hall at People's Congregational Church.

The United States stood alone when the UN voted to fix how Africa appears on world maps — every other member opposed it. Howard University Associate Provost for International Affairs Dr. Tanija Hope Navas joins Julianne Malveaux to explain why that non-binding resolution still matters. The stakes come into focus through a single number: only 6.4% of U.S. students who study abroad are Black or African American, a figure she connects to centuries of cartographic distortion.

Cultural anthropologist Dr. Sheila Walker pushes the conversation further. She has visited more than 40 of Africa's 54 or 55 countries, and wrote "Tarzan in the Classroom" on how Africa is taught in U.S. schools. From there she moves into the Kingdom of Kongo's cultural reach across the Americas — territory she has mapped in her documentary *Strange Familiar Faces in Unexpected Places*, which traces the African diaspora from Brazil to communities of Siddhi descendants in Karnataka, Gujarat, and Hyderabad.

shows.t: Morning Brew Jazz Notes Edition feat. Union City Radio
shows.desc:
As a child, Ellen Carter sneaked fast food into Nat Adderley's house in Teaneck — that's where they first encountered Cannonball Adderley, born September 15, 1928. The episode also marks the birth anniversaries of Joseph Jarman (September 14, 1937) — AACM co-founder, Shinshu Buddhist priest, and Army paratrooper injured in a Vietnam raid that killed 18 U.S. soldiers — and organist Jack McDuff (September 17), who gave George Benson his first break.

From there the story turns to Charlie Byrd, who carried bossa nova recordings by João Gilberto and Antônio Carlos Jobim back from Brazil and played them for Stan Getz at his home. The two recorded *Jazz Samba* live at Pierce Hall at All Souls Unitarian Church in Washington, D.C. in 1962. It closes with liner notes in which Byrd, plagued by chronic respiratory difficulties near the end of his life, told a writer over breakfast: "I'm not used to looking back.

The program moves from there into R&B and soul from the same era, love songs and ballads woven in alongside the hip-hop, before Coka-Lani closes out by thanking listeners who checked in, including Hazel and the Butterfly Lady. *Behind the Mic* airs every Monday morning from 2 to 5.

Carl Malcolm took the main stage at Adams Morgan Day Festival that weekend, one stop on a string of DMV events that Teacha and DJ Smooth Devastation recap mid-show. A DSA Association sound system gathering in Indian Head, Maryland drew crews from North Carolina, New York, Baltimore, and Virginia, and a private Ghana fundraising event in Bowie, Maryland honored Nana Peppy Parks. The hosts also preview a Sound Clash on the 19th: Cannabis from Antigua versus Franchise Sound out of Virginia.

The first hour covers foundation reggae and dancehall — Tanya Stevens, Rap Simeon, Icarus, and an original Barry Brown selection. Jerry Culture Sound then takes the second hour into dub and roots classics.

shows.desc: Rick Zeron opens his two-hour set on *This Is Reggae Music* with Gregory Isaacs' "Night Nurse," then moves through roots, lovers rock, and contemporary dancehall. Sitting in for Tony Carr on Sunday, September 13, 2026, Zeron pauses to mention a listener conversation about Miss Lou. He describes her as one of Jamaica's folk heroes. The episode closes with Zeron handing off to Radio Andy and the Reggae Experience.

Roberto dos Santos opens with a dedication to DJ Babalicious, who is set to appear on Fiesta DC's all-Brazilian stage on September 26th, and a shout-out to Grupo Raíces, performing samba con salsa every Wednesday at El Segredo de Rosita. This is *Beating Bow*, his two-hour Sunday Brazilian music program on WPFW. The set moves through João Bosco and Hamilton de Holanda's live "Linha de Passe," Seu Jorge, Chico César's "Mama África," and Naná Vasconcelos, before Alfredo Rodriguez, vocalist Alana Cinque, and Pedrito Martinez close out the hour with a Stevie Wonder cover.

shows.desc:
Tito Puente leaned into someone's microphone at a 1979 live concert at World Trade Center Plaza and credited Stevie Wonder with pressuring NARAS behind the scenes to create the first Grammy categories for Latin music. Host Jim Byers built this September 11th edition of *Latin Flavor Classic Edition* around that recording, dedicating the show to historian Joe Conzo Sr. on what would have been his birthday — Conzo collected and curated the tape.

The episode also honors bassist Israel Cachao López on the eve of his birthday, with selections from *Cachao y su Descarga 77*, a midnight tribute session recorded after the death of Noro Morales on the Alegre label in 1964. A live recording of El Jamaiquino from the Palladium Ballroom in 1954 surfaces here too — remarkable because owner Max Hyman otherwise banned recording entirely. Byers traces Conzo's work across liner notes and reissues: a 1978 Arcáneo reissue of Tito Rodríguez's *Three Loves Have I* and the Columbia Legacy release of *The Original Latin Dance King*.

songs.t: A Love Supreme, Pt. I – Acknowledgement

shows.desc:
The alternate take of "Flamenco Sketches" is the only complete alternate from the 1959 *Kind of Blue* sessions, found exclusively on the 50th-anniversary package, and host Miles Willis traces a line from that Columbia date straight to *Sketches of Spain*. Kevin Mahogany follows. Gene Lees deliberately loosened his English lyrics to Jobim's "Chovendo na Roseira" from the original Portuguese to make the song easier to sing, renaming it "Double Rainbow." Courtney Pine's *Modern Day Jazz Stories* gets examined as an early jazz and hip-hop synthesis: DJ Pogo's turntable tracks were prerecorded and tailored to Pine's compositions rather than improvised live.

The hour closes on Cassandra Wilson. Producer Craig Street asked her to list music that had genuinely moved her to tears, and when no jazz standards appeared on that list, the 1993 album *Blue Light Till Dawn* was built instead from Robert Johnson, Ann Peebles, and Wilson's own compositions.

Willard Jenkins opens this edition of *Open Sky* by honoring jazz centenarians of 2026, spinning Oscar Brown Jr.'s "But I Was Cool" from *Sin and Soul*, Jack McDuff's "Rock Candy" with Houston Person on tenor, and a Miles Davis–Coltrane sextet reading of Thelonious Monk's "Straight No Chaser." The 3 o'clock new-release hour brings a Ledisi–Gregory Porter duet on Dinah Washington's "You've Got What It Takes," from Ledisi's tribute album *For Dinah*, then Jason Moran's solo piano take on Duke Ellington's "Fleurette Africaine" from *Jason Moran Plays Duke Ellington*. His wife Alicia Hall Moran follows with "River" — both records on the couple's YES Records label.

Jenkins also previews that afternoon's WPFW benefit concert at Palisades Hub, with tracks from the two headlining acts: Baltimore bassist Chris Funn's Corner Store and Herman Burney's Two Bass Hit. Rounding out the hour are a Gary Bartz medley by the Baltimore Jazz Collective and a set from Luther Allison, winner of the previous week's D.C. Jazz Pre-Emerging Bands Competition.

shows.desc:
Jacari Sherman traces stepping back to the Negro Act of 1740, which banned drums in colonial South Carolina and forced enslaved and free Black people to make their bodies percussive instruments. His choreography for *The Fruits of Our Labor*, Step Afrika!'s production at Arena Stage, builds one section around Reverend C.L. Franklin's sermon "The Eagle Stirreth in Her Nest" — treating the congregation's responses as central to the movement as Franklin's own cadence. Sherman names "freedom" as the single word that unlocks the entire work. Miyuki Williams presents.

That history has a present address: Meridian Hill Malcolm X Park, where Steve Coleman of Washington Parks and People recalls 20,000 people gathering one month after Dr. King's assassination to hear Pearl Bailey perform. Producer Charvis Campbell details the full-day public affairs programming planned for WPFW's September 27th Jazz and Justice Festival at that same park. The episode closes with birthday tributes to blues pianist Charles Brown and Mel Tormé, who co-wrote "The Christmas Song" in 40 minutes on a sweltering summer day.

shows.desc:
Butch Warren grew up in Washington, D.C., became the go-to bassist for Blue Note Records in the late 1950s and early 1960s, then spent decades struggling with addiction and mental illness. On his Sunday morning program G-Strings, Tom Cole traces him through two Grant Green sessions — one with Herbie Hancock, one with Sonny Clark, the pianist who first brought Warren to Blue Note's attention. Victor Dvoshkin's "Song for Edward," written for Edward Cohen, the man who helped Dvoshkin emigrate from the Soviet Union "at a fraught time," draws a pointed parallel to the present.

The three-hour program is anchored by a benefit concert that afternoon at Palisades Hub, featuring Herman Burney's group Two Bass Hit and Baltimore bassist Chris Funn's group Corner Store.

shows.desc:
Scientists from Underwriters Laboratories, who wrote the specs allowing the Port Authority to insure the World Trade Center, told host Lona Alias that jet fuel could not burn hot enough to turn steel orange — and that the towers should have survived a 24-hour fire with their structure intact. Alias says she gathered those claims firsthand while working for INS in New York. She presents them here in this September 11 anniversary edition of *The Spirit of Jazz*, alongside her account of WPFW's post-9/11 investigative program *Peace Watch*, produced under executive producer Verna Avery Brown. That program brought in CIA briefer Ray McGovern; national counterterrorism coordinator Richard Clarke, whose book *Against All Enemies* she names; FBI whistleblower Coleen Rowley; and Ambassador Joseph Wilson, whose wife Valerie Plame was outed after he disputed the claim that Iraq sought uranium from Niger.

The three-hour broadcast's music moves from gospel and inspirational R&B — including the Sounds of Blackness, Dionne Warwick, Earth Wind and Fire, and an Isley Brothers album Alias identifies as recorded in a single take — to Sam Cooke's "A Change Is Gonna Come" and Nina Simone.

shows.desc: Kofi Kissi Dompere dedicates this episode of *African Rhythms and Extensions* to John Coltrane's 100th birthday, tracing Coltrane's expansion of jazz harmony and his role as a spiritual voice in the Black liberation struggles of the 1960s back to African polyrhythm. The music ranges across Eritrea, Kenya, Guinea, the Republic of the Congo, Senegal, Togo, Sierra Leone, and Cameroon, drawing in work by Mongo Santamaria and Armando Peraza alongside Congolese rumba and Cuban rhythmic traditions. Dompere closes with his standing reminder: "if you are drinking, don't drive; if you are driving, don't drink."

Bush Head Ed opened this Soul Controller Second Saturdays edition of *The Cypher* with a tribute to Peter Cullen — the voice of Optimus Prime — playing Big Daddy Kane's "Smooth Operator," with its line "transforming on stage like a Decepticon," alongside Gnarls Barkley's "Transformer" and Ty's "When Robots Go to War." Cullen had voiced the character from *Transformers*' 1984 cartoon debut through a forthcoming short film marking the franchise's 40th anniversary.

A Virgo-season birthday run covered Nas, Eazy-E, Doug E. Fresh, and Ludacris. Ed had caught Reese performing the 25th anniversary of *How I Do* at Songbird and followed that with her "Ice King" featuring Nas. Rapsody's "Pick a Side" from *God's Got an Afro and Gold Hoops* appeared alongside a posse cut from Storm the Unpredictable, Poor Righteous Teachers, Common and Pete Rock, and material from Nas and DJ Premier's "Pause Tapes" project. Ed broadcast the whole show after flying back from Alabama A&M on a 6 AM flight he nearly missed.

shows.desc:
Carl and Carol Jacobs, the Caribbean musicians whose song "Fix It Up" became a lasting part of Trinidad's popular music memory, told hosts Von Martin and Bryan Bernard how they deliberately fused calypso with rock, disco, and funk to draw younger listeners into the music's political and social messages. They also recalled doing background vocals for Kitchener, Sparrow, and Shadow in sessions that ran until 2 or 3 in the morning with one microphone and no flying tracks.

A second interview brought together Professor Opal Palmer-Adisa and Anya Gloden to discuss Louise Bennett-Coverley — how she validated Jamaican Nation Language by tracing its roots to Twi and other African languages, endured years of dismissal as a poet, and used humor and performance to defend the dignity of Jamaican women from the 1940s onward. Gloden noted that Miss Lou was her godmother and that as a child she would cross the hills of Gordon Town to get a bowl of soup from her. The hour also covered Caribbean news: kidnappings in Haiti, medication shortages in Trinidad and Tobago, and Howard University's investiture of the Eric Eustace Williams Endowed Chair in Caribbean Studies upon scholar Carol Boyce Davies.

shows.desc: Carl Davis never performed, yet he talked Gene Chandler into going solo and pushed "Duke of Earl" into existence over his own group's objections. Major Lance's daughter later became mayor of Atlanta. The second half of this *Roots and Fruits* marks what would have been B.B. King's 101st birthday on September 16th, with Wax drawing on the 40 one-hour interview programs he produced with King for XM's Bluesville. Early tracks highlight King's falsetto; duets pair him with Bonnie Raitt, Bobby Blue Bland, and Etta James.

Walter Williams of the O'Jays has performed through MS, barely able to move before stepping onstage — DJ Lance Reynolds drops that detail mid-set on this Virgo-themed episode of House of Soul. Reynolds plays birthday-season sets from Otis Redding, Freda Payne, the Fifth Dimension, Sylvester, Roy Ayers, Bubba Knight of Gladys Knight and the Pips, and Williams, among others. Between sets he sits down with Adina Gittens-Smith, co-founder of Belly Dancers of Color Collective, ahead of their tenth annual Honoring the Divine Masculine Day on September 19th in Upper Marlboro — an event combining tai chi, sound meditation, Egyptian yoga, drumming, and a "sacred flower shower" of white roses over the men present.

Near the end of the hour, Reynolds sets the celebration aside. His stepmother Andrea Beasley died the previous Thursday, and he remembers her by describing how she taught him Washington, D.C. — driving him to every T.G.I. Friday's in the region and showing him the city's back ways and alleys.

shows.desc: Cap'n Fly and Jas. Funk have been on WPFW for 36 years, and they remember it was a September when they first joined the station's family. The Oldies House Party rolls through the Dells' Chicago showmanship, basement-party classics, and hands-on dance instruction — the mashed potato, the tighten up, the popcorn, the limbo. Listeners call in, birthdays get called out, and the hosts name Willie Mitchell as the songwriter and producer behind the Al Green records played during the hour. Shout-outs land at Sam Caden's record store on 7th Street, a classic-car show at Anacostia Park, and a go-go night at the Charles County Fairgrounds with Backyard Band and Pocket 3.

Arthur McCloud, the Mellow Man himself, stops the music to read an original poem he wrote the day after September 11 — warning listeners that "we got attacked 3 times in less than 1 hour" and that America was "caught with our pants down." That pause marks the 15th anniversary. From there the Sexy Sensual Sounds Saturday set draws from Tyrone Davis, the Isley Brothers, Marvin Gaye, Natalie Cole, and Janet Jackson, followed by a tribute to Rodney Franklin, who died in mid-August, featuring "A Song for You" from the CD *Skydance*.

The Doo Wop Plus segment opens with Aki Starr's a cappella "Baby I'm for Real," then works through the Originals, the Brothers of Soul, and Barbara Mason.

Kwabena Nketiah's definition of improvisation as simultaneously "the way what is known is recreated" and "the process of invention." That frame holds the whole program together.

Buried in the set is an early Geri Allen recording — the title track from *Medasi*, cut when Allen was a freshman or sophomore at Howard University with the Nation African Liberation Arts Ensemble and poet Hakim Marabuti. shows.desc:
Vietnamese forces hauled roughly 212 artillery pieces up mountain slopes using ropes and human labor, then shelled the French garrison at Dien Bien Phu into surrender. Garland Nixon uses that pivot point on *News Views* to argue that every U.S. war since World War II has been built on lies. Former CIA briefer Ray McGovern and Colonel Lawrence Wilkerson, Colin Powell's former chief of staff, both told Nixon on air that the U.S. overthrew the Ukrainian government and is using Ukraine as a proxy against Russia.

The conversation moves from there through the looting of Iraqi and Venezuelan oil revenues to the concept of strategic depth as it applies to Russia, China, and an increasingly powerful Iran. Nixon's closing argument: neither party will change any of it.

Hosted by Jacqueline Luqman, this episode of *Darker Than Blue* uses the anniversary of the September 11, 2001 attacks as a framework for tracing U.S.-backed political violence across several other September 11ths: the 1973 CIA-supported coup that killed Chilean president Salvador Allende and installed Pinochet, whose regime tortured 27,255 people and executed 2,279; the 1977 beating death of South African Black Consciousness Movement founder Steve Biko by apartheid police; the 1990 stabbing murder of Guatemalan anthropologist Myrna Mack Chang, who had been documenting the U.S.-backed military's destruction of indigenous Maya communities; and the 1993 daylight killing in Haiti of Lavalas businessman Antoine Ismairi, connected to earlier attacks on a church where Father Jean-Bertrand Aristide had narrowly escaped death. Luqman also draws on a 2020 Yahoo News report in which FBI assistant director Jill Sanborn accidentally disclosed the name of Saudi diplomat Musaed Ahmed al-Jarrah — suspected of directing support to two of the 9/11 hijackers — and cites New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani's release of more than 170,000 pages of previously sealed city records, including the Harding memo and documents on World Trade Center 7, through a new public portal at nyc.gov/sept11docs.

Dr. Don Lottie Whitten, a physical therapist, opens Bobby Rox's Fantastic Friday Show with the argument that muscles function as an endocrine organ — releasing proteins called myokines that cross the blood-brain barrier and improve brain health. Strength training, she contends, can open pathways for glucose to enter muscle directly without raising insulin levels, making exercise act like medicine.

Audio clips from Dr. Francis Cress Welsing, Dr. Amos Wilson, Minister Louis Farrakhan, and Anthony Browder thread through the episode. Browder contends that the word "genius" derives from tapping into the genetic memory of ancestors carried in one's DNA. Rox anchors everything to September 11, 2001 — the date Jay-Z's *The Blueprint* dropped — while marking the US Open semifinal run of Hyattsville, Maryland native Francis Tiafoe, who would be the first Black American man to play in the US Open Championship since Arthur Ashe in 1972.

shows.desc:
New York Governor Kathy Hochul froze every operating account of the Seneca Nation, extracted $560 million, and directed more than $400 million of it to Bills owner Terry Pegula for a new stadium. John Cain connects that episode to his documentary film *The Long Hope*, which traces how the Doctrine of Christian Discovery and the Plenary Powers Doctrine continue to harm Seneca and Mohawk people today. He also marks the 10th anniversary of Colin Kaepernick's kneeling protest. Kaepernick took his team to the Super Bowl before being blackballed and has since been named the Muhammad Ali Humanitarian of the Year. The Washington Commanders still sell Redskins merchandise in their gift shops, and the NFL retains teams with Native mascots.

Cain flags a textual detail that NPR reporters recently got wrong. The phrase "excluding Indians not taxed" appears in the Apportionment Clause of both the original Constitution and the 14th Amendment, meaning Native people were never counted for congressional representation.

On the 53rd anniversary of the U.S.-backed coup against Salvador Allende — and the 50th anniversary of the Washington, D.C. car-bomb assassination of Orlando Letelier — host Oscar Fernandez speaks with historian and author Lynn Shapiro about her book on Fabiola Letelier. The Chilean human rights lawyer kicked down the door of a morgue to identify the bodies of the murdered Gallardo Moreno family, secured the first Latin American convictions of secret police chiefs for human rights violations, and won a unanimous Chilean Supreme Court ruling that crimes against humanity carry no statute of limitations.

Shapiro also discusses the pending U.S. deportation case of Armando Fernandez Larios, a DINA agent who surveilled Orlando Letelier, later pled guilty to a single count of accessory in the U.S., and has since lived in Miami. She describes how Chile's current Kast government is dismantling the National Search Program for the Disappeared by replacing experienced human rights staff — moves that six lawyers, sociologists, and family members of victims brought before the OAS in early August.

shows.t: Don't Forget The Blues - Ida Campbell
shows.desc:
Ida Campbell opens her September 11 broadcast by playing Patti LaBelle's "Walk Around Heaven" for listeners who lost someone that day, then reads a tribute sent by the mayor of Ocean City. The hour moves through Gospel, Al Green, and Leon Bridges, with a live blues calendar running from Graysonville, Maryland to Falls Church, Virginia.

Along the way, Campbell pauses to remember the recently deceased Cassandra Wilson, describing Wilson's "Subatomic Blues" as using scientific language to reach "the smallest particles of each matter" beneath human feeling. She closes with Freddie King and Albert King, signing off just ahead of her 75th birthday.
