shows.t: Community Watch & Comment - Friday / The Local Station Board Show (Last Frid
shows.desc:
Twenty-five years after 9/11, Ron Pinchback and Chip Jones open with a flat statement: "so many questions are still unanswered." *Community Watch and Comment* (Friday Edition) moves from there to Trump's pledge to give every U.S. adult $5,000 if Republicans win the midterms — bribery charges already floating — and an FCC report that Jimmy Kimmel was pressured not to interview a named guest. A prominent AI researcher warns that companies are stripping guardrails in a race to be first.

Callers push into harder territory. A Montgomery County case involves people allegedly held as slaves tied to data-center development. Roughly 200 women have died from ectopic pregnancies since abortion law changes. And a fight over flock cameras — license-plate readers at over $2,000 each — has Alexandria and other jurisdictions reconsidering their use.

Linda Sarsour was walking from her college campus in Sheepshead Bay, Brooklyn, toward Bay Ridge on September 11, 2001, catching burned paper falling from across the river. She arrived to find mosques gated and her mother refusing to wear her hijab. That day ended her plans to become a high school English teacher and pulled her into 25 years of activism — among them a class action lawsuit against the NYPD over mosque infiltrators, informants planted on whitewater rafting trips, and surveillance of coffee shop customers.

Historian Gerald Horne traces a line from Jimmy Carter and Zbigniew Brzezinski's 1970s alliance with religious zealots in Afghanistan — through the castration and lynching of Afghanistan's last left-leaning leader Najibullah, the Iraq invasion on "spurious" weapons-of-mass-destruction grounds, and China's rise during America's "forever war" distraction — to the current U.S.-Israeli war on Iran. The program also draws on engineer Jonathan Cole's documentary *False Flag Day* and a presentation by journalist James Corbett on the 9/11 money trail: Larry Silverstein's insurance payout, anomalous pre-attack trading, and a German data recovery firm's findings that the FBI later denied to the 9/11 Commission. Host Esther Iverem presents this edition of *On the Ground* on the 25th anniversary of the September 11th attacks.

"Racism ain't regional," Dear Silas told co-host Brittany Bell-Serrat — and Mississippi, he argued, is one of the Blackest states in the country. The Mississippi artist released two projects simultaneously: *Sophisticated Ratchet Red* (hip-hop) and *Sophisticated Ratchet Blue* (jazz), with the "Sophisticated Ratchet" name built around disrupting expectations and showing up authentically.

Jharrel Clay of Hip Hop Caucus then spoke with Dominique Morgan, a Black trans woman who grew the budget at Black and Pink National from $225,000 to $3.2 million and previously created content for Apple. Morgan talked Black trans identity, incarceration, and voting as one tool among many for community change. Telling people what to do at the ballot box backfires, she argued — helping people make informed decisions on their own terms works better.

shows.t: Morning Brew Jazz Edition feat. Union City Radio
shows.desc: Jaribu Shahid moved from the Sun Ra Orchestra (1978–80) through Roscoe Mitchell's band before joining the Art Ensemble of Chicago in 2004 — and his recent Detroit Jazz Fest artist-in-residency, where he led a tribute to the AACM, anchors Candy Shannon's birthday segment on the Friday Morning Brew. Commentator Skyler Borton covers the Treasury Department's $12.5 billion bond buyback amid foreign sell-offs and a First Circuit ruling blocking the administration's mail-in voting plan. Also in Borton's segment: Houthi control of the port of Mokka near the Bab-el-Mandeb Strait, and an Ohio resident's case that AI data center development is a speculative bubble requiring municipalities to demand upfront capital bonds before granting tax and zoning concessions. Music includes tracks from Charles Tolliver's remastered 1968 debut *Right Now and Then* — with Herbie Hancock, Ron Carter, and Gary Bartz — plus selections from Dee Dee Bridgewater's Horace Silver tribute and Cindy Blackman's *Someday*.

shows.desc:
A 65-year-old Black man can be biologically closer to 68 — not by calendar, but by what Dr. Tali Elliott called "sustained high-intensity trauma" and a "weathering effect" that accumulates over a lifetime. Dr. Jeffrey Johnson, coordinator of Black Men's Health at the African American Health Program, explained this to host Dr. Daryl Howard, alongside the stark gap: average life expectancy of 70.8 years for Black men versus 75.8 for white men. Johnson traced the Tuskegee Experiment's lasting grip on medical mistrust, then described his program's strategy of taking health screenings into barbershops, salons, and basketball courts, with a free Community Ambassador Training set for Saturday, 9 a.m. to noon.

That work of meeting people where they are finds a parallel in the history Kim Bishop and Troy Bishop bring to the program. They tell the story of Good Hope Union UMC in Colesville, Montgomery County — founded in 1870 by three freed Black farmers, John Powell, Tom Stewart, and Sam Jones, who bought the land from Sarah Watts. The congregation has counted the first ordained African American female pastor in the Baltimore-Washington Conference of the United Methodist Church and a Negro Leagues pitcher who played with the Newark Eagles, Birmingham Black Barons, and Atlanta Black Crackers. The Bishops describe plans to restore the 1913 sanctuary, ring its bell again, and host a free community health bazaar on September 19th.

Cedric DeLeon opens with a provocation: the empirical data, he argues, shows that Black workers — not white allies — were the primary architects of interracial solidarity in American unions. His new book *Freedom Train* presses that claim hard, even knowing it will unsettle labor studies circles. DeLeon brings organizer experience to the argument, having worked for the United Farm Workers, District 1199 SEIU, and the American Federation of Teachers between 1994 and 2006; he now teaches sociology and labor studies at the University of Massachusetts Amherst. From there he turns to a puzzle in the present: why record-high public approval of unions hasn't moved membership numbers. He points to employer misclassification of workers as independent contractors, automation, and the export of unionized jobs to the Global South. Host Renee draws him through the distinctions between social movement unionism, business unionism, and service unionism.

The conversation closes on a specific case. The 2017 UAW campaign at a majority-Black Nissan plant in Canton, Mississippi becomes a study in what happens when a union organizes for recognition without addressing the racial and social conditions workers face outside the plant gates — a limit, DeLeon suggests, that runs through the broader history *Freedom Train* sets out to tell.

David Roediger once called Toni Morrison to talk about a joke at the end of Malcolm X's autobiography. Morrison's argument, as Roediger tells Jon Jeter, was that immigrants' first English word — "okay" — represented learned submission to bosses, cops, and bureaucrats, and that the word likely derives from West African languages. Roediger, author of *The Wages of Whiteness* and the memoir *An Ordinary White: My Antiracist Education*, traces his own political education to growing up between a sundown town and Cairo, Illinois. There, city fathers closed a WPA-built swimming pool rather than desegregate it, and Cairo's Black mission church became an organizing center for a civil rights movement under armed attack by a white supremacist group called the White Hats.

That history of managed concession and violent reaction carries forward into the conversation's second half. Roediger and Jeter examine the Clinton-era strategy of using Black grievances to consolidate white voters, AOC's recent distancing from the Black Lives Matter movement, and whether socialist electoral politics can break that pattern. Roediger is a professor of history at the University of Kansas.

UAW president Sean Fain stood in Tabitha Arnold's studio, pointed to a figure in the bottom right of her tapestry, and said "that's what I did" — recognizing himself from his time working in Kokomo. Arnold spent 224 hours weaving that piece for Volkswagen workers during their union drive, the first successful unionization of an auto plant in the South, and brought it to rallies before the vote so factory workers could see themselves memorialized on the production line. That same instinct — art as witness to labor — runs through the rest of the hour. At the 10th Reuther Pollock Symposium in Wheeling, West Virginia, artist Eric Ruanne credited his father's union pension — paid out after his death — as what allowed him to quit his first job and pursue art.

In Tacoma, Chris Garlock hears from former Pierce County Central Labor Council president Vance Lely, who explains how the annual Labor Day commemoration at Ralph Chaplin's grave grew from one activist's solitary vigil into a gathering of 60 union members. From there, Tampa DSA organizers Roger Butterfield and Manny Ramirez walk through Ybor City's labor history, including a 1937 march of roughly 5,000 women on City Hall to protest the bombing of Guernica — led to a mayor named Robert E. Lee Chancey.

Jeffrey Sachs calls U.S. sanctions on Iran illegal and predicts they will fail. His Substack article "The Looming Failure of Operation Economic Outcast" makes the case: the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, representing roughly 42% of the world's population, will keep trading with Iran regardless, and China has already built payment channels that bypass the SWIFT dollar-clearing system. Sachs links the sell-off of U.S. Treasuries to what he terms the administration's "gangsterism," and sets America's roughly 750 overseas military bases against China's one confirmed overseas naval facility in Djibouti.

Journalist and author Sonali Kolhatkar turns to the domestic front with her new book "Breaking Ice: Community Defense Against State Terror and MAGA Fascism," drawn from interviews with frontline activists including Ron Góchez and Leonardo Martinez. She describes how organizations in Los Angeles deployed bullhorns, neighborhood patrols, and Know Your Rights cards to confront ICE operations. Because the strongest correlation to crime is inequality rather than policing, Kolhatkar argues, an abolitionist framework — redirecting budgets toward housing, mutual aid, and other community needs — applies equally to ICE, local police, and the U.S. military. Code Pink Radio host Marcy Winograd leads both conversations.

On the 25th anniversary of 9/11, *The Collision* host DZ and co-hosts Etan Thomas and Chuck Modiano argue that the attacks erased a nascent police-accountability movement — including NAACP conferences scheduled for October 2001 — and turned cops into untouchable heroes in stadiums and popular culture. Thomas recounts Trayvon Martin's brother telling him that mainstream media ignored the case until LeBron James and the Miami Heat wore hoodies. Modiano describes being among 50 protesters escorted out of a St. Louis Rams stadium after dropping a Black Lives Matter banner while Colin Kaepernick — starting quarterback that day — was on the field. The episode marks the 10th anniversary of Kaepernick's kneel on that same September 10, 2016 date.

The closing "16th Round" segment turns to Jalen Brunson hosting *Saturday Night Live*. Drawn from a conversation with Karen Russell, it notes that Bill Russell was the first athlete to host the show, in 1979.

During COVID, Ricardo A. Wilson II opened a box at Yale's Beinecke Library and found something scholars had missed: a Langston Hughes translation manuscript far more complete than anyone had noted — 18 authors, multiple drafts of most stories, correspondence proving Hughes wanted it published. Wilson, associate professor of English at Williams College and editor of *Troubled Lands: Stories of Mexico and Cuba as Translated by Langston Hughes* (Princeton University Press), tells host E. Ethelbert Miller how Hughes's agent Maxim Lieber — now believed to have been a Soviet spy — likely buried the collection to shield Hughes from HUAC.

The manuscript itself shows Hughes at work across three revisions of a single paragraph, quietly introducing the word "brownness," a concept absent from the original Spanish. Wilson reads aloud from "The Protector" by Marcelo Salinas, a story of a Cuban father and son stealing sweet potatoes in the dark to survive — a passage Miller connects to Hughes's own feelings about his absent father.

Caroline, a communal representative from Kenscoff's second communal section, counted at least 46 bodies with her own eyes after the August 23rd massacre. She tells host Eugenia Charles that local officials had already warned police about threats before the attack, yet nothing was done. She adds that gang members are holding more than 50 people hostage as leverage against government action.

Charles also plays an excerpt from a recent *Haiti on Our Mind* session with Jean Saint-Ville, known as Jafrik Afrika, a Pan-Africanist author based in Canada, who argues that Haitian fighters at the 1779 Battle of Savannah were children used as cannon fodder, not volunteers — a history he connects to the current UN-sanctioned multinational security force in Haiti. The episode also covers ICE's arrest of 1,328 people from Maryland and Virginia in the first two weeks of August; the release of Haitian businessman Dimitri Vob after more than 300 days in immigration detention; and Haiti's under-14 national soccer team winning the 2026 CFU Challenge Series.

Shani C. of the 411 Collective — a Washington, D.C. grassroots network of street artists, graffiti writers, and organizers active for about ten years — joins hosts Majé, Ahmad, and Tre'Logy of the Freedom Futures Collective to discuss the collective's mural at the Festival Center in Adams Morgan. The mural depicts figures including a former Black Panther turned reproductive justice leader who also produced a segment for WPFW, an arts organizer named Topper Carew who ran an architecture firm that fought displacement, domestic workers and street vendors, and Maha Halal, who has worked to elevate the issue of Islamophobia in U.S. policy. Shani also walks through the barriers behind large-scale public art — paint, equipment, artist pay, and the strings attached to institutional funding — and calls out the real estate industry's co-opting of murals and graffiti to advance development agendas, tracing graffiti's roots to Black and brown communities in the South Bronx.

The episode also features a Pride Purpose Power Top 5 Countdown and a DJ mix from DJ Kade of Washington, D.C. It closes with a conversation about Art All Night, a citywide celebration of art taking place that weekend across every ward in D.C.

Thirty Ward 8 teenagers read the Secure D.C. bill line by line, then wrote and delivered three-minute testimonies to the D.C. Council. Jackie Carter, founder of Children's Legacy Theater, tells host Sam P.K. Collins how that process works alongside historical productions — *The Meeting*, which imagines a conversation between Dr. King and Malcolm X, and *Fannie Lou Hamer: Until I'm Free* — to bring back students who had stopped showing up to school. Program manager Brittany Sestare joins Carter to describe their summer program, in which student playwrights wrote, cast, and directed their peers in original works. Carter has also taken her case to a Janice Lewis George listening forum, arguing that Ward 8 needs dedicated space on the St. Elizabeths campus for arts nonprofits and pointing to the $10.6 billion the arts brought into D.C. in 2016.

The conversation grows out of Collins's street-level interview with mayoral candidate Lewis George on her plans to use mayoral control of schools to address chronic absenteeism, literacy gaps, and special-education delivery.

Pink shut down her own comment section after, as host Zain Al-Amin puts it, she was "attacked by the world" — her response to Macklemore's concert declaration of support for Palestinian justice. Al-Amin also walks through a Haaretz exposé reporting that Netanyahu was warned by UAE leader bin Zayed ten days before the October 7th Hamas attack and allegedly never informed Israeli security or military authorities. The bulk of the hour goes to Laith Marouf, reporting live from Beirut on September 9th, 2026. Marouf covers Israel's failed attempts to capture Ali Tahrir Hill in southern Lebanon, the Lebanese government's reported willingness to extradite a former Palestinian Authority ambassador to the West Bank at Mahmoud Abbas's request, and Yemeni forces advancing toward Bab el-Mandeb while striking Saudi targets including the Aramco plant in Abha and King Khalid airbase. He also reports on Israel's air raid on an ammunition depot in the Idlib region of Syria.

Dr. Greg Carr told the audience at Sankofa Video, Books, and Café in Washington, D.C., that the Wayne Frederick Undergraduate Library across from Howard University "doesn't have a single book in it" and called the university structure itself "death." *AfricaNow!* host Mwiza Munthali presents this archival post-screening discussion, moderated by executive producer James Pope and recorded at Sankofa following a screening of the documentary *How to Build a Library*. The film follows two Kenyan women who took over management of Nairobi's Macmillan Memorial Library — a whites-only institution from its 1931 founding until independence — and attempted to decolonize it.

Carr, a Howard University Africana Studies professor, described students at Philadelphia Freedom Schools being handed Cedric Robinson and other demanding texts regardless of reading level: "we're going to bleed on these pages." Audience members joined the exchange, among them a Howard professor who learned to read at Chicago's Institute of Positive Education and a woman who taught all three of her children to read before kindergarten.

A whistleblower says federal officials are still blocking mail-in ballots despite a court order. Movement attorney Judith Browne Dianis walks through that and other concrete threats heading into the 2026 midterms — including Tarrant County, Texas's proposal to remove 92 polling sites — and gives out the Election Protection Hotline number: 1-866-OUR-VOTE.

Haiti Action Committee co-founder Pierre Labossiere describes a massacre in Kenscoff where survivors say they warned police two weeks in advance and were told the attack "will be worse than the one you survived before." He also recounts the death of Pierre Damas Bell, a 20-year-old TPS holder and scholarship student with an asylum hearing scheduled for October, whose ankle shackle prevented him from playing soccer and who died by suicide. Labossiere addresses the deportation flights and the claim that returnees receive $2,500 — sources on the ground, he says, put it closer to $60. The episode airs on Nana Gyamfi's *Sojourner Truth* and closes with notice of days of solidarity with Haiti running September 24th through the 27th.

Philip Aaron Lacy, a Howard University graduate who practiced architecture in Washington, D.C. for 40 years, tells host Faye Williams that January 6th drove him to research who actually built the U.S. Capitol. His book *They Laid the Stone* recovers the enslaved workers who constructed it between 1793 and 1864, known only by first names in slave ledgers, with no identified living descendants. One of them, Philip Reed, cast the statue that stands atop the dome. A site diagonally across from the Air and Space Museum once functioned as a slave dungeon.

That same evening, the Hirshhorn Museum hosts the premiere of *The Capital*, a film about the political battles over choosing the nation's capital, directed by Dr. Amy Anderson, daughter of former D.C. Mayor Sharon Pratt. The episode also notes a September 16th forum titled "Resolving the US-Provoked Crisis in Cuba" at New York Avenue Presbyterian Church, and closes with a tribute to Dick Gregory's 1976 cross-country run of 3,500 miles — roughly 7 million steps — sustained on fruit juices, vitamins, and water to draw attention to world hunger.

Dr. Marsha Coleman Adebayo says hundreds of African children died at a burial ground on River Road in Bethesda, Maryland between the mid-1700s and 1865 — and that a developer recently hired a DNA company, given permission to destroy 90% of the remains there before a self-storage unit could be built. As executive director of the Bethesda African Cemetery Coalition, Adebayo has fought Montgomery County, Maryland, in court for 11 years, winning at both the circuit and Maryland Supreme Court levels; she explains why she applies the United Nations definition of genocide to the case. She also traces how Black people were "terrorized out of their homes" in Bethesda with the support of the Ku Klux Klan and Montgomery County's Police Department. Host Denise Young then turns to Terry Blackwell of the Prince George's Community Collaborative Resolution Center and Dr. Anthony Bryant of Walker Mill Middle School, whose student peer mediation team won an international JAMS online competition in May. Several student mediators speak for themselves, among them lead mediator Dennis McCamery, who joined the program just last year after Dr. Bryant handed him an application immediately following a successful mediation.

Presbyterian minister William Sloane Coffin — once a CIA case officer who quit after the agency overthrew elected governments in Iran and Guatemala, then became Yale's chaplain — tells a 1968 New School for Social Research audience that armaments decrease national security rather than increase it. He traces U.S. complicity in Chinese suffering from the 19th century through the rejected diplomatic overtures of the 1950s and 60s, and argues that true unity demands belonging, not uniformity.

The second recording in this *From the Vault* episode, hosted by Brian DeShazer, turns to *Washington for Jesus* — a 1980 Pacifica program produced by Tim Frasca and Addie Gevins. It documents the April 29, 1980 rally on the National Mall, where an estimated 200,000 people heard Pat Robertson, Adrian Rogers, and Pat Boone speak. Across town, civil rights figure James Farmer and Howard University professor James Tinney — himself a born-again Pentecostal minister — held a counter-press conference charging that the organizers were using religious language to conceal a right-wing political agenda.

Dr. Bryan Kuwoba submitted a book interview to Jacobin magazine, incorporated every edit they requested, and was told it wouldn't run because it didn't "jive perfectly with our editorial line." He tells the panel that's the same wall Hubert Harrison hit over a century ago — driven out of the Socialist Party for placing Black workers at the center of socialist theory. Kuwoba's book *Hubert Harrison: Forbidden Genius of Black Radicalism* argues Harrison founded the Black Marxist tradition by secularizing Black Christian socialism, a contribution the left has spent decades burying.

That argument anchors "The Path Black to Socialism," a panel at the 2026 Socialism Conference in Chicago moderated by host Anthony Rogers-Wright, with Black Alliance for Peace members from Chicago and Nashville and a Party for Socialism and Liberation organizer from Omaha. The conversation moves through white paternalism in leftist spaces, the dismissal of Southern Black organizing, Claudia Jones's framework of super-exploitation, and Du Bois's general-strike thesis from *Black Reconstruction*.

The Ebola strain now spreading in Congo is Bundibugyo, a variant for which no vaccine exists. The doctor who first identified Ebola in 1976, Jean-Jacques Muyembe, is still alive and leading Congo's national biomedical research institute — yet for decades it was a Belgian scientist who received his samples that received the credit. Maurice Carney, Executive Director of Friends of the Congo, joins host Margaret Kimberley to put that history alongside the present: sanctioned businessman Dan Gertler collects roughly $200,000 a day in royalties from Congolese mining concessions while 80 percent of the country's 110 million people live on less than $3 a day.

The episode then moves to New York City, where tenant rights attorney and City Planning Commissioner Leah Goodridge had hosted a town hall on deed theft the previous night. Goodridge explains how speculators target fractional heirs — including estranged relatives — to force partition sales of homes in Brooklyn and Queens neighborhoods. The remedy, she argues, is prosecution of the thieves, not homeowner education.

Chris Carr built a 10-day, 150-performer festival in Brooklyn with no budget, then bought 15.6 acres of conservation land in upstate New York — where nothing larger than an 800-square-foot maintenance shed can be built — all while undergoing 13 months of immunotherapy for a rare melanoma that cost him a toe. On *Something to Say*, host Mazi Mutafa draws out how working that land has reshaped Carr's creative practice and his thinking about Black land ownership. Carr also traces the path that brought him there: teenage rapper in DC, where Jay Cooper of Teen Summit was an early influence, then Morehouse College, then Columbia grad school, and finally founding Brooklyn Wildlife.

The second hour belongs to Flex Matthews, a DC MC born in Augsburg, Bavaria, who told a hall monitor at Wheaton High School that "Flex Matthews" was his name when caught sneaking back in. He talks freestyling across reggae, folk, and jam bands, and offers his measure of a truly great freestyler: never saying the same thing twice.

Federal agents arrived at Cal Robinette's house with two helicopters, smashed a window, and dragged the union electrician into the rain in his underwear. Robinette is one of the Minneapolis 15, federally indicted workers whose unions responded by organizing worker assemblies across a dozen union locals to resist the Trump administration's mass ICE operations in the city. What those operations look like from the air comes into focus through a segment from the Tegna documentary *Air ICE*, which follows a single deportation flight, Tyson 57, through four stops in Ohio, Massachusetts, Indiana, and Louisiana in one day at an estimated cost of $119,000. On the ground in Alexandria, Louisiana, activists describe attending an obscure airport authority board meeting to expose a detention complex they say holds as many as 8,000 people.

The program turns from enforcement to foreign policy with lawyer and author Dan Kovalik, speaking with Pacifica's Thomas O'Rourke. Kovalik argues Russia held a legal right of collective self-defense to intervene in Ukraine, and contends the Bolivarian Revolution in Venezuela remained vulnerable because Chávez never succeeded in enshrining socialism in the constitution.

In 1986, Jeff Cohen would ask rooms full of activists why they'd protest federal buildings and city halls but never a media outlet. That gap, he tells the Project Censored Show's 40th-anniversary episode, was exactly what FAIR was built to close. Janine Jackson, FAIR's program director and host of Counterspin, offers a sharper example: a Time Magazine environmental issue sponsored entirely by Ford Motor Company, with an editor openly laughing that of course they wouldn't cover car pollution.

Media scholar Nolan Higdon then works through ten myths about AI, arguing that large language models are statistical prediction engines rather than anything resembling intelligence and that roughly 95% of corporate AI pilots fail. A Yale Institution for Social and Policy Studies study he cites found AI-generated local news more convincing to audiences than actual local news — making fabricated content a persuasion problem, not just an accuracy one.

Demolition debris from the White House East Wing — containing arsenic — was dumped into East Potomac Golf Links at Hains Point without testing for two weeks, then seeded over with grass. That disclosure comes from Rebecca Miller of the DC Preservation League, one of several voices in David Rabin's Community Watch and Comment challenging Trump's plan to convert the century-old public course into a championship-level facility. Golfer Alex Dixon, cyclist Nailet Broadnax, and Washington Area Bicyclists Association emeritus member Peter Harnick detail how the proposal would reshape Ohio Drive for everyone using it. Green Party House candidate Sam Husseini describes standing up at a National Press Club event to challenge Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, being walked out by security, and receiving a lifetime ban from the club.

Post-Classical Ensemble music director Ángel Ordóñez, curator Murray Horwitz, and jazz director Chuck Redd preview their September 23rd concert at the Shakespeare Theatre. It opens with Gershwin's "I Got Rhythm" and draws on the Coltrane-Ellington album for an arrangement of Ellington's "In a Sentimental Mood.

Alonzo Turner-Bey spent 31 years, 6 months, 16 days, and 5 hours in prison. On the day of this interview, he signed closing documents on a 2,700-square-foot, four-bedroom house. While earning $18 a month inside, he had sent $25 money orders to WPFW every few months. He now serves as Director of Returning Citizens Affairs for Prince George's County under County Executive Aisha Braveboy, and he tells host Roach Brown what it actually takes to reconnect with family and the job market after decades away — including the concept of "freedom guilt" as part of post-incarceration syndrome.

That conversation moves into the concrete. Turner-Bey walks through a Prince George's County program subsidizing CDL licenses and a forthcoming incentive-to-hire program offering businesses up to $5,000.

Imani Naumodja of the African Party of Independence of Guinea and Cape Verde explains how Senegal's post-independence CFA franc kept 50% of foreign currency reserves in the French Treasury—and how a disputed election installed a president in Guinea-Bissau who secretly handed Chevron 90% of the country's offshore petroleum without parliamentary approval. That clip comes from the Black Alliance for Peace's "Shut Down AFRICOM" series, featured here by Voices With Vision hosts Nefer Freeman and Brother Craig. A Sovereign Media segment traces terrorist attacks in the Sahel rising from 1% of global incidents in 2007 to 47% in 2023, linking that trajectory directly to the 2011 NATO intervention in Libya and the U.S.-backed Ethiopian invasion of Somalia in 2006.

The episode rounds out with an AJ+ clip on the petrodollar system and a reflection from the late Thomas Blood McCreary. McCreary describes how the Black Liberation Army was never infiltrated because "the BLA picked you," and recalls retaliatory actions taken after the killings at Attica and the death of George Jackson.

Hosted by Mimi Rosenberg, this Labor Day special of *Building Bridges* opens with Cristóbal Ceballos, executive director of the DuPage Workers Center. He reports that roughly 40 to 50 percent of ICE raids in the Chicagoland area have been thwarted by patrol units — a 300-person network that is 60 to 70 percent Anglo, African American, and trans volunteers. Fewer than 3 percent of people taken by ICE, he adds, have violent criminal records.

The program then travels to a reparations rally in Bedford-Stuyvesant, Brooklyn, where speakers from the December 12th Movement, the NAACP Brooklyn Chapter, the New York Civil Liberties Union's Racial Justice Center, and Tsuru for Solidarity — a Japanese American group whose members describe being imprisoned in horse stalls at Santa Anita Racetrack during World War II — draw a line from the 2001 Durban Declaration's finding that the transatlantic slave trade was a crime against humanity to present-day issues: deed theft, the Rockefeller drug laws, and the displacement of 200,000 Black residents from New York City. New York City Public Advocate Jamani Williams closes by noting that his own reparations claim, tracing his family to Grenada, would properly go to England.

Mimi Rosenberg opens this Labor Day edition of *Building Bridges, Never Walls* by marking the first Labor Day without co-host Ken Nash — labor librarian, trade unionist, and 30-year presence on the program — who died the previous December. Ben Carroll of the Southern Workers Assembly then describes a network of more than 30 workers' assemblies across the South, along with a deliberate strategy of placing recruited workers inside electric vehicle and battery plants in North Carolina, South Carolina, and Georgia. That includes the world's largest BMW plant in Spartanburg, South Carolina, which ships 60 percent of its output overseas. Scholar and activist Abdul Akhalimat connects that new industrial landscape to Black community organizing.

Carroll also describes coordinating with other unions toward a general strike on May Day 2028. The hour closes with Cristóbal Savasos of the DuPage Workers Center, who offers a pointed fact: Chicago ranks first in the nation in food and beverage production, and 75 percent or more of the workers who harvest and manufacture that food lack documents.

Cassandra Wilson died the previous Wednesday in Jackson, Mississippi, where she was born in 1955, and host Katia devoted the full hour to her memory. Katia had worked for District Curators and produced what she believed was Wilson's first Washington, D.C. concert, in the fall of 1990. Wilson came back later to play a benefit for WPFW at Bethesda Blues and Jazz, and the last time Katia saw her was at the Cape Town Jazz Festival, where Wilson had a suite overlooking Table Mountain and was joined by longtime musicians Brandon Ross and Lonnie Plaxico.

The program moved through recordings spanning Wilson's career: early JMT label tracks "Electra Magnolia" and "Blue and Green," covers of Patsy Cline's "Crazy," Neil Young's "Harvest Moon," and Van Morrison's "Tupelo Honey," and "Vietnam Blues," "Fragile," and "Wichita Lineman." Between songs, Katia returned to the same observation — that what set Wilson apart was her ability to make any cover entirely her own.

Lifeguarding is probably 85% prevention," says a 59-year Asbury Park lifeguard explaining why drownings on guarded beaches are near zero. That claim opens an hour drawn from six podcasts across the Labor Radio Podcast Network. Two United Steelworkers members who work 2,150 feet underground at the Waste Isolation Pilot Plant in New Mexico — the only facility in the world that disposes of nuclear waste underground — describe it as "its own little city" with ambulances, electricians, and fire protection. A Calgary freelance journalist traces her turning point to an all-nighter at an architecture firm when a boss arrived at 3 a.m. demanding drawing changes, realizing then "this is why workers unionize."

Australian construction workers from the Concrete Gang react to police raiding union officials' homes, cops walking through asking "how did you afford this?" From there the hour turns to Colorado labor history: the 1927 Columbine Mine Massacre, the IWW's role in what historians call the most successful strike in Colorado history, and Big Bill Haywood's connection to the founding of the IWW. Hosted by Chris Garlock with Patrick Dixon and Harold Phillips.

Historian Donna Haverty Stack, author of *America's Forgotten Holiday*, opens the hour with a pointed correction: the first Labor Day parade in 1882 had socialist organizers at its core, and the AFL deliberately rewrote that history after the Haymarket bombing made radical associations toxic. From there, NewsGuild President John Schloess puts a number on the crisis — roughly 60% of the country's journalists cannot afford to live in the communities they cover, with some Guild members using food pantries. He traces an organizing wave running from a 10-person nonprofit newsroom in rural Maine to an 8-person shop in Washington State's Skagit Valley.

Mayda Rosenstein of UAW Local 2110 closes the *Labor Heritage Power Hour* by naming what has kept cultural-sector wages depressed: the assumption that museum work is "a labor of love," and that it helps to have a trust fund. A wave of organizing that began in 2018 has since brought in the Guggenheim, the Whitney, the MFA Boston, and the Met. This Labor Day special aired Monday, September 7, 2026.

Eighty-four percent of maternal deaths in Washington, D.C. are Black women, and the July closure of the postpartum and antepartum unit at Washington Hospital Center is making things worse. A community forum on the issue is set for September 9th at People's Church with mayor-elect Janice Lewis George. National Nurses United director Jazmyn reports that Medicare for All now has 115 House co-sponsors and 17 in the Senate — the most ever — with Senator Chris Van Hollen and Representatives April McClain Delaney and Sarah Elfreth signing on for the first time last December.

Calling in from the Greenbelt Labor Day parade, Metropolitan Washington AFL-CIO president Sam Epps reports that workers at Verbal Beginnings, a Rockville company serving people with developmental disabilities, have been on strike for seven weeks through Teamsters 639. A recent Gallup poll puts union favorability at 71% nationally, with 47 million workers who want to join one but cannot. To Heal DC host Joni Eisenberg anchors the two-hour Labor Day program.

Josh Williams has a pointed explanation for why Americans celebrate Labor Day in September instead of May 1st: labor leaders accepted the separation from International Workers' Day as a compromise after the holiday was branded communist during the McCarthy era. That history sets the frame for this Labor Day edition of *To Heal DC*, hosted by Joni.

Nurses Renelsa Caudill and Luke Filomena, both members of National Nurses United at Washington Hospital Center, take on Palantir — the data company already under contract with the Department of Defense and ICE — which is now selling hospital scheduling software under names like HCA Inspire and Timpani. They argue the software optimizes for profit rather than safe staffing ratios. Caudill and Filomena also detail Washington Hospital Center's closure of its maternity unit in July 2026, after which the hospital recorded 15 diversions of laboring patients to other facilities in just five weeks, including one diversion that lasted 24 hours.

When sharecropper Robert Lee Hill tried to organize the Progressive Farmers and Householders Union in Arkansas, white law enforcement and vigilantes responded by killing hundreds of African Americans in what became the 1919 Elaine Massacre. Journalist and attorney Faye McCray traces that violence alongside earlier history: Black caulkers organizing at the Washington Navy Yard in the 1830s, and 214 delegates at the 1869 Colored National Labor Union convention petitioning Congress to subdivide Southern public lands into 40-acre farms with low-interest loans — a petition Congress ignored.

That unbroken line of suppressed labor organizing carries into the present. Dr. Annie McClellan, author of *Beneath the Wage: Tips, Tasks, and Gigs in the Age of Service Work*, explains how the federal tipped minimum wage was frozen at $2.13 an hour under Bill Clinton in the 1990s, details how DoorDash and Uber have been caught applying customer tips toward their own guaranteed-wage obligations, and describes how AI is "deskilling" white-collar work much as machinery once deskilled manufacturing.

Ray McGovern — 27-year CIA analyst who briefed Reagan's five most senior national security advisers one-on-one — tells host Garland Nixon exactly how Victoria Nuland named "Yats" as the man to install in Ukraine during her intercepted call with Pyatt. McGovern walks through the evidence that the U.S. orchestrated the 2014 Ukrainian government overthrow, then explains why a peace deal initialed in Istanbul collapsed after Boris Johnson told Zelensky the West would not back it. He also recounts what he learned traveling to Russia with Oliver Stone: Putin's older brother died during the 900-day siege of Leningrad and lies buried in a mass grave holding an estimated 800,000 to 900,000 people. Nixon opens the hour with his own analysis, arguing that the three rules of winning an election all reduce to turning out your base, and predicting that whichever party loses the midterms will claim the election was stolen.

William Holden legally reported only $50,000 of his earnings from *The Bridge on the River Kwai* — and the government had quietly built the mechanism that made it possible. On *Darker Than Blue*, host Jacqueline Luqman argues that the famous 91% top marginal tax rate of the 1950s was essentially propaganda. The wealthiest 1% paid an effective federal income tax rate of just 16.9%, thanks to deliberate loopholes: accelerated depreciation on real estate, income-deferral arrangements nobody was penalized for using. The postwar boom's actual revenue came from a broadened middle-class tax base, corporate taxes, and Cold War defense spending.

Beneath that prosperity sat documented exclusions. Luqman examines specific income figures comparing white and Black family earnings in 1950 and 1960, the deliberate denial of GI Bill benefits to non-white veterans, and Cherokee and Navajo family incomes in the early 1950s. The picture that emerges shapes her closing argument: "tax the rich" is an insufficient political demand precisely because the rich have never been made to pay the rates advertised, and the government has always engineered the code to ensure they wouldn't.

shows.t: Resistance Radio with John and Regan
shows.desc: New York Governor Kathy Hochul extracted over half a billion dollars from Seneca gaming revenue and handed it to the billionaire owner of the Buffalo Bills for a new stadium — and Interior Secretary Deb Haaland said nothing. On *Resistance Radio*, host John Kane uses that sequence to anchor his argument that Native people living on their own territories should not vote in U.S. state or national elections. Seneca Nation President J.C. Seneca's endorsement of Republican gubernatorial candidate Bruce Blakeman — who supports the predictive markets Kane says could kill Native gaming — sharpens the case. Kane traces the legal framework behind federal power over Native peoples: the Doctrine of Christian Discovery, the trust doctrine, and the plenary powers doctrine, all developed under Chief Justice John Marshall, with Ruth Bader Ginsburg citing the Doctrine of Christian Discovery as recently as 2005. No Democrat in Congress, Kane notes, has ever publicly opposed any of the three doctrines. The episode also covers the Two Row Wampum as a framework for Native independence, the broken promise to include residential school history in New York State's curriculum, and the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act as an exercise of plenary powers that handed states leverage over Native casinos.

Bretton Louis, a professor of anthropology and African American and Africana studies at the University of Kentucky, calls the French indemnity imposed on Haiti outright extortion — 100 to 150 million gold francs demanded of a nation that had just freed itself. His Black Agenda Report article "Anti-Haitianism: A Hemispheric Rejection of Black Humanity" frames that debt as the opening move in a pattern stretching across centuries. Host Oscar Fernandez of the Latino Media Collective walks Louis through it: the 1915 U.S. Marine invasion that removed gold from Haitian banks, the 1980s HIV crisis, and the Supreme Court revocation of Temporary Protected Status for 300,000 to 350,000 Haitians. Saint-Domingue, Louis notes, once produced two-fifths of the world's sugar and nearly half of its coffee before that wealth was systematically stripped away.

From there the conversation moves to New York's Democratic primary, where "Haitian" was deployed as an anti-Black slur against congressional candidate Daryalisa Ávila Chevalier. Louis also examines how the Bahamas legally assigns Haitian nationality to children born there of Haitian parents, a citizenship structure he compares to policies in the Dominican Republic and the United States.

shows.t: Community Watch & Comment - Friday / The Local Station Board Show (Last Frid
shows.desc:
A federal judge's restraining order has blocked the Trump administration's plan to overhaul mail-in ballot distribution through the U.S. Postal Service — a plan a Postal Service whistleblower said was designed to fail and would disenfranchise voters before a ballot ever reached them. Ron Pinchback and Chip Jones host *Community Watch and Comment* (Friday Edition) as callers weigh in on whether to switch from mail-in to in-person voting.

A 77-year-old caller from Georgia recounts her father's 27 years at the Savannah post office. Another caller argues the country has been in a state of armistice since the Civil War, and that the vote is the "soft power" holding it together.

Elon Musk's Colossus 1 data center sits in Boxtown, a Freedmen's community in Memphis where the cancer rate is already four times the national average. It runs on natural gas turbines. Dr. Sokobe Wilson, founder of CEJA Inc. and professor at the University of Maryland School of Public Health, walks Cross the Producer through how that fits a pattern: hyperscale facilities consuming roughly five million gallons of water a day, and low-frequency noise that bounces over barriers and disrupts sleep for miles. Unlike high-frequency sound, that noise can't be blocked by walls or fences.

Wilson also draws a direct line from redlining to the two-week outage in Gary, Indiana, showing how power shutoffs land hardest on Black communities. The conversation closes on her 12th annual Environmental Justice and Health Disparities Symposium, "EJ 2076: Make America Just Again," running September 14–19 with keynotes from Justin Pearson and Peggy Shepard and in-person sessions at Bowie State University.

Vaughn Bennett, a DC firefighter turned chess instructor, says the DC Chess League excluded Black DC residents from tournaments, scholarships, and leadership for nearly 80 years — a history the US Chess Federation documented in a 2022 report. Bennett has taught more than 7,000 children across 25 years. Baba Oso, a founding member of Kankuran West African Dance and Music Company, traces the banning of the drum under slavery to its role as a communication and healing tool, and previews the group's 43rd-anniversary performance at Crampton Auditorium at Howard University. Natani Victoria Lim of Embracing Equity, an Albuquerque-based nonprofit, describes its virtual workshops on building cultures of belonging in schools and a debate over whether to strip equity-related language from its website under current political pressure — a debate the team resolved by keeping the name and the mission intact. This episode of *#YouMustLearn* airs Thursday, September 3, 2026.

Vicente Martinez spent eight years as a Starbucks barista in Denton, Texas, and qualified for company health insurance exactly once. Starbucks controls the scheduling that determines eligibility. Martinez and fellow bargaining delegate Jasmine Lolly of Buffalo, New York, join host Renee Bowser to explain why Starbucks Workers United has called a nationwide boycott, citing hundreds of alleged unfair labor practices and stores running five workers during peak hours instead of thirteen.

The union has also pressed to remove silica powder from blended-drink recipes after workers reported lung irritation. Still unresolved at the bargaining table: a $17 starting wage, guaranteed minimum staffing of three workers on the floor, and just-cause protections. The boycott pledge is at boycottstarbucks.net.

Dr. Suzanne Claxton grew up with an Iranian adoptive father, lived in Iran in 1975–76, watched poverty grind Black residents in D.C., and saw a third-grade teacher in southern Oklahoma shame Native children. Those experiences shaped her rejection of white identity before she had language for it. In this conversation with host Jon Jeter of *Short Money: Dissecting Racial Capitalism*, Claxton — an adjunct philosophy professor specializing in Heidegger — works through what it means to identify, or refuse to identify, as white.

The conversation moves from Theodore Allen's *The Invention of the White Race* and AOC's recent distancing from defund-the-police language to Plato's Allegory of the Cave as a metaphor for racial mythology. It arrives, finally, at Heidegger's concept of *poiesis* — the poet and storyteller as the figures most capable of seeing beyond "the merely actual into the realm of the possible" — as a framework for why personal narrative is indispensable to social transformation.

Detroit's riverfront holds North America's largest public artwork dedicated to organized labor: *Transcending*, 63 feet of steel arches, bronze reliefs, and workers' quotations. Michigan Labor History Society guides John Dick and Dave Elsila walk Chris Garlock and his listeners through it in this episode of *Labor Heritage Power Hour*. From there, Dick turns to Hitsville, USA, where Freddie Gorman — a Detroit letter carrier and part-time songwriter — supplied the hook that turned Berry Gordy's unfinished song into "Please Mr. Postman," Motown's first number one hit. Gorman was then edged out of the Holland-Dozier-Gorman songwriting team and returned to carrying mail until retirement.

Harvard historian Kelly Goodman picks up the thread of Detroit labor history by tracing the teachers' 43-day strike of 1973, which began on Labor Day in resistance to merit pay and the automation of classroom work, through to the Chicago Teachers Union strikes of 2012 and 2019, and on to a 2022 Massachusetts ballot initiative that imposed a 4% surtax on incomes above $1 million to fund free community college and restore education cuts. The hour closes with singer and activist Hallie Hammer, who names "Union Maid" as her favorite labor song for putting union women at the center of the fight.

Donghao Wang, a postdoc at the University of Michigan, jumped from a university building hours after being questioned by a federal agent. His case is one of several Megan Russell details in a Code Pink webinar on the China Is Not Our Enemy campaign, whose origins co-founder Jodi Evans traces to a surge in anti-China sentiment she noticed on her Facebook page in late 2019.

The episode opens, though, before that — with public testimony before the Los Angeles Unified School District board, where speakers from Code Pink, Jewish Voice for Peace, and CAIR urged members to reject a settlement in Brandeis v. California. That lawsuit would hand the Brandeis Center — led by former Trump appointee Kenneth Marcus — authority over teacher training on antisemitism and a seat on a committee reviewing ethnic studies curriculum. Code Pink Radio host Marcy Winograd presents both segments.

The NBA just hit Steve Ballmer with a $30 million fine, a one-year ban, and five consecutive first-round draft picks stripped from the Los Angeles Clippers — 2029 through 2033 — after the team paid companies to hand Kawhi Leonard no-show sponsorship contracts as a way around the salary cap. Kawhi's Uncle Dennis received a five-year ban of his own. Dave Zirin, Chuck Modiano, and Kevin McNutt tear through every layer of the punishment on *The Collision*.

The episode also marks ten years since Colin Kaepernick first took a knee, and the hosts take up Howard Bryant's argument that today's players have been effectively silenced into writing messages on their cleats. Zirin turns the lens on himself: his book *The Kaepernick Effect* got it wrong, he says, by expecting Kaepernick's blackballing to become an animating spirit for other athletes — when it became instead a ghost tale used to warn players to toe the line. Chuck Modiano closes with an eye on the upcoming FIBA Women's World Cup and women's basketball.

Alice Madison kept a secret for years: Jane Kenyon's letters described a relationship with her former doctor, and Madison redacted those passages from copies sent to editor Chad Ricklesworth while Donald Hall was still alive. Hall's own writing had made the marriage "seem very idyllic," she tells host E. Ethelbert Miller — but the letters reveal a "questing and somewhat restless and very intelligent, discontented spirit." The conversation moves through Kenyon's years on Nardil and Prozac and the three-way writing workshop Madison ran with Kenyon and Joyce Pesteroff, all of it orbiting the book at the center of the discussion: *What Clever Friends: The Selected Letters of Jane Kenyon and Alice Madison*, edited by Ricklesworth and published by the University of Michigan Press.

Madison also traces her own education as a fiction writer to coverless books by Tillie Olsen and Grace Paley, picked up from an illegal discount bookstore.

Eugenia Charles had been Yvon Florival's agent for years, first meeting him when he designed sets for Théâtre Mapou productions, including a staging of a Jacques Roumain play. Florival died August 25, 2026, at 72. He had won a 1992 Congressional Black Caucus Spouse Quincy Jones Award and shown work at the White House Eisenhower Executive Building, the National Museum of American History, and the French Embassy in Washington. Charles devotes much of this episode of *Konbit Lakay* to his life and career.

She also follows the case of Pierre Damas Belle, a recent high school graduate and JROTC member in Springfield, Ohio, who was fitted with an ICE ankle bracelet during his first week of college and fell into depression — his father holds government immigration policy responsible. From there, Charles walks Haitian community members through concrete steps: finding a licensed immigration attorney before a crisis, understanding the new public charge test taking effect September 18th, and seeking mental health support. USCIS will now review credit reports as part of green card applications.

Hamza of Washington Area Road Skaters, Ashley of Skate Baltimore and We Are Skate DC, and Bree of Roll Club Delaware sat down during Skate DC Weekend to talk concrete logistics: beginner clinics, volunteer marshals, corkers holding intersections, and free Wednesday-night meetups where the only requirement is bringing your own skates. Entry-level skates start at $200, and Delaware lost its Ellesmere Skating Center in the early 2000s, sending state skaters to DC and Philadelphia just to find community. The three also name hostile architecture directly — skate blockers added to Freedom Plaza's ledges after renovation. Their vision runs toward skater-designed public spaces and school programming built on the institutional support other physical activities already receive.

The episode also features the Pride Purpose Power Top 5 Countdown and an open mic drop mix from DC-born DJ Tay. Produced by the Freedom Futures Collective.

Marcellus Queen once threw his keys to a detained youth mid-fight — eight staff against one kid — so the boy could lock himself in a safe room. That act cost Queen his job at D.C.'s Youth Services Center, where children with serious mental health conditions share space with the general population, staff are undertrained, and one worker can be responsible for 15 kids with no padded rooms in sight. Queen, now founder and executive director of Representation for the Bottom, speaks with host Sam PK Collins about those conditions and about losing his longtime collaborator Shama King, whom he found dead the day after the two of them handed out 300 pairs of Jordans to youth at a back-to-school event.

The episode opens with local news: D.C. mayoral nominee Janice Lewis George's eight-ward listening tour and a D.C. Council hearing set for September 24th on the Vaccine Administration Protection Amendment Act, which would shield local healthcare providers from liability for vaccine-related injuries.

Israel always means you cease and we fire," says Beirut-based analyst Leith Marouf on Zain Al-Amin's show — his explanation for why Hezbollah had held back for more than three weeks before launching an offensive drone strike on Israeli troops near Ali al-Tahrir Hill the day of the broadcast. Marouf tallies what he describes as three years of accumulated Israeli military losses: more than 70 percent of its tanks gone, roughly 80 percent of its Humvees, Iron Dome batteries destroyed in the north, and U.S. PAC-3 stockpiles in Jordan drawn down 30 percent in a single day of exchanges with Iran. Lebanese President Joseph Aoun's invocation of the late Imam Musa Sadr at a commemoration ceremony drew a public rebuke from the Amal Movement, Speaker Nabih Berri, and Hezbollah, who disputed the reference. An NBC News interview captured on camera the beating of Palestinian woman Aida Ahmed Abdullah by Israeli settlers in the West Bank. Israeli investors are quietly acquiring properties and shoreline in Cyprus and along the Kalamata coast of Greece.

Destiny Blackwell is organizing Amazon workers in Garner, North Carolina with CAUSE (Carolina Amazonians United for Solidarity and Empowerment). She describes coworkers sleeping in their cars and missing rent while working for what she calls the richest company in the world, and argues that Amazon's tax cuts for employing HBCU students and disabled workers are subsidies that should go directly to workers' wages. Chris Hollis of Black Workers for Justice and UE 150 recounts how Virginia Beach municipal workers staged an illegal wildcat stoppage at Waste Management on a Wednesday — the day upper-class residents needed trash pickup — and won new equipment, a 10% raise, and eventually a $15 minimum wage.

Historian Robin D.G. Kelley traces Jim Crow segregation and right-to-work laws as ruling-class responses to interracial organizing, focusing on the largely African American female Local 22 of the Food, Tobacco, and Agriculture and Allied Workers Union at RJ Reynolds in Winston-Salem, which fought sexual harassment and ran voter registration drives before the Taft-Hartley Act of 1947 stripped unions of much of that power. This Labor Day edition of *AfricaNow!*, hosted by Mwiza Munthali, draws from the program's archive around the Southern Workers Power Program's first point: the right to organize, collectively bargain, and strike.

Mildred Taylor says a warden at Stewart Detention Center told her husband Rodney — a double amputee detained there for 471 days — "this is not Uber Eats" when he requested charged prosthetics, a shower stool, and appropriate meals. Each time Mildred spoke to media, those accommodations were taken away. Her testimony anchors a Black August panel hosted by the Black Alliance for Just Immigration, alongside Manuela, a Cameroonian woman detained at Adelanto, who describes being chained, fed spoiled food, and threatened with solitary confinement for refusing meals, then monitored after release through ankle GPS and the BI SmartLink app. Shirley Leslie of Critical Resistance connects those conditions to the prison industrial complex and details prisoner-led hunger strikes that won a reduction of indefinite solitary confinement in California.

The program then turns to Esther Arma, founder of the Arma Institute of Emotional Justice, who defines the "emotional mammy" as a Black woman expected to center the feelings of white people and all men regardless of the cost to her own health. Her short film *Goodbye to the Emotional Mammy* screens at the Black Women Nonprofit Leaders Forum in Alhambra, California on September 3rd, organized by Dawn Brown of EmpowerHer Institute.

Former Washington, D.C. Mayor Sharon Pratt and her daughter Dr. Aimee Dixon Anthony, director of the documentary series *The Capitol*, joined host Dr. Faye Williams on *Wake Up and Stay Woke* to discuss what the film recovers: that Benjamin Banneker — a free African American whose astronomical knowledge came from a West African tradition — used a photographic memory to reconstruct Pierre L'Enfant's plans after L'Enfant was fired and walked off with the original drawings, and that the capital ended up on the Potomac rather than in Pennsylvania partly because slaveholders feared Pennsylvania's law emancipating any enslaved person held there longer than six months. The episode also featured Talib Muhammad, a Howard-trained engineer and lawyer who described his legal fight after the D.C. Board of Elections gave him 30 minutes to complete 311 pages of petition forms — time the court later confirmed was treated differently than what Democratic candidates received — with a ruling issued just the day before the broadcast. The premiere of *The Capitol* was scheduled for September 9th at the Hirshhorn Museum, with streaming on WETA+ the following day.

Mississippi held back Nolan Wells's brain and trachea from the second pathologist — and forensic expert Dr. Nicole Jackson says that's not standard protocol. Wells was 18, a Black college football player who vanished July 4th on Horn Island off the Gulf of Mississippi; his three white companions came home, and his body turned up on the beach two days later. Host Verna Avery Brown brings Jackson onto **What's at Stake** to explain what those retained tissues would reveal about strangulation, aspiration, or blunt force trauma, and why their withholding from Dr. Roger Mitchell matters. Jackson has performed upwards of 2,000 autopsies and served as medical examiner for Chicago and Seattle.

The question of what a grand jury will do with any of this brings in law professor Justin Hansford, executive director of the Thurgood Marshall Civil Rights Center at Howard University. Drawing on his time near Ferguson during the 2014 Michael Brown grand jury, Hansford lays out how Mississippi prosecutors hold near-total control over what a secret, transcript-free grand jury sees. If no indictment comes back, he says, the Wells family's only remaining path runs through the Department of Justice.

Amina Claudine Myers corrects the record mid-conversation: she was not a co-founder of the AACM, as host Katia had introduced her, but an early member. The actual founders included Muhal Richard Abrams and Steve McCall, and it was Ajaramu who gave Myers her African name and brought her into the organization. DC pianist Janelle Gill traveled to San Francisco specifically to meet Myers backstage after an Emmanuel Wilkins residency at SFJAZZ, arriving with Palo Santo perfume and a proposal for a collaboration — one that grew from Gill's artist-in-residency at the DC Jazz Festival.

Myers also discusses two works in progress: a Harriet Tubman symphony and a piece about Navajo code writers. The conversation leads up to their joint performance on September 5th at the DC Jazz Festival.

Akili Shakur is calling from her car — still without power two weeks after a derecho hit Gary, Indiana on August 11th — because NIPSCO never put Gary on its power-restoration list. Host Anthony Rogers-Wright adds context: Lake County, where Gary sits, received $715,404 across three federally declared disasters between 2011 and 2024, roughly $1 per resident, against $84,871,273 — $191 per person — for Santa Barbara County, California over the same period, figures drawn from a Harvard Kennedy School study. Shakur also points to Gary's mayor, Eddie Melton, whose past employment with NIPSCO she says explains his slow criticism of the utility.

*Black Agenda Report* executive editor Margaret Kimberley takes up the case of Venezuelan diplomat Alex Saab, freed in a prisoner swap and returned to Venezuela in 2023, only to be handed back to the United States in May and publicly smeared by Venezuelan officials. Kimberley reads that reversal as proof that the U.S. is now "giving direct orders to the Venezuelans" and that Venezuela has lost its sovereignty.

Sam Husseini was physically removed from a State Department briefing by Antony Blinken, then banned from the National Press Club after questioning Chuck Schumer about Israel at a Public Citizen anti-corruption event. Black Agenda Report host Margaret Kimberley talks with him about his Green Party challenge to Maryland's 4th District incumbent Glenn Ivey, who has taken more than $7 million from AIPAC and holds at least $100,000 of his own money in NVIDIA.

Akili Shakur calls in from Gary, Indiana — speaking from her car because her power is out. A derecho knocked out electricity across the city for two weeks, and Gary, a 70% Black city in a red state, was left off NIPSCO's restoration list entirely. It was Black Lives Matter grassroots, not the utility, that distributed dry ice so residents could keep food and medicine cold.

The Black Panther Party ran sickle cell screenings in the late 1960s and helped pressure Congress into passing the Sickle Cell Control Act. That history comes from Barbara Harrison, Assistant Director for Community Outreach and Education at Howard University's Center for Sickle Cell Disease, which the Act funded into existence in 1972. Harrison traces the disease's geographic spread directly to the transatlantic slave trade and lays out a stark funding gap: cystic fibrosis, affecting roughly 30,000 Americans, has received three to four times more research funding than sickle cell, which affects 100,000, and has 12 to 13 approved drugs compared to sickle cell's three.

Host Mazi Mutafa also sits down with actor Jacob Ming-Trent about his one-man show *How Shakespeare Saved My Life* at the Folger Theatre, then with MCs Do Me Right and Night Train 357, who discuss hip-hop history, their collaborations with pioneers like Chuck D, and an upcoming show at The Pocket in DC.

Dan Kovalik once sued Coca-Cola, Drummond Mining, and Occidental Petroleum under the Alien Tort Claims Act for allegedly sponsoring paramilitary violence against union members. He tells Pacifica's Thomas O'Rourke why Colombia's newly elected president — a former cartel lawyer nicknamed El Tigre — won through voter suppression, diaspora votes, and frustration over armed-group violence. U.S. military aid of $10 billion produced zero reduction in coca production. Kovalik had accompanied Colombian President Gustavo Petro to Washington in February.

That organizing thread — institutions that resist accountability — runs through the rest of the hour. National Nurses Union members rallied outside Palantir's former Palo Alto headquarters, accusing the company of using AI tools to cut hospital staffing and of helping ICE detain a union nurse colleague. Philadelphia Teamsters Local 623 secretary-treasurer Richard Hooker Jr. — the first Black leader in his local's history — describes how his Fearless slate filed election-fraud charges against Teamsters President Sean O'Brien that the Department of Labor received, reviewed, and left unresolved.

Flock Safety pushed a software update that silently turned its drones into flying license plate readers — no new contracts, no public notice. Beryl Lipton of the Electronic Frontier Foundation explains how that happened, tracing it back to drone-as-first-responder programs that began in Chula Vista, California in 2018 and now dispatch drones to every call for service, including reports of "suspicious persons." That pattern of expanding surveillance without public accountability carries directly into the second conversation, where Ian Head of the Center for Constitutional Rights' Open Records Project describes filing a FOIA request with ICE in December 2020 and waiting four years for a response.

When the Trump administration placed the HHS FOIA office on leave to halt document production in active litigation, multiple judges ruled that agencies cannot evade FOIA by firing their FOIA officers. Host Eleanor Goldfield leads both conversations on *The Project Censored Radio Show*.

Richard Pryor walked into Lorton prison, saw a gymnasium packed with roughly 1,000 incarcerated men, and wept. Roach Brown, host of *Crossroads Today*, was there, and he tells it live from Ben's Chili Bowl on this unscheduled open-phone hour, hosted by David Rabin after both booked guests canceled. Pryor went on to arrange for Brown's prison drama group, the Inner Voices, to perform at the Apollo Theater, Sing Sing, and Walpole State Prison.

The open phone draws callers who press Brown on returning-citizen voting rights in D.C. and Maryland, including the history of Public Law 179, introduced by Arrington Dixon in 1979 or 1980, and a Pennsylvania case where a woman received 53 years under felony murder rules for acting as a lookout. Brown also addresses the unmarked graves found at the Cheltenham boys' school in Maryland and shares the story of a man who had not encountered an automatic-flush toilet or a cellphone in 50 years.

Andrea James told host Roach Brown she refused to run as a Democrat for one reason: "I need people to focus on issues." She argues that the Democratic governor and legislature in Massachusetts have failed Black and working-class communities, and are pushing ahead with a $350 million women's prison built to hold roughly 200 people. James is running for governor of Massachusetts as an independent. She gathered more than 11,000 signatures, clearing the 10,000 required to reach the November general election ballot.

A former attorney who served federal prison time for wire fraud, she went on to found the National Council for Incarcerated and Formerly Incarcerated Women and Girls. She also traced her family's seven generations in Boston, including her grandmother Corinne Alleyne, who broke the color barrier as the city's first Black nurse.

The August 25, 2026 edition of *Voices with Vision* opens with a recorded commentary by political prisoner Mumia Abu-Jamal, who spent 28 years on death row in solitary confinement, including eight years in isolation for refusing to cut his hair. From there the program turns to Roger Wareham, a human rights lawyer and December 12th Movement organizer, who spent more than a decade learning from Cuban diplomats how to fight over semicolons and hyphens in UN language. He walks through how that effort secured the 2001 Durban Declaration, which named the transatlantic slave trade a crime against humanity and established that reparations are owed. He details how the U.S. and Israel walked out of that conference, then tracks a March 2026 UN resolution that passed 123–3 — the United States, Israel, and Argentina voting against — and strengthened the declaration further.

The program closes at Pan-African Community Action's People's Community Health Walk in Hyattsville, where organizers offered free blood pressure screenings, fresh produce from a local farm, hygiene kits, and a session on how to read lab results. Hosts Nephthys Freeman and Brother Craig present the show.

Kasisi Sadiki opens by explaining why her father Kamau Sadiki keeps being denied parole: he refused to tell authorities where Assata Shakur was hiding. Host Mimi Rosenberg convenes six women with roots in the Young Lords and Black Panther movements for this special edition of *Building Bridges: Women on the Liberation Road*. A recorded clip of Assata Shakur describes the torture of Sekou Odinga — cigarettes extinguished on his body, a beating severe enough that his spleen was removed. From there the conversation turns to *Freedom Ain't Free*, a jazz, poetry, and spoken-word CD originally made as a fundraiser for Odinga.

The guests range across Young Lords cadre work, COINTELPRO, and Puerto Rico's ongoing displacement crisis before arriving at a question that runs through all of it: who counts as a political prisoner. They make the case for redefining the category to include women like Joanne Little, who acted in self-defense.

Rosemary Mealy left her job as a child psychologist in Philadelphia, drove to Chicago, and walked into the blood-soaked rooms where Fred Hampton and Mark Clark were assassinated. That visit ended her career and began something else. This special edition of *Building Bridges*, hosted by Mimi Rosenberg, gathers six women across two generations of Black and Puerto Rican liberation movements. Among them is Olga Robles Toro, who joined the Young Lords at 16 after organizing against the systematic defunding of Bronx schools, and Kasisi Sadiki, who describes arriving at a Georgia prison with her mother and children to visit her father — imprisoned former Black Panther Kamau Sadiki — only to be turned away at the gate. That was the moment she committed to building a campaign for his release.

The hour is framed as a Black August tribute, calling the names of movement ancestors while pressing the question of what women inside these organizations had to fight for even among their own comrades.

At thirteen, Mumia Abu-Jamal was beaten by white men and a police officer after opposing a George Wallace rally in Philadelphia in 1968. Ambrose Lane Jr., host of *To the East*, traces what followed: Abu-Jamal organizing the Philadelphia chapter of the Black Panther Party as a teenager, building a radio journalism career that put him across from Bob Marley and Alex Haley, and then the 1981 shooting of officer Daniel Faulkner and forty-plus years of appeals that converted his death sentence to life without parole. Assata Shakur appears in a recorded statement explaining why Abu-Jamal's case mattered.

Lane's Black history segment covers August 31 through September 6, moving from Gabriel Prosser's 1800 slave revolt in Virginia to the 1885 killing of 28 Chinese workers by white miners in Rock Springs, Wyoming, and the Lincoln Motion Picture Company's 1919 release of *A Man's Duty*, identified as the first feature-length African American film.

Bob Dole took to the Senate floor and threatened NPR's funding — and according to Noelle Hanrahan, founder of Prison Radio, that threat is the direct reason prisons banned recording equipment. Hanrahan tells host Katea Stitt how Democracy Now dropped from 26 stations to 13 after it began airing commentaries by Mumia Abu-Jamal.

Abu-Jamal himself then calls in from SCI Mahanoy. His PhD dissertation takes up the transformation between the man who wrote *Black Skin, White Masks* and the man who wrote *The Wretched of the Earth* — two versions of Frantz Fanon — and from there he moves to fear as a tool of empire, the ICE killing of Alex Preddy in Minneapolis, and AI as a mechanism for concentrating wealth among the super-rich. The episode is part of WPFW's Black August special, broadcast Monday, August 31, 2026.

Felipe Luciano opens with one detail: Denise Oliver-Velez once walked out of a police car after an arrest at the First Spanish Methodist Church. It sets the tone for what he tells host Fahima Sekh about a life that shaped American political history. Luciano — poet, Emmy Award-winning journalist, and co-founder of both the Young Lords and the Last Poets — describes how Oliver-Velez, an African American woman fluent in Puerto Rican political history, became the only woman on the Young Lords' Central Committee. She helped draft what became the Patient's Bill of Rights following the group's takeover of Lincoln Hospital's nurses' residence and illustrated the party's newspaper *Palante*.

The work didn't stop there. Oliver-Velez co-founded the Black Filmmakers Foundation with her first husband Warrington Hudlin, taught Caribbean diaspora history at SUNY New Paltz, and worked to get people into treatment during the crack epidemic. She was also a founding member and first program director of WPFW. She died July 15th.

Gabriel Prosser's plan was precise: seize the armory, kidnap the governor or James Madison, and trade them for freedom. Lawrence Hamm, chair of the People's Organization for Progress in New Jersey, walks host Joni through that 1800 Virginia rebellion and the execution of roughly 26 of its participants — pardoned posthumously by Tim Kaine centuries later. From there the two move through Black August's bloodier landmarks: the Peekskill riots of August 27 and September 4, 1949, when racist mobs and police coordinating with the Klan attacked concertgoers at Paul Robeson's concerts. Emmett Till's killers confessed in a paid *Life* magazine interview and were acquitted by an all-white jury — which is exactly why the March on Washington was scheduled for August 28th.

Hamm connects the ongoing power outage in Gary, Indiana to that city's role hosting the 1972 National Black Political Convention, and the hour closes on Hurricane Katrina's August 29, 2005 anniversary.

Felipe Luciano — poet, co-founder of The Last Poets, Young Lords activist — says losing Johanna Fernández left him unable to leave his house: "a sister from another mother." This August 31, 2026 episode of *To Heal DC*, hosted by Joni, marks Black August with an hour-long tribute to Fernández, the scholar-activist who died at 55 and wrote *The Young Lords: A Radical History*. Luciano credits her as the first to push Puerto Ricans to seriously engage with Mumia Abu-Jamal's case in the 1990s.

Pam Africa, chairwoman of the International Concerned Family and Friends of Mumia Abu-Jamal, describes how Fernández organized a packed event for Mumia at Philadelphia's Constitutional Center, and walked into a hospital unannounced to find him during a diabetic crisis. Historian Robyn Spencer-Antoine, who trained alongside Fernández at Columbia in the 1990s, joins Zaid Mohammed of the Malcolm X Commemoration Committee and DC community radio figure Kimon Freeman, who reads aloud a personal inscription Fernández wrote in his copy of her book in May 2021.

Julianne Malveaux hosts two conversations on the last day of Black August. The first is with Dr. Felipe Hinojosa of Baylor University, a close collaborator of the late scholar Johanna Fernández, whose book *The Young Lords* won the major awards of the Organization of American Historians and drew on nearly 100 pages of footnotes and repeated oral-history interviews with movement members. Hinojosa describes how Fernández resisted reducing the Young Lords to "the brown version of the Black Panther Party" and how she documented the group's machismo while insisting on the movement's significance in its own right — including the Young Lords' development of a patient bill of rights during their occupation of Lincoln Hospital.

The second guest, Chrissy Williams, whose great-aunt was a survivor of the 1921 Tulsa massacre, describes finding over 60 bodies at Oaklawn Cemetery, the city's reburial of massacre victims while a white man in a kilt played bagpipes over the remains, and the discovery of Greenwood artifacts stored in boxes next to a trash can in a janitor's closet. Her $1.5 million Mellon Foundation-funded Vernon Witness Experience and Museum is being built in the basement of Historic Vernon AME Church, where handmade nails bent eastward from the force of the bombing still hold the structure up.

Retired Army Colonel Lawrence Wilkerson, who served as Chief of Staff to Secretary of State Colin Powell, tells host Garland Nixon that a recent report found U.S. sanctions have killed 38 million people worldwide since 1972 — half of them women and children. He recalls Madeleine Albright saying on the record that 500,000 Iraqi children's deaths were worth it to remove Saddam Hussein. Wilkerson assesses that the U.S. military has expended most of its conventional munitions, that Iran destroyed American radar and surveillance infrastructure across Bahrain, Jordan, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and Kuwait, and that carriers have been kept 1,000 nautical miles out in the Indian Ocean because Iran's hypervelocity missiles could sink them.
