Nixon and Wilkerson take up Congress's failure on war powers, the $32 million spent to defeat Tom Massie, and Wilkerson's warning that January 6th was a coup attempt whose organizers have since studied their own mistakes.

In Louisiana, the same day Union troops withdrew, white residents burned freedmen's schoolhouses to the ground. That detail comes from W.E.B. Du Bois's *Black Reconstruction in America, 1860–1880*, and host Jacqueline Luqman reads aloud at length from it — specifically the chapter "Founding the Public School" — in response to listeners who challenged his previous show's argument that American opposition to tax-funded social programs is rooted in racial hatred. The evidence Du Bois marshals keeps accumulating: four young men in Adams County, Mississippi conspired to murder a Black school's teacher; in North Carolina, two women teachers were told by a county sheriff they would not be allowed to leave their steamer; North Carolina collected $136,076 for education in 1870 and delivered only $38,931 to the Department of Education.

Luqman also foregrounds Du Bois's conclusion that "the state public school system was formed mainly by Negro Reconstruction governments" — a history Du Bois argues was systematically suppressed by white historians.

shows.t: Resistance Radio with John and Regan
shows.desc: Resistance Radio host John Kane argues that the four Native Democratic candidates running in current U.S. elections — Peggy Flanagan (Minnesota Senate), Mary Peltola (Alaska Senate), Sharice Davids (Kansas House), and Deb Haaland (New Mexico governor) — are American candidates, not Native ones, and should be understood as such. He focuses at length on Haaland's tenure as Interior Secretary, contending that she deliberately delayed federal involvement while New York Governor Kathy Hochul froze the Seneca Nation's bank accounts, forcing the Nation to pay nearly $600 million — most of which went to billionaire Buffalo Bills owner Terry Pegula for a new stadium — and that Haaland's promised rule changes to address the imbalance in the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act never materialized before she left office. Kane also breaks down the Seneca Nation's upcoming tribal elections, where outgoing president J.C. Seneca is proposing to keep half of an escrow account built from slot revenue while still paying the other half to the state in hopes of eventually securing mobile gaming rights — an arrangement Kane argues is legally unnecessary and financially harmful to a nation where 30% of the population still lives below the poverty line.

Lorenzo Salgado Araujo's son Ronaldo told a press conference his father ran from two unmarked cars because he thought someone was stealing his work tools — not to evade ICE. Had the agents shown any law enforcement emblem, Ronaldo said, "he would have complied." Host Oscar Fernandez of the Latino Media Collective spent the hour on the July 2025 ICE shooting deaths of Araujo in Houston's Magnolia Park neighborhood and Juan Sebastian Durán Guerrero in Biddeford, Maine. Guests Egberto Willis, host of a Houston Pacifica program, and freelance writer Arturo Dominguez walked through video evidence they say contradicts the official account given by U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz, then described protests and competing responses from the Houston mayor and Harris County DA. Journalist Laura Jadid, heard in a clip, described receiving a tentative ICE job offer — including a final position as a deportation officer — without completing a background check or signing a domestic violence waiver. The ex-wife of David Briette, the ICE agent identified in the Maine shooting, said in audio that Briette asked her to lie about his character and that she had witnessed abuse directed at both her and their daughter.

shows.t: Community Watch & Comment - Friday / The Local Station Board Show (Last Frid
shows.desc:
Dr. Ron Daniels called in live from the National Mall on the anniversary of the 1963 March on Washington — standing, he said, where he had also stood as a young activist 63 years earlier. He was there for a new march organized by the National Action Group with Al Sharpton, and reported buses arriving from Houston, New York, and elsewhere. A councilman-at-large made a pitch for DC statehood, and Black Women Wins drew a strong response from the crowd.

Host Ryan Pinchback and co-host Chip Jones then opened the phones. An 86-year-old who had been present at the 1963 march called in, as did a listener who argued the current march suffered from poor publicity. Another caller invoked Lenin's *Left-Wing Communism: An Infantile Disorder* to challenge what he called a purist streak in today's left that dismisses voting and elections.

Heather McTeer Toney tells host Brittany Bell-Serrat that petrochemical pollution is "if not already, the number one driver of increased emissions." Toney — former mayor of Greenville, Mississippi, former EPA Region 4 Administrator, and now Executive Director of Beyond Petrochemicals — describes how her organization works in Louisiana, Texas, Ohio, Pennsylvania, and West Virginia by following communities that identify themselves as overburdened, rather than "parachuting in." She was serving as mayor during Hurricane Katrina and watched displaced residents arrive in Greenville, and that experience shapes her argument that race and economic inequality cannot be separated from climate response.

The conversation moves through Alpha Kappa Alpha Sorority, the HBCU Climate Change Consortium, and Black churches as entry points for broadening climate organizing. Toney also addresses the deaths of Nolan Wells and Tayshia Fortune and, as the mother of two Black sons, the need to break "the repetition of the behavior".

Toussaint L'Ouverture was lured to a meeting under a false promise of safety, captured, and left to die — and a lieutenant "a little over 20" finished the revolution and declared Haitian independence in 1804. Dr. Daryl Howard opens *#YouMustLearn* with that account before welcoming Baba Ayize and Dr. Azoma Miller, a professor of African American Studies at Ohio University, to discuss a Black August webinar they are co-hosting through the Asen of Kemet, an African-centered fraternity founded at Morehouse as an alternative to the Divine Nine. The two argue that George Jackson, Assata Shakur, and Fred Hampton are largely absent from mainstream education. Ongoing efforts to remove exhibits about George Washington enslaving Africans at his Philadelphia house, they contend, make erasure active, not passive.

That conversation about what gets left out gives way to a look at what Words, Beats & Life is building on the ground. Mwiza Munthali, executive director of the nearly 25-year-old hip-hop nonprofit, describes their upcoming Game Day — a free intergenerational event built around chess, checkers, dominoes, Uno, spades, mahjong, and video games. This summer was the first since 2020 when young people in their programs told staff they had made friends with kids from other neighborhoods they had never met.

Ryan Marshall, organizer and Joint Apprenticeship Training Committee member of Ironworkers Local 5, opens with a striking promise: members who work thirty years can retire on a pension that pays more than their working wage, plus an annuity that may reach $1 million. The union's four-year apprenticeship requires only seventh-grade math and no high school diploma. Marshall's own credits include the Frederick Douglass Bridge, the Wharf, and the upcoming Commander Stadium. He also describes a federal Department of Labor investigation into a job site where non-union ironworkers were misclassified as independent contractors — a problem he says affects 23 percent of construction workers in Washington, D.C.

Host Renee Bowser closes with news from a different front: an arbitrator ruled in favor of Washington Post opinion journalist Karen Attia, finding she did not commit gross misconduct and rejecting the Post's attempt to hold her responsible for threats made against her by outside actors.

When Olinka Greene and Geechee Yaw gave a Juneteenth talk at Jefferson City Correctional Center in Missouri, they spoke about the 1878 Great Fireburn of St. Croix — the uprising in which women burned down plantations while chanting "more fire." The phrase spread through the prison population so fast that administrators held a formal meeting, banned inmates from saying or writing it, and barred both speakers from returning. The two had arrived to find over 100 inmates who'd decorated the gymnasium with a hand-drawn Black historical timeline stretching from ancient Egypt to the present, including a freehand poster-board map of all the continents drawn by one of the prisoners. The prison's NAACP chapter, Greene and Yaw said, was more politically radical than most chapters outside prison walls.

In the days after the event, the wing most prone to daily fights stopped fighting. Host Jon Jeter, a former Washington Post foreign correspondent and author of *Flatbroke and the Free Market*, draws out these details across the hour.

David Sherba's factory in Brunswick, Ohio, has built between 4,000 and 5,000 Scabby the Rats since the first one was made on May 4, 1992. Host Chris Garlock visits Inflatable Images to hear how the process shifted from hand-airbrushing — three or four days per rat — to digital printing and computer patterning.

Carmen Rodriguez interviews historian Eladio Bobadilla about his book *Dangerous Migration*, which documents how the UFW under Cesar Chavez turned undocumented workers over to the Border Patrol and ran its own border enforcement operation. Bobadilla connects the fear-based narratives used against immigrants today to a pattern reaching back to Benjamin Franklin's warnings about Germans. Rounding out the hour, labor arts news briefs cover the Boston Symphony Orchestra's unanimous vote to authorize its first strike in 145 years, a unionization drive in the newsroom of the Illinois Daily Herald, and a tentative agreement that narrowly averted a strike by SEIU members at the Cleveland Public Library.

Flávio Bolsonaro announced his presidential candidacy standing next to Netanyahu in Israel — while his father Jair remains under house arrest. Medea Benjamin, co-founder of Code Pink and just back from Brazil, reports on that scene and explains how Lula's Bolsa Família program now reaches roughly 1 in 4 Brazilian families. The conversation turns from Brazil to Gaza, where Code Pink Palestine campaigner Janine brings birth-rate data: 57,000 births in 2022, dropping to 38,000 in 2024, then falling another 67% across a six-month span. Those figures anchor a new petition pressing the Center for Reproductive Rights to address Israel's impact on Palestinian women.

Host Marcie Winograd and Benjamin also take up Section 1217 of the NDAA, the Flock camera surveillance backlash spreading across roughly 57 municipalities, and a quiz identifying which think tanks are tied to the U.S.-Israel lobby.

Chuck Modiano calls Caitlin Clark not just not the WNBA MVP — not even a top-10 player. Her league-record rookie turnovers, a 3-point percentage ranking 32nd despite the third-most attempts, and a stat her supporters cite — "points created" — that appears nowhere among basketballreference.com's 94 statistics. August 27 marks ten years since Colin Kaepernick knelt, and Modiano traces that protest back through the back-to-back killings of Alton Sterling and Philando Castile. He connects Len Bias's 1986 overdose to the Drug Abuse Act, the crack possession mandatory minimums it introduced, and the crack-powder cocaine sentencing disparity that followed. Callers push into athlete economic power — one citing Junior Bridgeman's $1.4 billion estate built on fast-food franchises after his Milwaukee Bucks career — and into Kaepernick's Know Your Rights organization financing over 150 private autopsies for families seeking transparency in police-related deaths.

Véronique Tadjo traveled to Rwanda in 1998 with eleven other African writers on a project called "Rwanda: Writing as a Duty to Memory." The trip took four years to arrange because the Rwandan government had to be persuaded to accept the group. What shook her most wasn't the scale of the genocide but how ordinary the survivors looked — people she might have known at home. E. Ethelbert Miller also asks about her novel *In the Company of Men*, in which the Ebola virus speaks as its own character. Tadjo argues that deforestation and illegal gold mining are pushing animals closer to human settlements, fueling outbreaks in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

The conversation reaches back further too. *Lord of the Dance*, her 1988 book, started when she heard a hymn at a London wedding and decided to retell it with a Senufo mask as the central figure.

Caroline, a communal representative for the second section of Banga, told interviewer Woody Sanon she personally counted at least 46 bodies after the August 23rd massacre in Kenscoff, Haiti — a figure that excluded victims who died outside homes or went missing. She also told Sanon that local officials had warned police inspector Cadet that Kenscoff was at serious risk before the attack, yet no preventive action was taken. At a recent *Haiti on Our Mind* event at Sankofa, Pan-Africanist writer Jean-Séville Jafrik Afrika argued that the 1779 Battle of Savannah sent African captives — including a 12-year-old Henri Christophe — as cannon fodder, and drew a direct line from that history to Kenyan and Rwandan troops currently deployed to Haiti under UN mandate.

The programme's news segments move from that context to developments closer to the present: Haiti's under-14 boys soccer team winning the 2026 CFU Challenge Series in Punta Cana; businessman Dimitri Vob's release after more than 300 days in immigration detention; a federal judge's invalidation of the Trump administration's visa ban affecting 75 countries, including Haiti; and ICE's arrest of 1,328 people across Maryland and Virginia in the first two weeks of August. Eugenia Charles hosts.

Washington DC poet Janari, appearing on this episode of *New World Order*, performed a new piece titled "Overly Good" describing a firsthand account of being stopped by undercover officers, transported to jail, and held in a cell where another detainee was begging for water and saying he couldn't breathe. Janari then discussed the extended National Guard deployment in DC — confirmed by the Pentagon to run through Inauguration Day 2029 — and what "respected safety" means versus enforced safety, drawing on an observation of a spider dismantling its own web to recycle materials and build a stronger one the next morning. Valentine, a middle school cohort lead with the Black Swan Academy, described how the organization runs school-based campaigns — one cohort targeting lack of menstrual products at an all-girls school, another challenging a school lunch vendor shared with DC prisons — and explained that youth testifying before DC Council this year cited both the National Guard deployment and a youth curfew as central concerns.

When Dr. LaJoy Johnson-Law's daughter A'Bria — born at 23 weeks and one pound six ounces — lost her special education services, Johnson-Law filed a complaint with OSSE and eventually testified before the D.C. Council. That path brought her to her current seat as Ward 8's representative on the D.C. State Board of Education, and she joins host Brother Sam P.K. Collins to explain why she pushed the Board to pass a resolution on real ID access for students. With National Guard, FBI, and other federal law enforcement visible near Ward 8 schools, high schoolers who look older need documentation beyond a school ID. She also breaks down why chronic absenteeism data misleads: lumping excused and unexcused absences together without asking why students are missing school distorts the picture.

The conversation closes on a more encouraging note. D.C. schools have posted a fourth consecutive year of CAPE standardized test score gains, with double-digit math increases at Savoy Elementary and Gar-Field Elementary.

Sailors aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln have tried to go overboard after more than 200 days at sea without a single port call. On *The Resistance Report*, Jon Elmer tracks day 1,049 of Israel's genocide in Gaza alongside the widening U.S.-Iran war. Iran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz has cut tanker traffic from 140 ships per day to a fraction of that, and the American Enterprise Institute puts the cost of rebuilding damaged U.S. bases in the region at more than $5 billion. At least 45 MQ-9 Reaper drones have been shot down, the production line has been halted for more than two years, and the U.S. Air Force is now below 50% drone capacity.

Hezbollah has released previously unseen FPV drone strike footage from the battle around Beaufort Castle. The Pacifica Headlines segment reports on the Israeli military's raid on the UNRWA Qalandiya Training Center in occupied East Jerusalem.

Professor Gaye McDougall walked into the December 2022 Geneva launch of the UN Permanent Forum on People of African Descent and found the same room she had first entered decades earlier — when she was the only person from the African diaspora present — now holding 600 to 700 people of African descent from around the world. In this archival conversation on AfricaNow!, hosted by Mwiza Munthali, McDougall explains how George Floyd's murder supplied the final push to get the Forum "across the goal line" after Western countries had spent years dragging their feet.

McDougall brought rare standing to that fight: six years as the first UN Special Rapporteur on Minority Issues, a seat on the UN Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination, and a hand in shaping the 2001 Durban Conference. She breaks down the Forum's ten-member composition and its unsettled position between the General Assembly and the Human Rights Council, and she calls its founding resolution "a blank piece of paper" — one that leaves members to define their own power on reparations and beyond.

At a White House press conference, Ethel L. Payne demanded that President Eisenhower support desegregating interstate travel — and the next day her question was front-page news across the country. Payne was a Chicago Defender journalist whose Montgomery bus boycott coverage included an early observation that civil rights leadership was shifting to men of the cloth, yet she was writing for a Black press white Americans didn't know existed. Biographer James McGrath Morris, author of *Eye on the Struggle*, describes finding her papers in unopened boxes.

The hour also features what the program identifies as the first interview with Rosa Parks after her 1955 arrest, recorded in 1956. Parks describes paying her fare at the front of the bus, walking around to the rear in the rain, being convicted, and watching the boycott take hold after word spread by telephone and a single newspaper article. Produced by Askia Muhammad for *From the Vault*.

Louis Romaine returned from Cuba in May with a delegation organized by Dr. Ron Daniels and the Institute of the Black World — a group that sat down with elected officials, everyday Cubans, and the Cuban president. He traces U.S. hostility toward the island back to the 1854 Ostend Manifesto, in which American diplomats secretly urged President Pierce to seize Cuba by force, fearing it would become an independent Black republic like Haiti. A July 20th State Department report labeling Black internationalism a form of foreign subversion, Romaine argues, runs on the same fear of Black self-determination.

Washington, D.C. spoken word artist and boxer Azaira the Poet describes serving 18 months at Clarksburg Correctional Facility as a teenager, taking up boxing after surviving domestic violence, and performing at Howard University for Children's Mental Health Awareness Day. She performs two poems, including "Trap or Die," which moves through gentrification, absent fathers, and postpartum struggles. Host Dr. Ife Williams leads the conversation throughout on Wake Up and Stay Woke.

Baltimore is sitting on $32 million designated for the city's African community, and the commission deciding how to distribute it includes Dr. Ray Wimbush, a psychologist and reparations scholar who joins this conversation on *What's at Stake*. Host Denise Young is joined by Wimbush, Dr. Denise Wright, and Dayvon Love, director of public policy for Leaders of a Beautiful Struggle, to mark the 25th anniversary of the 2001 Durban Conference — where 18,000 people gathered and the U.S. and Israel walked out. A March 2026 UN General Assembly resolution, led by Ghana's president, declared the transatlantic slave trade the gravest crime against humanity ever committed. Only the U.S., Argentina, and Israel voted against it.

Love details a strategy of taxing university endowments above $2 billion to fund reparations, alongside a planned 2027 Maryland bill that would bar the state from doing business with Sinclair Broadcasting. He also explains why pressuring Congressman Jamie Raskin to move H.R. 40 out of the House Judiciary Committee could force Hakeem Jeffries into a public position on reparations.

We keep us safe" became a live practice, not just a slogan, at Black Lives Matter Plaza during the George Floyd uprising — where free food, water, street medics, and midnight yoga ran alongside protests. Frankie Sebron and co-host Chuck Moty trace the phrase from that moment to the current federal occupation of DC. Sebron left DC classrooms in 2021 after a decade teaching in public, charter, and Washington County schools, concluding she was "playing triage" while kids arrived with needs rooted in systemic failures.

The episode moves through the organizations that have built mutual aid and accountability infrastructure since then. The DC Safety Squad built filmpolicedc.org to document an alphabet soup of agencies. Court Watch trained at least 500 people to observe arraignments. The Informed Juror Project monitored a carceral system whose lockup lists hit 125 names in a single day. Moty brings something more personal to the conversation: he was kettled with 60 others at a Delaney Hall protest in New Jersey, and plastic handcuffs left his right hand numb for nearly three months. He uses that experience to reason through what indefinite ICE detention does to a person psychologically. The debut episode of *We Keep Us Safe*, part of WPFW's Liberation on My Mind series, aired August 25, 2026.

The Amazon River is audible in the background as Anthony Rogers-Wright reports live from COP30 in Belém, Brazil — where the UN and Brazilian government denied Afro-descendants standalone constituency status within the UNFCCC, and more than 1,600 oil and gas lobbyists were on the grounds. From there, David Cobb makes the case that the Democratic Party's move to put South Carolina first in the 2028 presidential primary forces candidates to build real relationships with Black, Latino, Arab American, and Indigenous grassroots organizers rather than route around them through traditional gatekeepers.

The Black Alliance for Peace's push to shift the movement's framing from environmental justice to environmental liberation runs through the same terrain. So does the Battle of Blair Mountain, which surfaces as a model of multiracial labor solidarity, and the proliferation of data centers, examined as an organizing issue pulling together communities across racial and political lines.

Seven detentions in a single Friday. That is what Guerline Joseph, founder and executive director of the Haitian Bridge Alliance, reported after the Supreme Court upheld the end of Temporary Protected Status for Haitians on June 25th — followed by 600 calls to the Alliance's hotline in two weeks. Residents in Springfield, Ohio are receiving letters offering a choice between deportation and an ankle monitor. Joseph identifies Senate Bill S.4814 as the only remaining legislative remedy and notes that 80 percent of affected Haitians work in healthcare.

Black Agenda Report host Margaret Kimberley turns from that crisis to Gerald Pereira, chairperson of the Organization for the Victory of the People in Guyana, who traces how the U.S.-led Shield of the Americas coalition has resulted in fishing boats being bombed in the Caribbean, killing two brothers from Trinidad. Pereira also details how the U.S. Defense Department has purchased a bauxite mine in Guyana and pressured the government to expel Cuba's medical brigade, whose doctors had been treating patients in remote jungle communities where no local physicians would go.

*Something to Say* (WPFW 89.3 FM) host Patrick Washington interviews performance poet and educator Nathan Richardson, who has spent 14 years portraying Frederick Douglass in partnership with the National Park Service at Cedar Hill in Anacostia — and in the episode delivers a sustained passage from Douglass's 1852 "What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?" address, explaining that he first recognized Douglass as a spoken word poet by hearing "the iambic pentameter leap off the page." The first hour also features author Avery Drummer (stage name Sienna B. Faroozi), who reads from her poetry collection *Blue Manitarian* and from her essay in *Triumph in the Trenches Volume 3* — a survival guide for Black professionals — where she writes about being undiagnosed and neurodivergent while attending Spelman. Co-host Mazi Mutafa takes over for the second hour, speaking with the Cooperative Opportunity Project's Gary about CommunityCon (September 19, Bowie, Maryland) and with Lydia Curtis of Siddiqui Educational Safari, whose group recently brought five D.C. youth to Cartagena and Medellín to meet with the Afro-Colombian Rosa Parks Foundation, and who is now recruiting a cast for a 15-minute street theater piece about union-busting dancers, to be performed October 24 in Columbia Heights.

*Capitalism, Race, and Democracy*, hosted by Thomas O'Rourke, opens with ILWU Local 10 President Mike Viaggianti speaking outside a Contra Costa County courthouse, where ten picketers arrested during the C&H Sugar Refinery strike faced charges. Viaggianti describes sheriff's deputies attacking workers "from behind" as they were leaving the facility. Filmmaker and activist Boots Riley, who attended the same hearing, argues that the strike is educationally valuable precisely because workers were visibly keeping scabs out, making the mechanics of class power legible to people who have never seen a real strike.

The episode then turns to Teamsters National Black Caucus chair Dr. Robin Cooper, who describes a convention in New Orleans where microphones were cut off to prevent the meeting from starting. She also recounts a male-dominated board's attempt to remove her from her seat, and members' five-year-old demands for financial transparency that organizers had repeatedly scheduled for Saturday night — when, she says, most attendees have already left.

Abby Martin and Mike Preisner got inside weapons contractor conferences and boarded a RIMPAC warship in the Pacific to make *Earth's Greatest Enemy*, a grassroots-funded documentary identifying the Pentagon as the world's largest polluter. Martin, co-winner of the 18th annual Izzy Award, tells hosts Mickey Huff and Eleanor Goldfield that corporate media won't touch the story because it requires questioning the premise of U.S. military force.

That reluctance has a long history. Media scholar Victor Pickard, C. Edwin Baker Professor at the University of Pennsylvania's Annenberg School for Communication, traces how the U.S. handed public airwaves to CBS and NBC in the early 1930s and stripped the Fairness Doctrine in 1987. The U.S. now spends $1.59 per capita on public media — a figure Pickard says has effectively dropped to zero after recent federal cuts. He also flags the Nexstar-Tegna merger, which FCC chair Brendan Carr is greenlighting despite a 39% ownership cap, as an instance of the current administration not changing media law but ignoring it.

On this episode of *Community Watch and Comment*, host David Rabin speaks with former Biden administration Head Start director Khari Garvin and National Head Start Association Deputy Director Tommy Sheridan about the Trump administration's proposed rewrite of Head Start's program performance standards — a document that would shrink from 122 pages to roughly a dozen. Garvin walks through specific rollbacks in the proposal: raising infant-to-teacher ratios from 1-to-4 to as high as 1-to-11 in some states, making health and dental screenings optional, removing pay parity requirements for teachers, and mandating English-only instruction — changes he calls "a carcass" of the original program, while Sheridan notes the public comment period runs until October 6th. The second half features Institute for Policy Studies Program Director Lindsay Kashgarian, whose organization's blueprint *Forging a Democracy That Works for All* documents that the United States' 977 billionaires now hold over $9 trillion in wealth — a 32% increase in a single year — and proposes an annual federal wealth tax on fortunes above $50 million, taxing investment income at least at the same rate as wages, and cutting the Pentagon budget in half, which Kashgarian says would, in year one alone, erase all medical debt and all private student loan debt in the country.

Marlo Hargrove built Baltimore's FACE Program — Freedom Advocates Celebrating Ex-Offenders — over 26 years without a single grant, charging residents roughly half what comparable programs charge. He conceived the model while serving six months in a treatment program, after cycling in and out of trouble from age 13 to 30, having lost both parents before he was a teenager. He tells host Roach Brown that he recently named one of his houses after a deceased mutual friend, and describes how the program connects residents with employment, food banks, and wraparound services.

The conversation opens out from there. A live call from a public defender in Prince George's County brings a specific case into the room: her client lost custody of her children while incarcerated and, as a result, cannot access family housing programs.

Mumia Abu-Jamal, recording from prison, describes spending 28 years on death row in solitary confinement, then 8 additional years in "the hole" for refusing to cut his hair, and watching men smear themselves with feces and howl for hours. Hosts Nefre Freeman and Brother Craig present his commentary as the closing installment of their station's Black August series.

Human rights lawyer Roger Wareham of the December 12th Movement explains how his organization spent more than a decade learning parliamentary tactics from Cuban diplomats to lobby the United Nations — work that produced the 2001 Durban Declaration, the first international document to name the transatlantic slave trade a crime against humanity and affirm that reparations are owed. A March 2026 UN resolution strengthened that language, passing 123 to 3, with the United States, Israel, and Argentina casting the only dissenting votes. The episode closes with voices from Pan-African Community Action's People's Community Health Walk, which ran from Anacostia Park to the RISE Demonstration Center and offered blood pressure screenings, produce from a Hyattsville farm, hygiene kits, and a presentation on reading lab results.

Abdul Akalimat — Professor Emeritus at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, also known as Gerald McWorther — opens with a pointed self-criticism: "we've become our own audience." Black Studies, he argues, has delinked from the Black community and failed to standardize its curriculum. James Counts Early, who spent 32 years at the Smithsonian including as Assistant Secretary for Education and Public Service, joins him in pressing the point further. The current attacks on Black Studies, DEI, and affirmative action are not, in their reading, isolated culture-war skirmishes but a coordinated effort to dismantle liberal capitalist democracy itself.

Early traces that project to what Marco Rubio called Europe's interrupted "civilizing mission," and draws on Du Bois's 1953 revision of his own race thesis to insist that race and class must be read together. Any Black liberation politics disconnected from broader working-class struggle is, in Akalimat's word, "fantasy." Host Mimi Rosenberg presses both guests on what a genuine multiracial democracy would require — and it is that question that pulls the conversation back, finally, to where Akalimat began.

Marsha P. Johnson remembered "I Heard It Through the Grapevine" playing on the jukebox at Stonewall the night the riots began. Host Cory Bae (Sweet Cory Bae) builds that recollection into the centerpiece of this installment of Suge's Line Radio, drawing on Tourmaline's book about Johnson's life to frame the Stonewall uprising as days of resistance by gender-marginalized people subjected to laws requiring clothing that matched their assigned gender at birth. Johnson — queer activist, costume designer, and co-founder of Street Transvestite Action Revolutionaries (STAR) — appears on the cover of Earth, Wind & Fire's *Touch the World*, which is why the show opens with two singles from that album.

From there, Bae covers the origins of Black Music Month, signed into law by President Jimmy Carter, and recent accounts of police aggression at Pride celebrations in Sherelle Parker's Philadelphia.

White people did not exist on planet Earth until 1681." That's the claim Dr. Jacqueline Battalora makes in a lecture host Ambrose Lane Jr. plays on this episode of To The East, tracing the word "white" to Maryland and Virginia colonial anti-miscegenation laws. The 1664 Maryland statute accidentally encouraged the interracial marriages it meant to stop; the corrected 1681 law is where "white" first enters colonial statute. A Black history segment covers the week of August 24th, from Edith Sampson's 1950 appointment as the first African American U.N. representative to the 1983 March on Washington. Valerie Watts, editor of HWRE Lifestyle Magazine, then discusses her October 23rd national livestream symposium at Medgar Evers College in Brooklyn, focused on the Black church's role in economic empowerment, property ownership, and political power.

Dr. Theodore Watkins, a surgeon-turned-holistic-medicine practitioner, devotes this episode of *To Your Health* to the physiology of walking, drawing on his own "Walk for Life" program he ran with residents of Harvard Towers — a high-rise near 16th and Harvard — where elderly patients who had rarely left their apartments eventually walked to the National Zoo. Watkins explains in clinical detail how the calf muscles (the soleus and gastrocnemius) act as a mechanical sump pump returning blood to the heart, how walking produces nitric oxide that relaxes arterial walls, and how a glucose transporter called GLUT4 clears blood sugar without insulin — relevant, he argues, to reversing rather than merely managing diabetes and early-stage Alzheimer's. Callers raise questions about neuropathy, hypoglycemia, and a brain parasite linked to a public official, and Watkins cites research suggesting that breast, colorectal, and prostate cancer survivors who walk regularly can see a 30 to 40 percent reduction in cancer-specific and all-cause mortality.

Virginia stocked the Potomac, York, James, and Rappahannock rivers with blue catfish in the early 1970s, betting the fish wouldn't survive the Chesapeake Bay's brackish water. That miscalculation produced an estimated 100 million catfish by 2011, with the population still growing. Host Stacia LaMira draws on clips from Straight Arrow News and the Virginia Farm Bureau, where watermen and researchers describe a canceled trophy striped bass season, a 75% yield loss when processing catfish, and dock prices too low to cover costs. Maryland's responses include a 2019 Blue Catfish Initiative Purchasing Program and chef symposiums, and one school-lunch item — a blue catfish sandwich called the "catty patty," named to evoke SpongeBob's Krabby Patty — that students say tastes similar to crab cakes.

A "Doctor's Orders" segment covers a 2024 study finding that marigold petal tea produced a 51% reduction in body-weight gain in a rat model, with anti-obesity activity the researchers compared to the drug orlistat. The programme closes with a "Story of Food" segment tracing white potato pie — a custard dessert with colonial English roots tied to surplus potato harvests — most associated with Maryland's Eastern Shore, where a lemon-slice version is called a Maryland Sunrise.

Senator John Tyler Morgan — a former Klansman — described Black suffrage as a load to be rid of "by burning down the barn to kill the rats." DC historian C.R. Gibbs cites Morgan's role in stripping the vote from every DC resident after the Civil War, then traces Josephine Butler's leadership of the DC Statehood Party from 1977 through the 1990s. Walter Fauntroy's statehood bill cleared the House District Committee but never reached the floor. Eleanor Holmes Norton's 1993 bill lost 277 to 153. DC Statehood Party candidate Kamau Freeman adds that Butler's organizing directly stopped a planned expressway through the Brookland neighborhood.

WPFW morning host Brother Jamil will debut a one-man play about his life at the Billie Holiday Theater in Bedford-Stuyvesant on August 29th and 30th.

Josephine Dorothy Butler's school bus was stoned, and her father lost his job for supporting Black children's education. She grew up to co-found the D.C. Statehood Party in 1971 — a history historian C.R. Gibbs brought to host Joni on *Heal DC*. Butler came from a Prince George's County family of tobacco sharecroppers and went on to organize laundry workers, government cafeteria employees, and Veterans Administration workers before being "disinvited" from that last job for being too active. Her statehood strategy, as Gibbs traced it, meant traveling state to state on the logic that ratification would require winning over state legislatures. She and fellow Statehood Party founders Julius Hobson and Hilda Mason argued the 1973 Home Rule Act left Congress with veto power over the city's budget, control of its courts, and the ability to tax non-resident workers — what some dismissed as "home fool" rather than home rule.

The episode draws on clips from the Free DC Mixtape and places the broadcast within Black August, noting the 1949 Peekskill riot in which Paul Robeson was burned in effigy ahead of a concert.

An AI resume-screening bot was up to two-thirds more likely to accept a résumé written on ChatGPT than one written on a rival platform like Gemini or Claude — machine "homophily," Howard Ross and Jake Ross tell Julianne Malveaux, that mirrors the human impulse to hire people like oneself. The pair join MALVEAUX! to discuss the second edition of *Everyday Bias*, which they co-authored. A Zillow algorithm underestimated home values in predominantly Black neighborhoods by training on data shaped by redlining. Cambridge scholar Jason Arday's suicide followed a targeted plagiarism search that combed his work at a scale rarely applied to white male academics — and when the same technology was turned on one critic's wife's dissertation, it found plagiarism there too.

The conversation also covers the outgroup homogeneity effect in political discourse, the Facebook "like" button replacing self-worth with dopamine-driven validation, and what Howard Ross calls the shift from a parent-child power structure to working as peers with his son.

Garland Nixon says the food shortage on the USS Abraham Lincoln isn't Pentagon incompetence — Iran destroyed the warehouses storing those supplies at the U.S. naval base in Bahrain, and blaming logistics is a way of refusing to say the U.S. lost the war. Callers from Germany, Maryland, and Baltimore push the conversation into military recruitment and the $4 trillion cost of the Iraq and Afghanistan wars. Nixon reads from a 2007 Reuters article on Citgo, the Venezuelan state-owned oil company that supplied heating oil at 40 percent below market price to poor Americans in 23 states before the program ended. He also invokes Jimmy Carter's line that the United States is "the most warlike nation in the history of the world" and takes up Israel's reported construction of an execution facility for Palestinians.

Jacqueline Luqman opens *Darker Than Blue* with a pointed challenge: military spending and tax cuts are funded the same way socialist programs are — through government revenue. China's state-owned enterprises returned 574 billion yuan to the government in 2025, a 12-fold increase over a decade, with central SOEs contributing an average of 29.7% of profits. Cuba allocated nearly 100 billion pesos in 2026 to subsidize electricity, medicine, and public transport, under a decades-long U.S. blockade. The academic study *Slavery, Reconstruction, and Bureaucratic Capability in the American South* grounds Luqman's argument that post-Reconstruction white elites built cross-class coalitions to gut tax collection specifically to keep government funds from reaching formerly enslaved people. That racial history, she argues, is the root of "taxation is theft" politics still debated today. The episode closes by stacking what Americans pay privately for healthcare, childcare, and college against what a higher income tax rate would replace.

shows.t: Resistance Radio with John and Regan
shows.desc:
At a county fair in California, John Kane couldn't buy a funnel cake with cash. That detail anchors a longer argument on *Resistance Radio* tracing surveillance from flock cameras debated on the Cattaraugus Territory of the Seneca Nation — where Kane is broadcasting — through RFID chips in enhanced tribal IDs built to satisfy the Department of Homeland Security's Western Hemisphere Travel Initiative. Kane turns to language next, contending that "sovereignty" describes governmental power over people and land rather than freedom. The 1924 declaration of Native American citizenship, he argues, was imposed without consent — a point he ties to his film *The Long Hope*.

The broadcast also covers the Navy's internal discussions about renaming the USS Doris Miller, a carrier under construction honoring the first African American to receive the Navy Cross, under President Trump.

Latino Media Collective host Oscar Fernandez interviews Javier Puente — chair and associate professor of Latin American and Latino Studies at Smith College and author of the NACLA article "The Return of Fujimorismo" — about what Keiko Fujimori's narrow election as Peru's first woman president (50.13% of the vote, a margin of fewer than 50,000 ballots) means for a country already shaped by her father's 1992 self-coup, the overnight price shocks of Fujishock, and decades of states of emergency that left Ayacucho under suspended constitutional rights for the entirety of the internal conflict. Puente traces how Keiko turned three presidential losses into a congressional majority that toppled successive presidents, and explains terruqueo — the tactic of branding leftists, indigenous activists, human rights defenders, and LGBTQ people as Sendero Luminoso sympathizers — as the mechanism that keeps organized opposition off balance. The conversation also covers why the grassroots No a Keiko movement, despite blocking her three times, has yet to develop the kind of opposition suited to confronting Fujimorismo in power rather than on the campaign trail.

shows.t: Community Watch & Comment - Friday / The Local Station Board Show (Last Frid
shows.desc:
Police pulled children as young as 6 from an SUV at gunpoint because a Flock camera matched the wrong plate — the alert was tied to a motorcycle from another jurisdiction. The family won nearly $2 million in that lawsuit, and that case anchors Friday's open-phones hour on *Community Watch and Comment* with hosts Brian Pinchback and Chip Jones. A 45-year-old Black caller invokes James Baldwin to make the point that Flock cameras are simply a newcomer's introduction to what Black drivers have faced their entire lives without any technological pretext.

The money follows. Silicon Valley venture capitalists have put over a billion dollars into lobbying for these AI-assisted license plate surveillance systems now being installed in communities nationwide, and callers push on what that spending could mean if directed at healthcare or other public needs instead.

A city racial equity assessment found that young people with one police contact are 121 times more likely to have a repeated negative interaction — and that number anchors this conversation on Washington, D.C.'s "teen takeover" media narrative. Host Rev Yearwood speaks with Yasmin Salina, co-founder of the Hustlers Guild and sixth-generation Washingtonian building school-to-career pipelines through sports and entertainment, and Nicole Newman, executive director of Critical Exposure. Salina puts the math plainly: it costs over $35,000 a year to incarcerate someone, yet organizations serving hundreds of youth are routinely handed that same figure in grants.

Newman's organization, Critical Exposure, has worked with D.C. youth on campaigns ranging from school facilities funding to mental health resources. The young people themselves are pushing back on the curfew and calling for free transportation, family-sized housing, and year-round workforce development programs modeled on the Summer Youth Employment Program.

Andre Kearns can trace his family to Emmanuel and Joan Cumbo — captives from the Kingdom of Ndongo in present-day Angola who arrived at Port Comfort around 1628 — and to his third great-grandfather William B. Harvell, sold as a child named Buck in an 1832 bill of sale. After emancipation, Harvell became a landowner, founded a church, and established a school that launched five generations of HBCU attendance in Kearns's family, with a sixth generation now at Howard. Kearns, a Washington D.C. native, genealogist, and author, sits down with the #YouMustLearn program on WPFW to tell that story.

The episode also turns to the DiverseCITY Fund's fall grant cycle, open to Black and brown-led organizations with budgets under $50,999 that do organizing, advocacy, or healing justice work in D.C. Board member Nkechi Feaster — who first encountered the fund while living in a family shelter at D.C. General — explains how its community grantmaking model deliberately removes the barriers that typically block impacted residents from both funding decisions and funding itself. Rounding out the hour, holistic health practitioner and Black Love Day founder Mama Ayo Handy Kendi previews WPFW's 5th annual 5K walk/run on September 12th at Bladensburg Waterfront Park, describing new additions that include walking meditation and strength training.

Nearly 40% of green jobs require a high school diploma or less — and those positions pay 8 to 9% more per hour than national averages. That is the research Devashree Saha, Director of the Clean Energy Economy Program at the World Resources Institute, brings to host Renee Bowser, drawing on Brookings Institution findings. Saha puts the global picture in sharp relief: 35 million clean energy jobs now exist worldwide, edging out 32 million in fossil fuels. In the United States alone, nearly 3.6 million clean energy jobs existed at the end of 2024, with energy efficiency holding the largest share, and over 60% of new utility-scale solar, wind, and battery manufacturing projects are sited in Republican congressional districts.

The numbers, though, only go so far. Saha argues that transportation, childcare, and what she calls "wraparound services" are the real barriers keeping lower-income workers from reaching training programs. She also warns against training workers too narrowly for technologies whose market demand can shift with policy changes.

Moses African Cemetery was formally established in 1911 on land used for burial since the slavery era, but that history has not protected it. A sewage trench was dug through it in the 1930s. Its tombstones were demolished for a parking lot. A storage facility is now going up on a parcel where the developer's own excavators have turned up human bones sized to belong to children. Robert Stubblefield, a volunteer with the Bethesda African Cemetery Coalition and worshiper at Macedonia Baptist Church, explains how the River Road community of freed people was dismantled through higher utility bills, tax liens, and Klan violence — including the beating of Harvey Matthews' father and grandfather until they signed away their farm. Macedonia Baptist Church is the sole surviving institution of a neighborhood that once had a colored school, a beer hall, and a semi-pro baseball team.

Host Jon Jeter, author of *Class War in America*, fills in the context of slave breeding on Montgomery County plantations, where the recorded life expectancy of enslaved Africans was roughly 20 years. Against that backdrop, Stubblefield traces the coalition's legal fights through three courts, culminating in a Maryland Supreme Court ruling that descendant communities can sue for equitable relief. A court date on the developer of Parcel 242 is set for September 24th.

Pete Seeger performing "The Preacher and the Slave" in 1960 opens a listener-request hour marking the 115th anniversary of the IWW's Little Red Songbook — 38 editions between 1909 and 2010, with a 39th now in progress. Host Chris Garlock also airs Labor Heritage Foundation co-founder Saul Schneiderman singing an a cappella "Dump the Bosses Off Your Back." The hour's centerpiece is labor historian Nick Jurevich interviewing veteran organizer Phil Cohen about his memoir *Maximum Leverage: From the Street to the Picket Line*. Cohen drove illegal gypsy cabs in New York at 17, lived in a Skid Row hotel while clearing a stack of arrest warrants, and eventually rebuilt union locals from 30% to 80% membership. Among the tactics he describes: having workers fan out down separate aisles of a Sam's Club simultaneously so managers couldn't stop them all at once.

The labor arts news rounds out the hour. Video game workers rallied in six states against Xbox layoffs, the Traverse City Philharmonic voted to join the American Federation of Musicians, and workers ratified a first contract at Dallas Black Dance Theatre.

Terry Madsen, a Mexico City-based podcaster, tells Code Pink Radio host Marcie Winograd that 19 Latin American countries have joined the Trump administration's Shield of the Americas and Counter-Cartel Coalition — what Madsen calls "Monroe Doctrine 2.0 on steroids" — while Brazil, Cuba, Mexico, Nicaragua, and Venezuela refused rather than relinquish sovereignty. Cuba's current conditions, Madsen says, resemble a war zone: under sanctions, the state is barred from purchasing petroleum while private companies can.

The conversation turns to K-12 classrooms. Winograd speaks with Liz Jackson, legal director of K-12 Legal Defense, about that organization's intervention in a Brandeis Center for Human Rights lawsuit against the state of California and the California Department of Education. The suit seeks to compel nearly 400,000 school staff to undergo antisemitism training coordinated by the plaintiffs and to install curriculum monitors in 14 school districts. Jackson also details a recently settled federal case against the Sequoia Union High School District, in which the district agreed to a plaintiff-selected censor to prescreen all Israel-Palestine curriculum and adopted a definition of antisemitism under which calling Israel "a racist endeavor" is officially prohibited.

Etan Thomas walked out of the National Association of Black Journalists convention and onto *The Collision* with a firsthand account: young journalists at his panel named Stephen A. Smith "Exhibit A" for the rift between athletes and the media. Smith had just responded to the NABJ's Thumbs Down Award by appearing on Sean Hannity's Fox News show, where Hannity questioned why an organization specifically for Black journalists needs to exist — a claim Smith did not correct. Attendees told Thomas that independent shows like *The Collision* say things corporate journalists wish they could say. Chuck Modiano marks ten years since Colin Kaepernick took a knee on August 19, 2016, arguing the NFL's willingness to lose games rather than sign Kaepernick was no accident. He ties that to ESPN's removal of Black journalists Jemele Hill, Bomani Jones, Howard Bryant, Ryan Clark, and Cam Newton as a deliberate institutional pattern.

Onika Mays spent more than a decade teaching yoga and mindfulness at Rikers Island Correctional Facility, and she tells host E. Ethelbert Miller what it actually took to work there: arriving on the Q100 bus each morning, calling on her ancestors before leaving home, spraying liquid sage in her office, and stripping off her clothes the moment she got back. She reads from her book *Sit With Me*, describing the jail's ten facilities, power plant, solitary complex, and a barge that once housed incarcerated people and now houses migrants — all visible from the bridge. She also explains why she sees the criminal justice system not as broken but as working exactly as designed.

The conversation moves through her years as a bookseller and the role bell hooks's *All About Love* played in the women's facility, before turning to a harder question: whether the Buddhist concept of metta can coexist with Pan-Africanism. It ends on something concrete — what the constant noise and lights-on dorm conditions do to a person's nervous system within three days.

Haiti is heading toward a December 13th election with roughly 104 political parties already in the certification process, and the CEP is pressing them to merge into coalitions. To help secure the vote, a Japan–OAS cooperation agreement delivers a $3 million grant to expand Haiti's national identification system and procure 350,000 blank biometric cards before the election.

Host Eugenia Charles tracks six Haitian and Haitian American candidates on Florida's primary ballot, among them Florida State Representative Doty Joseph seeking the Democratic gubernatorial nomination and physician Dr. Rudolph Moïse running in District 24 to succeed retiring Congresswoman Frederica Wilson. A recorded segment from Ezuli Danto on the 1791 Bois-Caïman gathering opens a broader discussion of what democracy and freedom mean under Haiti's current government. Charles argues that Prime Minister Alix Didier Filsaime has lost more territory to gangs than existed before he took office and is paying over $35,000 a month in legal fees to stay in power.

George Carter III grew up in New Orleans's 9th Ward, survived Hurricane Katrina, and was killed in an act of intercommunal violence. Before he died, he imagined schools with mood detectors instead of metal detectors and strawberry gardens instead of suspension rooms. That vision opens a conversation with Jomo, National Information Coordinator for the Malcolm X Grassroots Movement, on this Black August episode of *New World Order*.

Jomo traces Black August to California prisons in the 1960s and '70s, where incarcerated people studied and trained to join the broader freedom struggle upon release, and to mourning the murder of a political prisoner that ended nearly a decade of organizing. He introduces "Black thrival" and the "revolutionary potential of Black youth," drawing on *Educating for the Insurgency*, which documents that many people who escaped enslavement were between 13 and 29 years old. The episode, produced by the youth artivist collective Freedom Futures Collective, also covers the Malcolm X Grassroots Movement's Wednesday programming at the Black Workers and Wellness Center, their organizing framework of people's assemblies, people's self-defense, and political prisoners, and a Pride Purpose Power Top 5 Countdown of independent artivist music.

Matt Miller noticed men in his community were "walking around looking like bank robbers" — so District Dads at Martha's Table built a fashion showcase. Alumni dads will model four scenes of four different styles at the Outfitters clothing boutique on Martin Luther King Avenue, where everything is free to community members. Miller also walks host Brother Sam PK Collins through District Dads' 17-week fatherhood curriculum, which draws participants ages 16 to 77 and ends with five weeks on emotional wellness.

Xavier Brown and Jamila White describe the Black Environmental Fellowship, a six-week summer program for youth from east of the Anacostia River. Fellows toured Harriet Tubman's birthplace on the Eastern Shore, visited Black-owned land formerly used to enslave ancestors, and camped in Southern Maryland. The program closed with fellows presenting on the Kwanzaa principles — wearing sashes handmade in Accra — to their community.

A folkloric lullaby in Arabic, anonymous and sung at the concert All Together for Palestine, opens the hour before Leith Marouf takes over.

Marouf — founder of Palestine TV and host Zain Al-Amin's named authority on Lebanon, Gaza, and the Arab world — argues that Morocco's King deliberately released 40,000 amnestied petty criminals toward the Spanish enclave of Ceuta within 24 to 48 hours, punishment for Spain's rhetorical support for Palestinians. The King's father, Marouf claims, accepted $50 per Jewish Moroccan expelled to Palestine to help establish the Zionist colony. A mine outside Barcelona, he says, produces the vast majority of the white phosphorus used on Palestine and South Lebanon, and Spanish territorial waters on both sides of the Strait of Gibraltar give ordinary citizens legal standing to blockade weapons shipments to Israel without government permission.

This episode of *Africa Now*, hosted by Mwiza Munthali, features a conversation with writer Arun Kundnani about the political life of Jamil Al-Amin, formerly known as H. Rap Brown — including the detail that, when FBI files obtained through Freedom of Information requests listed Al-Amin's possessions at the time of his arrests, the books he was carrying were works by Nkrumah, Fanon, and Robert Williams. Kundnani traces how Al-Amin, elected SNCC chair at 23 and named in J. Edgar Hoover's 1967 COINTELPRO memo alongside three others, argued at the National Conference for New Politics that Black people constituted "an internal colony" and that America was enacting genocide through Vietnam draft casualties, child poverty, mass incarceration, and disproportionate targeting in reproductive health. The conversation also covers Al-Amin's conversion to Islam in the New York State prison system in 1971, his argument that Islam made activists "COINTELPRO-proof," and his organizing alongside Puerto Rican and Chicano movements — all framed around Kundnani's ongoing biography project, the first of its kind on Al-Amin.

Roger McAfee, a white farmer from Fresno whom Angela Davis had never met, put up his farm as collateral to bail her out of jail. He then needed movement members to guard it after the Ku Klux Klan shot some of his animals. Aretha Franklin had publicly pledged to pay, but it was McAfee who acted. Davis makes that correction speaking at USC's Bovard Auditorium on February 23, 2015, before 1,500 people, in conversation with Dr. Michelle Turner.

She also addresses her co-defendant Ruchell Magee, still imprisoned after more than 50 years, and names Leonard Peltier and Mumia Abu-Jamal among political prisoners she connects to ongoing racist violence. Davis links the ideology of colorblindness to a failure to reckon with the history of lynching. The episode opens with a montage of Pacifica Radio Archives recordings of Davis spanning 1969 to 2011, compiled by Mark Torres.

Dr. Willie Jolly's grandmother ran a beauty shop in Philadelphia until she died at 88 — doing three heads that morning, a pocket full of money in her smock. On *Wake Up and Stay Woke*, host E. Faye Williams asks Jolly, author of *Rich Is Good, Wealthy Is Better*, to explain the difference between the two: rich is money you earn from what you do, wealthy is money you generate from what you own, usually while you sleep. Jolly lays out five types of wealth — financial, health, relationship, reputational, and intellectual capital — and five money mindsets that range from day-to-day survival to generational planning. He also describes a trust structure he uses with his own family that requires heirs to submit a W-2 each year to receive 5 percent of their earnings as their inheritance payment. Williams, who references her book *This Is Me* and her past run for U.S. Congress in Louisiana, also presses Jolly on voting and what it takes to write a book.

On July 4th, Nolan Wells — an 18-year-old Black college athlete — went missing during a boat trip to Horn Island, Mississippi; his three white companions returned home without him, had the boat scrubbed down at 3 AM, and immediately retained lawyers. Host Verna Avery Brown connects his case to at least 22 Black individuals found dead under suspicious hanging circumstances since March 2025. Eric K. Ward, Executive Vice President of Race Forward and Senior Advisor to the Southern Poverty Law Center, argues the cluster demands federal investigation and says Black communities should look to bodies like the UN Working Group of Experts on People of African Descent when domestic government fails. The second half turns to author Andrew Oake, whose two-volume *Unusual for Their Time: On the Road with America's First Ladies* draws on two to three years of travel to recover overlooked histories. Those include Martha Washington managing 8,000 tobacco acres before marrying George Washington, Dolley Madison being expelled from the Quaker Church over her necklines before marrying James Madison, and Martha Jefferson's deathbed request that Thomas Jefferson never remarry — which he honored.

Dennis Banks walked into his own trial in Custer, South Dakota wearing full Native American regalia and Nike shoes. Alice Walker tells that story in a Stanford University lecture recorded ten days after Banks's death — he was her friend and a leader of the American Indian Movement — which she delivered wearing a squash blossom necklace in mourning. Walker argues that turning away from others' pain leaves an "arrow in the heart" that festers until people become, as she puts it, like those they hate. Among the wounded she names the children of Che Guevara, Medgar Evers, and Malcolm X.

She also reads her own poems, including tributes to Michael Jackson and Martin Luther King Jr., and speaks about Whitney Houston and Prince — and what she sees as the harm of pressing artists to perform identities not their own.

David Cobb, Green Party member and host of *Redneck Gone Green*, says a real grassroots organizer can do "with $10 what it takes $1,000" in high-cost media markets. He and *Full Spectrum* host Anthony Rogers-Wright take that as a starting point for the Democratic National Committee's decision to move South Carolina, Nevada, New Mexico, and Michigan earlier in the 2028 presidential primary calendar — a shift Cobb argues forces candidates to engage Black, Latino, Arab American, and Indigenous communities from the start rather than as afterthoughts.

Rogers-Wright recorded the second segment on the ground in Belém, Brazil at COP30, where over 1,600 oil and gas lobbyists were present and the UN and Brazilian government rejected Afro-descendant self-agency as a standalone constituency. Those failures at the international level feed back into the conversation with Cobb: together they connect the dynamics at COP30 to data center proliferation, the Battle of Blair Mountain, and the original Rainbow Coalition built by Fred Hampton.

"I woke up illegal." A 23-year-old woman from Gonaïves said that to Guerline Joseph after the Trump administration ended the CHNV parole program she had used to enter the United States legally at age 19. Now in Brooklyn, she fears ICE the same way she once feared armed groups in Haiti. Joseph, founder of the Haitian Bridge Alliance, tells Black Agenda Report host Margaret Kimberley that the Alliance's hotline received over 600 calls in two weeks, including seven detentions in a single day, among more than 300,000 affected Haitians — 80% of whom work in healthcare.

The program's reach extends well beyond Haiti. Gerald Carrera of the Organization for the Victory of the People in Guyana argues that the Shield of the Americas coalition is less about drug cartels than about U.S. control of regional resources. Boats bombed in the Caribbean under the program were carrying fishermen, not drugs. The U.S. Defense Department has purchased a Guyanese bauxite mine, and Secretary of State Rubio ordered the expulsion of Cuba's medical brigade, which Carrera says had kept Guyana's rural health system from collapsing.

Sarah Collins Rudolph, the sole survivor among the five girls in the 16th Street Baptist Church bombing, told a panel that those survivors, unlike 9/11 survivors, never received physical therapy, help, or compensation. Isisara Bey, artistic director of the March On Festival, was sitting across from her when she said it. Now Bey and festival director of audience development Nina preview the 13th annual March On Festival, running September 29 through October. It opens with a Friday-night rally at Metropolitan AME Church — the site of Frederick Douglass's last public address — pairing a conversation on allyship with a performance by original Freedom Singer Rutha Mae Harris and Maimouna Youssef. A Saturday event at the Atlas Theater examines three New Orleans families — the Francises, the Morials, and the Landreus — whose civil rights work ran across the 20th and 21st centuries.

Host Mazi Mutafa speaks with Words Beats and Life Academy Assistant Director David Jones about a six-week summer arts apprenticeship for DC youth ages 14–19. Patrick Washington interviews 2023 Virginia State Youth Poet Laureate Kashvi Rahmani, who discusses her forthcoming collection *Saffron Skies and Kajal Cries* and a work-in-progress film about Indian traditionalism and generational conflict, with a book release event at the Kennedy Center's River Terrace Theater on August 26th.

Ian Lustig, co-author of *Israel's Lobby: America in the Grip of a Foreign Power*, says Netanyahu privately met with Trump before the Iran attack and "together they planned that war." Lustig also argues the Israel lobby helped produce the invasion of Iraq, and that lobby strategy manuals shifted over decades from substantive policy defense to instructing advocates to call critics antisemites rather than engage their arguments. Street interviews from a Wednesday protest in New Orleans include a palliative care physician describing her arrest at an ICE protest after identifying herself as a doctor, and an organizer detailing Louisiana's 8,000 ICE detainees — second only to Texas — held in rural northern parishes near a facility 200 miles from New Orleans where Mahmoud Khalil was briefly detained. WPFW News covers Florida primary races pitting DSA candidates against Debbie Wasserman Schultz and Alex Vindman. The Congo Ebola outbreak has killed at least 2,300 people, spread to a sixth province, and the WHO has raised only about 60% of the $115 million needed for the response.

Florida's Board of Governors chancellor declared every introductory sociology textbook non-compliant with state law, then routed all faculty guidance through phone calls so no paper trail would exist. Zachary Levinson, a sociology professor at Florida International University, walks through what followed: a secret committee whose records remain sealed, and sociology removed from the general education curriculum entirely.

Nolan Higdon traces how that moment became possible. His book *MAG Academy* documents the decades of neoliberal restructuring that flipped tenure-track faculty from roughly 70% of the workforce in the 1980s to roughly 30–35% today. Higdon argues corporate DEI functioned as social-justice branding for a system that simultaneously funneled more faculty of color into the most precarious, lowest-paid positions. This edition of *Project Censored* aired on Pacifica Radio on Tuesday, August 18, 2026.

On the morning of September 21, 1976, a car bomb killed Orlando Letelier and Ronni Moffitt at Sheridan Circle on Embassy Row — less than two miles from the White House. Moffitt was 25, an Institute for Policy Studies staffer who had opened a music center in a low-income Washington neighborhood where people could borrow instruments for free. David Rabin, who presents the program as Host Dave Raven, speaks with IPS Global Economy Project Director Sarah Anderson about three former Chilean secret police agents sentenced to 15 years in prison for Moffitt's murder, nearly 50 years after the assassination, and about American operative Michael Townley — who taped the bomb under the car — still living in U.S. witness protection. Elliot Nagan of the Substack publication Money Trail traces Trump's "communists are coming" rhetoric back through Roy Cohn and the McCarthy era. Organizer Burton Bollag describes a weekly Saturday demonstration outside D.C.'s Holocaust Museum, where he and a small group hand out leaflets connecting the museum's historical mission to what the Committee to Protect Journalists has called the deadliest and most deliberate effort to kill journalists it has ever documented.

Andrea James collected more than 11,000 signatures to land on the Massachusetts gubernatorial ballot, running as an independent after a federal wire fraud conviction sent her to prison. A Boston attorney who founded the National Council for Incarcerated and Formerly Incarcerated Women and Girls, she told host Roach Brown that African Americans are 7% of Massachusetts' population but 51% of its jail and prison population. Her platform centers on affordable housing, universal healthcare, equitably funded education, and childcare — the same pressures, she argues, that drive women into incarceration.

The conversation moves to the current Massachusetts governor's proposal to spend $360 million on a new women's prison to house roughly 200 people, then to the legislature's 2020 decision to strip incarcerated people of the right to vote — a move that followed prisoners at Norfolk State Prison organizing their families against tough-on-crime legislation.

Mumia Abu-Jamal mourns Dr. Johanna Fernandez — his former advocate, dead at 55 — recalling the black blazer and black slacks she wore daily as her "armor." He first met her after a labor historian brought her to visit him on death row.

Hosts Netfa Freeman and Craig draw on Pan-African Community Action's August 12th political education session, "Taking It to the Streets: The Long Tradition of Revolutionary Youth Resistance." Jalil Muntaqim, introduced as one of the longest-held political prisoners of warfare in the country, explains that Black August originated inside California prisons, where enslaved Africans banded together against the Aryan Brotherhood and neo-Nazi guards — naming George Jackson, Jonathan Jackson, and others as central figures. That history runs alongside a clip from the 1968 NET Journal documentary *Color Us Black*, filmed during the student takeover of Howard University, and discussion of COINTELPRO's targeting of youth organizers. The session closes with Pan-African Community Action's Community Control DC platform, whose first demand is that youth shall govern youth resources.

After the Confederacy fell in 1865, defeated Confederate officers W.W. Loring, H.H. Sibley, Samuel Lockett, and Raleigh Colston traveled to Cairo to help Egypt plan an invasion of Ethiopia — the goal being a fresh supply of enslaved labor. Historian Gerald Horne lays this out for host Mimi Rosenberg, alongside the parallel story of ex-enslavers relocating to Brazil and Cuba, where slavery remained legal into the 1880s. His new book, *Slavery, the Slave Trade, and the Roots of U.S. Imperialism*, traces the network further: Zanzibar as a hub of U.S.-connected slave trading in the 1840s, Ottoman Turkey castrating enslaved African men to staff imperial harems, Saudi rulers arriving in Washington as late as 1957 with enslaved Africans.

Horne argues that the 9th-century Zanj Revolt in Iraq, the Haitian Revolution, and Ethiopia's defeat of Italian invaders in 1896 each forced measurable contractions of the slave system. The post-Civil War rise of American labor unions, he contends, was a direct consequence of removing enslaved people as a drag on wages.

A Black patient arrives at the emergency room in crisis and nearly gets turned away because hospital staff didn't know how to remove a lace front wig. A Black nurse intervened. Hosts Daffo the Flowa and Jay Barber use that case to anchor a Fellowship Hall conversation about how mental health care became stigmatized in Black communities, tracing a line from the Tuskegee syphilis study through white-dominated psychiatric institutions that routinely labeled Black patients insane. The Lafarge Clinic in Harlem — established in the 1940s through a partnership with local religious leadership as the neighborhood's first dedicated mental health services — shows how the Black church stepped in to fill that gap.

The hour closes with Baltimore house DJ and producer Charisma, also known as K-Tronic, blending gospel and deep house, then Donny Hathaway's "Someday We'll All Be Free." The episode also lists free D.C. mental health resources and Black mental health Instagram accounts for listeners seeking support.

D.C. Attorney General Brian Schwab and At-Large Councilmember Christina Henderson sent a joint letter alleging the Department of Behavioral Health illegally directed $10.7 million in opioid settlement funds toward unauthorized purposes — and host Ambrose Lane Jr. reads every word of it on air. Among the alleged misuses: approximately $2.3 million put toward covering the District's Medicaid local match, a purpose the letter says does not meet the legal criteria for those funds. Lane is himself one of over 40 signatories on a related community letter, and he says he is writing an article asking whether the money is being stolen. From there he traces a week of Black history from August 17–23, identifying the 1989 murder of Yusef Hawkins in Bensonhurst, New York as the basis for the Public Enemy song "Fight the Power."

The program then turns to an extended segment from the Geopolitical Economy Report tying together Japan's yen carry trade, the Bank of Japan's nearly $1.2 trillion in U.S. Treasury holdings, and the U.S. Treasury's use of euro reserves to prop up the yen. Economist Barry Eichengreen's verdict: the dollar is "not the attractive reserve currency it once was.

Richard Van Dyke walked 4.5 to 5 miles a day, steamed unseasoned asparagus and kale, and brought his hemoglobin A1c from 6.5 down to 5.5 — then came off diabetes medication entirely. Attorney Patricia Grady grew organic vegetables across four garden plots at her church, drank 64 ounces of alkaline water daily, and watched her blood pressure drop from readings as high as 180–190 to 118/77. Host Dr. Theodore Watkins, now approaching 50 years since his medical school portrait went up on the wall, argues that lifestyle intervention was once the first line of treatment in medical textbooks before it largely disappeared from practice. On *To Your Health*, he interviews both patients about the diet changes, cleansing program, and daily check-ins that drove those results.

Van Dyke and Grady walk through the specifics of what the shift looked like for each of them.

Mayor Muriel Bowser's $3.875 million grant is now open to independently owned D.C. brick-and-mortar restaurants and retailers with no more than three locations that lost revenue in 2025. From that, host Seysha Lamira turns to Poplar Island in the Chesapeake Bay, where dredge material from Port of Baltimore shipping channels has rebuilt a 1,700-acre wildlife habitat supporting over 260 bird species and a growing diamondback terrapin population.

The island has its own buried history. Waterman Willie Rowe once salvaged headstones from Poplar Island's submerged cemetery and kept them in his yard for more than 50 years before Lee Howarth's family recovered them and returned them to the island. The episode features music from local artists Chloe Jai and Yusuf Latif.

A Maryland man tells *Make It Plain* host Reverend Mark Thompson he has not voted in nearly 70 years. That call opens a wide-ranging phones segment on third-party politics — the Umoja Party, the Working Families Party, the DSA — alongside a Virginia political consultant running four Northern Virginia races who argues the Democratic Party would be four separate parties if it were in Europe.

Terrence Woodbury, president of HIT Strategies, then presents findings from his organization's *State of Black Opposition and Engagement* research. Among the results: 62% of Black respondents said no one had asked them to join resistance activities, and Black approval of ICE sits at 6%. The share of Black Americans taking three or more civic actions climbed from 64% in October 2025 to 75% by April, a rise Woodbury ties partly to what he calls the "Kale decision" and escalating attacks on Black political power in the South. His polling also shows that corporations and special interests rank above Donald Trump on Black voters' list of who is most responsible for undermining democracy.

Gerald Horne calls Nat Turner's 1831 Southampton rebellion a revolt of "the unpaid sector of the working class," and that framing sets the tone for the entire hour. Horne, author of more than 40 books and Chair of History and African American Studies at the University of Houston, joins civil rights activist Larry Hamm on *To Heal DC* with host Joni to mark the 195th anniversary of the uprising. He connects it to a lesser-known 1835 slave revolt across a wide swath of Mississippi, and argues that August 1st — the date of Caribbean emancipation — deserves recognition alongside Juneteenth as a date of solidarity.

The second half becomes an impromptu tribute to Rami Cheeks: a native Washingtonian who co-founded the Clubhouse, a Black LGBTQ social club in mid-1970s D.C., helped build Us Helping Us, one of the first Black HIV/AIDS organizations in the city, and established a Unity Fellowship Church congregation in Detroit in 1994. Chuck Hicks recalls that Cheeks and Andre Scott secured a $350,000 grant for Black-led AIDS organizations and persuaded the D.C. mayor to require HIV/AIDS training for all District government employees. Beatitude Zachary Jones of the Unity Fellowship Church movement also appears among the guests.

When unemployment falls because workers stop looking, that's not progress — Dr. Kyle Moore, newly appointed chief economist at the Century Foundation, explains why July's drop signals stagnation and why Black workers depend on a tight labor market to make any movement toward equity. He connects Strait of Hormuz disruptions and the administration's tariff reversals to prices corporations have no obligation to lower, even after courts ruled those tariffs illegal. Then Dr. Starsky Wilson, CEO of the Children's Defense Fund, walks through the administration's proposed Head Start rule changes: higher student-to-teacher ratios, removal of prohibitions on corporal punishment and seclusion, an English-only provision, and a ban on "preferencing" — in a program whose enrollment is 29% Black and 40% Hispanic.
