Garland Nixon opens with a number: Niger gets roughly $2 an ounce for uranium that France then sells for around $250. That gap, he argues, is the through-line connecting every U.S. war since World War II — not ideology, but colonial extraction. Iraq's oil revenue has flowed into a New York bank since the invasion, with Washington withholding it to block an elected prime minister. U.S. bombers hit poor Black neighborhoods in Panama during the operation to remove Noriega, deployed partly, Nixon says, to demonstrate capability to the Soviet Union.

The calls that follow push the conversation in different directions. A caller who identifies as part-Iranian pushes back hard on Nixon's figures for Iranian protest casualties. A 92-year-old listener who has known Nixon since childhood calls in to pledge. Nixon closes by explaining why he broke with the Democratic Socialists of America — their repetition, he says, of CIA talking points on Venezuela and Cuba.

On this episode of *Darker Than Blue*, the host covers two major stories: the mental health crisis aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, whose 5,000 sailors have spent a record 250 consecutive days at sea during combat operations against Iran, with Navy Times and Stars and Stripes reporting multiple attempts by sailors to jump overboard, moldy showers, broken toilets, and rations reduced at one point to half a cup of rice and two tortillas — conditions Trump, when asked at Joint Base Andrews, dismissed by saying the deployment was "not nearly long enough." The host also walks through Luigi Mangione's guilty plea in the killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson, reading Mangione's own courtroom statement describing years of untreated back pain, his email to UnitedHealthcare posing as an investor managing over $50 billion in assets to learn the conference location, and his use of a 3D printer to forge part of a firearm. Throughout, the host ties both stories to her own neighborhood near Joint Base Andrews, where military helicopters have been flying over daily since the bombing of Iran began.

shows.t: Resistance Radio with John and Regan
shows.desc:
Sharice Davids endorsed Markwayne Mullin for a Homeland Security post on one basis alone: he said he was Native. John Kane, broadcasting from the Cattaraugus territory of the Seneca Nation, uses that move to anchor a broader argument — that voting party lines is not civic engagement, and Native political figures are not exempt from the standard. Deb Haaland's gubernatorial run in New Mexico, he contends, rides institutional momentum, not grassroots origins. Peggy Flanagan served as lieutenant governor under Tim Walz while ICE operations intensified in Minnesota, and Kane puts the question of what she accomplished on the table.

He also connects the Osage murders depicted in *Killers of the Flower Moon* to the Tulsa Massacre roughly 50 miles away — Kane had the book's author on an earlier program and asked him directly about that omission. The hour was recorded during a WPFW fund drive, with co-host Jackie Luckman joining Kane throughout.

At St. Matthew's St. Joseph's Episcopal Church — a documented Underground Railroad hub since the 1840s — Detroit hosted a People's Tribunal in June 2026 to coordinate resistance to ICE. Abayomi Azikiwe, editor of the Pan-African Newswire, tells host Oscar Fernandez how the event grew out of Detroit Will Breathe, the Black Lives Matter group formed after George Floyd's death, drawing small community groups from across Michigan. Azikiwe details conditions at the Northlake immigration detention facility in Baldwin, Michigan — 3.5 hours from Detroit — where detainees have recorded accounts of rotten food, beatings, racial targeting of Black and Latino inmates, and solitary confinement. Five women have died in recent months at the state's only women's detention facility, in Washtenaw County.

The conversation also covers how flock surveillance cameras and Michigan's ban on driver's licenses for undocumented residents make racial profiling routine on Detroit's southwest side, including the targeting of African migrants from countries like Senegal alongside Latin American migrants. A community campaign successfully stopped a planned ICE detention center near Detroit Metropolitan Airport in Romulus.

shows.t: Community Watch & Comment - Friday / The Local Station Board Show (Last Frid
shows.desc: **Community Watch and Comment** with hosts Ron Pinchback and Chip Jones opens with two policy debates drawing listener calls: a South Carolina Republican congresswoman's bill to reinstate the death penalty in D.C. — which one co-host notes would bypass DC residents' vote entirely — and the Department of Homeland Security's plan to equip ICE agents with shock gloves that deliver a debilitating electrical charge through skin contact and, unlike tasers, leave no marks. Callers raise the Innocence Project's record of exonerating people of color on death row, the closure of Lorton prison and its aftermath, and a listener named Joni reminds the hosts that WPFW's own former program director Tom Porter led the campaign against the death penalty in D.C. in the early 1990s, a piece of the station's history she ties to its approaching 50th anniversary.

A major petrochemical company called the FBI on Dr. Lemire Toran simply for writing a report on human health impacts. Toran, a Howard University professor in its new Department of Earth, Environment, and Equity, discusses his book *Unlearned Power: Strengthening Communities in the Age of Environmental Crisis*, which moves from the Onondaga Nation through communities across the country. The title carries a double meaning: rethinking literal energy systems, and dismantling the political and socioeconomic arrangements that have placed Black, brown, and Indigenous communities in what host Rev. Yearwood calls "the path of least resistance."

Yearwood brings his own recent work into the conversation. At the NABJ conference in Atlanta, he argued that the progressive climate movement is in a "crisis of imagination" and must do better at storytelling and narrative — a conviction that runs through his own work producing climate documentaries, including *Plastic Detox*, currently on Netflix.

Mongo Santamaría composed "Afro Blue" before John Coltrane made it famous, then scored a 1962 hit with Herbie Hancock's "Watermelon Man." Rusty Hassan's *Afro-Cuban Connection* uses that arc to anchor a centennial tribute to Cuba, tracing the thread between Cuban music and American jazz. From Santamaría, the episode moves through Irakere, the Cuban group that included Paquito D'Rivera and Arturo Sandoval and landed a Columbia Records contract after Dizzy Gillespie's return visit to the island. Hassan also recalls seeing Celia Cruz perform on a chilly night at the Sylvan Theater near the Washington Monument.

The hour opens and closes with a deliberate pairing: the Afro-Cuban Jazz Orchestra of Chico O'Farrill's "Egoist's Dream" beside his son Arturo O'Farrill's *Dreaming in Lions*, the two recordings linked by their titles as a programming choice.

Mario Bauza introduced Dizzy Gillespie to percussionist Chano Pozo, and what followed were the 1947–48 recordings — "Manteca" among them — that Pozo made with Gillespie's big band before he was killed in New York City. Rusty Hassan's Thursday late-night program, recast as "the Afro-Cuban Connection," builds outward from that origin to trace the musical bond between Cuban and American jazz musicians from the 1940s onward.

The episode moves through Chano Pozo's recordings with James Moody and Art Blakey's 1947 big band work, then follows Blakey to his 1949 trip to Africa. A Cuban track by Raul Paz, drawn from Hassan's wife's copy of *Putumayo Presents the Latin Party*, sits alongside Mongo Santamaría recorded live at the Black Hawk. The broadcast is part of WPFW's all-day tribute marking the centennial of Fidel Castro's birth, with a challenge grant in place to double listener donations made during the fundraising drive.

shows.t: The Rich and Varied Sounds of Cuban Music
shows.desc:
Kathleen Franks and Brother Jamil open this two-hour Cuban music special with Chucho Valdés and his ensemble Irakere — the group that once counted Arturo Sandoval among its members. The occasion is the centennial birthday of Fidel Castro, and the program moves chronologically, from bolero queen Olga Guillot and Bebo Valdés singing "Corazón Loco" to the Buena Vista Social Club's "Chan Chan."

From there the program turns to younger voices. Daimé Arónsina, described as Cuba's finest young female singer, and Yusa, a singer-songwriter from Havana's Buena Vista district who received two nominations at the 2003 BBC Radio 3 World Music Awards, both weave Afro-Cuban jazz together with hip-hop and rap influences.

When the Shelburne Hotel demanded a $10,000 deposit from Cuba's UN delegation and accused them of plucking live chickens, Malcolm X personally invited Fidel Castro to stay at Harlem's Black-owned Hotel Teresa instead. That 1960 standoff opens this Cuba Libre special hosted by Anthony Rogers-Wright. Scholar-musician Joe Consol Sr. traces the African roots of Afro-Cuban jazz through Mario Bauzá and Machito forming the Afro-Cubans in 1941 and composing "Tanga" in 1943.

The music shares the hour with the present. Manolo de los Santos of the People's Forum describes Cuba's national grid collapsing five times in one year under a US oil blockade that, according to the Center for Economic and Policy Research, has more than doubled Cuba's infant mortality rate. Cuba's answer to that crisis was 49 new solar parks brought online, pushing solar-generated electricity from 5.8 percent to over 20 percent of national output in roughly twelve months, with equipment and financing from China.

shows.t: Participatory Democracy and Social Transformation in Cuba
shows.desc:
On the 100th birthday of Fidel Castro (August 13, 1926), host Baba Izay's #YouMustLearn program features an interview with Cuban Deputy Head of Mission Sister Dieguez. She describes how Cuba's 2022 Families Code went through more than 70,000 community meetings and was revised by 60% before passage. She also reports that an executive order issued since January has left more than 96,000 Cubans waiting for surgeries, including 12,000 children.

The second voice in the program is filmmaker Catherine Murphy, whose documentary *Maestra* examines Cuba's 1961 literacy campaign. Fidel Castro announced at the UN General Assembly that Cuba would become fully literate within one year — and it did, reducing illiteracy from above 40% in some rural areas to below 4%. Murphy notes that *Maestra* is available to stream free on Kanopy with a public library card and will screen at Sankofa on August 29th, hosted by Africa World Now Project.

Mark Friedman of the Hands Off Cuba Committee puts a number on what the U.S. blockade means right now: 7,000 containers of food, medical supplies, and solar panels stranded in Caribbean and European ports because no shipping company will challenge it. One oil tanker allowed through in seven months. Daily blackouts of up to 22 or 24 hours that he says have contributed to the deaths of 1,800 infants in hospital ICU units.

That account sets the frame for the rest of the hour on *Unionism Drives Community*, hosted by Renee Bowser. Amber Longo, a Teamsters organizer at an Amazon warehouse in California's Inland Empire, attended the May Day parade in Havana and watched Cuban workers march past the U.S. Embassy on electric motorbikes — a direct demonstration against the fuel blockade. She also describes a meeting with the president of the Central de Trabajadores de Cuba, where she learned that three elected workers sit on every factory executive board alongside one manager and one Communist Party representative. César Omar Sánchez of the National Network on Cuba joins as the third guest.

shows.t: Playing Dirty: Rubio’s War on Cuban Athletes
shows.desc:
A Cuban basketball team beat the United States in Havana in 2024 — the first time in 53 years — and then Marco Rubio's visa policy barred them from traveling to compete on American soil. Chuck Modiano speaks with Reid Lindsay, journalist and documentary filmmaker with Belly of the Beast, about how that policy is playing out across Cuban athletics on *The Collision*. Lindsay's documentary *Safe at Home* profiles a pitcher who signed with Cleveland for $300,000, renounced the contract, kept the signing bonus, and went home to the Cuban countryside. That story opens onto a broader pattern: the MLB deal negotiated during the Obama opening would have let players remain in Cuba until their mid-twenties before signing abroad, but Trump cancelled it in his first term.

The conversation moves to the May 2025 secondary sanctions threatening foreign companies and their family members for doing business with Cuba, and to the longer history behind these policies. Lindsay traces the Cuban American lobbying apparatus back to advice and organizational help from AIPAC in the early 1980s.

Obi Agbonna — playwright, organizer, and producer — co-produced the Kutulumela Bolingo with Russell Schultz, son of former Black Panther Russell Maroon Schultz: a 30-song double album honoring Assata Shakur and Pauline Lumumba and supporting the roughly 4,000 Cuban doctors currently working on the African continent. Agbonna joins development intern Sunit Teklaab and co-host Netfa Freeman to trace Cuba's solidarity with Africa well past the Angola campaign, back to the first Cuban medical mission to Algeria in 1963, and through the training of 3,000 Zimbabwean teachers in Cuba between 1986 and 1996 — a program Agbonna credits for Zimbabwe's 97% literacy rate. He details how Fidel Castro deliberately recognized non-Marxist African revolutionary leaders — Kwame Nkrumah, Sékou Touré, and Thomas Sankara, the first African head of state to receive the Martí Award — as an explicit challenge to Soviet criteria for authentic revolutionaries.

The hour features album tracks including "Wounded Wombs" and "Mothers in the Revolution," and draws a line between two acts of resistance separated by decades. One is Pauline Lumumba's bare-breasted march of 100 women on the United Nations headquarters in the Congo. The other is the ongoing campaign to remove Assata Shakur from the U.S. terrorism list and lift the $2 million bounty on her head.

shows.t: Culture and the Human Resilience of the Cuban People
shows.desc:
Fidel Castro was mid-speech, drinks in hand all around, and Alice Walker had to sit down — she couldn't follow a Castro lecture and keep standing at the same time. Walker, who grew up in the Deep South, tells host Katea Stitt on *Cuba Libre* that Castro's 1959 rise "meant everything" to poor Black Southerners being lynched and beaten. She also recounts Celia Sánchez's largely unrecognized work steering the revolution against the sexual exploitation of children by mobsters running gambling operations on the island. Walker has made four trips to Cuba in total.

That history of connection runs forward into the present. Busboys and Poets founder Andy Shallal describes the 2024 unveiling of a bust of Langston Hughes at the House of Poetry in Old Havana, sculpted by Cuban sculptor Duett Laskay. Hughes had translated the poems of Cuban national poet Nicolás Guillén into a collection also titled *Cuba Libre*, and the two men's verse shared a foundation in blues and son rhythms.

shows.t: Diversity and Engagement in the Diaspora
shows.desc:
Danny Valdez grew up in Miami believing his grandfather had been jailed for his beliefs — then discovered the man was actually a cop under the previous regime who had been funneling money to anti-revolutionary groups. That unraveling led Valdez to co-found Cuban Americans for Cuba, an organization he describes as a Cuban American counterweight to AIPAC. In March, he traveled to Havana as part of the Nuestra América convoy, organized in response to the Trump administration's oil blockade on Cuba; strangers on the street stopped the group to thank them for coming.

This hour is part of WPFW's 24-hour Cuba Libre programming marking the centennial birthday of Fidel Castro. The conversation also takes in the Venceremos Brigade's decades of annual work-delegations to Cuba, the 2019 Cuban constitutional reforms that followed the Obama-era normalization period, and Cuba's development of medications for Alzheimer's, lung cancer, and a diabetes treatment credited with preventing amputations.

DJ Abby closes with Bobby Céspedes's *Si Agua No Llueve, Maíz No Crece* — "If it doesn't rain, corn doesn't grow" — framing it as commentary on current conditions and a call to lift the U.S. blockade on Cuba. That closing choice is one thread in a larger design: this *Cuba Libre* broadcast on WPFW marks the centennial birthday of Fidel Castro with a daylong fundraiser built around what DJ Abby calls an "ajiaco" mix, named for a Cuban stew she describes as a metaphor for the Cuban people — multiple elements and textures blending, against America's melting-pot homogenization.

Two all-women salsa orchestras anchor the music, Son Damas and Orquesta Anacoana, alongside Los Van Van, Daimé Arocena, Ibeji, and Céspedes. Host Katea Stitt will also speak with Alice Walker and Andy Shallal about Cuba and Castro — Walker among those who met Castro many times.

In 1984, Benjamin Chavis Jr. introduced Fidel Castro at a United Methodist Church in Havana — the first time Castro had entered a Christian church since the Cuban Revolution. Chavis was there as a PhD student at Union Theological Seminary with the Black Theology Project, on the same visit that brought Jesse Jackson to negotiate the release of Cuban political prisoners. Speaking with host Julianne Malveaux, Chavis also describes being present with Cuban troops during the 1980s Battle of Cuito Canavale in Angola, where Castro had conditioned troop withdrawal on South Africa freeing Nelson Mandela, while the Reagan administration backed the apartheid regime's designs on Angola, Namibia, Botswana, Zambia, and Zimbabwe.

Malveaux brings her own witness to the conversation. In May she traveled to Cuba with a delegation led by Ron Daniels of the Center for the Black World, and she reports a baby who died when an incubator lost power during a rolling blackout. A medical student from the Bronx struggled to find vegetarian food because of transportation shortages, and a hospital visit left a colleague with a bill of eight dollars.

shows.t: The ELAM Model and Health as a Human Right
shows.desc:
Sitting across from Fidel Castro in Havana in 2001, Dr. Lucy Pérez suggested Cuba's meningitis vaccine could bring "fiscal resources" to the island. Castro turned her down flat. He also declined her invitation to the National Medical Association's annual convention in Hawaii, saying the only U.S. hotel he would stay in was the Hotel Teresa in Harlem. Pérez, past president of the NMA and former Black Panther Party member, traces her relationship with the Cuban health model back to her teenage years running a Free People's Clinic on Sutter Avenue in Brooklyn and teaching health door-to-door through the Party.

Her 2001 delegation visit to the Latin American School of Medicine found students receiving full tuition, housing, and food in exchange for a commitment to return and serve underserved communities in the United States. That same solidarity is the lens through which she examines Cuba's response to Hurricane Katrina — Castro offered a medical team for a full year while the Bush administration committed only six months — and the current toll of sanctions on Cuba's power grid, which Pérez says has left 100,000 surgeries unperformed and dialysis patients without treatment.

shows.t: Cuba: Master of its Own Destiny
shows.desc:
A waiting list of 100,000 Cubans needing surgery — 12,000 of them children — exists because a January 2025 executive order cut off oil supplies, leaving hospitals with only 2–3 hours of electricity per day. Cuba's Ambassador to the United Nations, Ernesto Soberón Guzmán, adds that 36,000 pregnant women cannot get an ultrasound. Bob Schwartz of Global Health Partners reports Cuba's infant mortality rate has nearly doubled to 10 deaths per 1,000 live births. His organization has worked to supply two Havana hospitals with incubators, ventilators, and prenatal nutrition, part of more than $280 million in medical supplies donated over three decades.

That history of deprivation did not begin in January 2025. Cultural scholar James Early traces the blockade to Eisenhower administration documents explicitly naming hunger and desperation as tools of regime change, then draws a line from that history through Malcolm X's welcome of the Cuban UN delegation in Harlem to today's push for congressional action. The program is hosted by Mimi Rosenberg.

shows.t: Buena Vista Social Club and Beyond
shows.desc:
A Washington judge ordered Kennedy Center trustees to pay jazz musician Chuck Redd $252,000 in legal fees — news Craig Williams broke mid-broadcast on his Morning Brew Classic Jazz Edition. The lawsuit stemmed from the cancellation of Redd's Christmas show, and a "Hands Around the Kennedy Center" rally was set for September 18th.

Williams used Ry Cooder's 1997 Buena Vista Social Club project, later paired with a Wim Wenders film, as an entry point into Cuban jazz's longer history. Roy Hargrove's Crisol band — featuring Chucho Valdés, Gary Bartz, and Russell Malone — shared the program with Mongo Santamaría's "Afro Blue" and "Elephant Pants." Jerry Gonzalez took on Monk's "Misterioso" from *Rumba para Monk*. Gonzalo Rubalcaba played "Transparency" alongside the late Charlie Haden on *Tokyo Adagio*, with further duets pairing Hilario Durán with David Virales.

shows.t: The Music Bed Presents Dalé Liberaciión
shows.desc:
DJ Cody V closes a three-hour set with Common's "Song for Assata," first telling listeners that ballistics evidence showed Assata Shakur could not have held the gun in question — and that her comrades later broke her out of prison before she lived in Cuba. That moment caps a centennial birthday tribute to Fidel Castro broadcast on WPFW, moving through classic Cuban boleros and Afro-Cuban music: Omara Portuondo, Ibrahim Ferrer, Antonio Machín, Tito Puente, and Dizzy Gillespie's rendition of Manteca.

The set is part of a full day of Cuba Libre programming. Program director Katea Stitt secured a $10,000 matching grant for it, which Craig Williams joins to announce. DJ Cody V previews the rest of the 24-hour schedule: Cuba's role in African liberation, the new Cuban Family Code, and a 2 p.m. hour featuring Alice Walker and Andy Shallal.

Fidel Castro's centennial birthday prompted WPFW to run a full 24-hour tribute to Cuba, and Saiz Kamaluddin opened it at midnight with this special edition of *Life Music*. The playlist ran from Celia Cruz and Tito Puente to Orquesta Revé, Harry Belafonte, the Fania All-Stars, Pancho Sanchez, and Johnny Pacheco, with Pérez Prado's "Patricia" in the mix alongside Kenny Dorham's "Aphrodisiac" from his album *Afro-Cuban*. Between sets, Kamaluddin told listeners that later in the day they would hear stories, information about current conditions in Cuba, and ways to help. The broadcast ran from midnight to 2 a.m.

Eugenia Charles opens by arguing that the Bois-Caïman gathering of 1791 was not primarily a spiritual ceremony but a strategic political meeting — one that took twelve years to organize, carried out underground by women and men traveling routes unknown to slave masters in Saint-Domingue. That reframing anchors the anniversary episode of Konbit Lakay. The second half airs a segment from a WBAI special report on the TPS crisis, including New York Mayor Mamdani's statement explaining that the city was forced to separate Haitian municipal workers after the Supreme Court's 6-3 decision lifted a stay on ending TPS for 350,000 Haitians. Civil rights attorney Norman Siegel joins other guests to debate whether the city's move will trigger a cascading compliance effect across both the public and private sectors.

Ahmad performed at a Free D.C. Project rally the day before this recording, marking one year since Trump sent the National Guard to take over MPD. That event is the entry point into a Black August episode built around the four tenets — study, fast, train, and fight — that incarcerated people at San Quentin Prison first observed in 1979 to honor George Jackson and other Black freedom fighters.

Young members of the Freedom Futures Collective take turns at the mic, weaving original music through roundtable conversation about community control over food and funding, the racial wealth gap, and police brutality. One host reaches for Maya Angelou's "Still I Rise" and her work alongside Martin Luther King and Malcolm X to argue that training should point toward liberation, not personal success. The collective names what they hope will no longer define Black life in America by 2076.

FBI agents don't give up easily. When a teenager turned them away the day after they watched National Guard pull a kid off a Lime bike, they came back with a taunt: they read out the names of the kid's incarcerated friends. Jawana Hardy, U.S. Air Force veteran and founder of Guns Down Friday, tells host Brother Sam PK Collins exactly how that unfolded, and how a Know Your Rights training led by Black Swan Academy made it possible.

Poet Janari Mitchell describes being handcuffed by four Park Police officers at Anacostia Metro Station on June 29th — the first day of a summer youth employment program — having her shoelaces and shorts drawstring removed, and sitting at the Park Police station at Haines Point for hours before charges were dropped. Mitchell names it plainly: a pattern of data collection and surveillance targeting Black youth. Both guests are speaking from communities east of the Anacostia River, at the one-year mark of what Collins calls the federal occupation of Washington, DC.

Ta-Nehisi Coates grew up watching the nightly news with his Baltimore parents, who talked about Israelis and Palestinians in terms of "who was oppressed, who was not." He later dismissed that framing as too simple, then traveled, wrote *The Message*, and concluded that "the basic morality that I had grown up with actually probably had more to say about the world." In November 2023 he hosted a private gathering at his home, bringing together Palestinian Americans and Black journalists to talk through what was happening and what was coming.

Host Zain Al-Amin, a WPFW volunteer for seven or eight years, anchors the interview in the argument that domestic and international injustice are inextricable, citing the Martin Luther King line about bombs dropped on Vietnam falling on American cities. One measure of what that means in practice: a journalist Al-Amin had lined up to speak from South Lebanon went dark for two weeks — she was in an area under bombardment.

At Busboys and Poets, Linda Penzey-Gunther reads aloud from her book *No to Nuclear* about the assassination of Patrice Lumumba, then pivots to Operation Plumbat, a covert Israeli operation that smuggled Congolese uranium to the Dimona nuclear center. The ore came from the Shinkolobwe mine in the Belgian Congo, grading at roughly 65% purity against 0.5% in Canada or Czechoslovakia — which is why it mattered so much to the Manhattan Project. Maurice Carney, executive director of Friends of the Congo, traces that supply chain forward into present-day conflict over the DRC's minerals.

Penzey-Gunther also covers Navajo miners told uranium extraction was their "patriotic duty," who worked without protective gear and are now surrounded by at least 500 abandoned mines on their land. Host Mwiza Munthali closes with a pledge-drive segment dedicating the fundraising goal to WPFW's first program director, Denise Oliver-Vélez, a Young Lord and Black Panther.

Marion Barry walked out of a Howard University appointment, saw a van pull up, and broke down crying — it was full of Black male amputees arriving for dialysis. Kim Dickens recounts that moment, and it anchors *To Heal D.C.*, which tracks why Washington, D.C. has the highest kidney disease rate of any city in the United States, with some Southeast D.C. zip codes running four times the national average. Dr. Clive Callender, the transplant surgeon who performed Barry's own 2009 kidney transplant, makes that case.

Dr. Theodore Watkins goes further: lab reference ranges classify stage-two and stage-three kidney failure as normal, most physicians never share GFR numbers with patients, and Watkins describes reversing late-stage kidney failure using a plant-based diet and activated charcoal. The episode also hears from Katea Stitt, who gave a kidney to performance poet Sekou Sundiata around 2000 and found that six friends volunteered to be tested at Westchester Medical Center while only one family member did.

Diane Powell, founder and director of Community and Family Builders, wants you to notice the unopened mail, the accumulating boxes from excessive ordering, the forgotten steps for making coffee. These are warning signs of dementia, and she's specific about why Black women need to hear them. African Americans are twice as likely to develop dementia as their white counterparts, two-thirds of those diagnosed are women, and over 7 million people in the U.S. currently live with the disease. Powell gives out the Alzheimer's Association 24/7 hotline number on air.

That same clarity about where people are and what they don't yet know carries into the second conversation. Dr. Hattie Washington — Florida's 2026 Mother of the Year — describes walking onto Norfolk State's campus without having applied, not knowing college required an application or tuition. That story threads into her new book *Happy Motherhood Every Day*, launching on National Relaxation Day, August 15th. Host Faye Williams leads both conversations on *Wake Up and Stay Woke*, Wednesday, August 12, 2026.

Yajide Orenmila, president of the African National Women's Organization, calls it the "Arrest CPS" campaign — launched in 2016 after two Philadelphia mothers sought help and lost their children instead. On *What's at Stake*, host Denise Young pairs Orenmila with Dr. Annie Woodley Brown, retired Howard University professor of social work, to press on whether Child Protective Services protects Black children or polices Black families. Orenmila argues that when poverty-related neglect triggers removal, the money follows the child to foster care while the original family gets nothing — or gets sent to anger management classes they didn't need, arriving angry only because their children were taken. Dr. Woodley Brown answers with the history of family preservation programs, kinship care, and the professional development of "cultural competency" in risk assessment to prevent one-size-fits-all removal.

The hour also carries audio from a series by the late journalist and activist Ambrose I. Lane Sr., reading verbatim from 1690s South Carolina statutes — including the law specifying the exact grades of cloth enslaved people were permitted to wear.

Muhammad al-Kuwaiti, speaking one month before he was killed, described losing his wife, his son, and every piece of archived work he had made since 2005 in a single strike. His words come from the Living Record Project, an unreleased oral archive built by Writers Against the War on Gaza from testimony by Gaza journalists about their killed colleagues. Translated from Arabic by volunteers and read aloud, these testimonies were aired for the first time anywhere on Liberation on Our Minds, broadcast August 11, 2026, by the DMV chapter of the Palestinian Youth Movement. A WAWAG member named Sami explained that the project emerged from criticism that Western memorials cast martyred journalists as isolated individual heroes rather than a collective. He also described the challenge of building a website that resists reducing people to "little boxes on a web page or numbers in a database."

The archive holds other voices. A colleague remembers Anas al-Sharif saying he spoke "the language of the street" deliberately, so his message would reach "the ignorant before the educated." A colleague of Mahmoud al-Nauq describes how he opened his home in Deir el-Balah to everyone fleeing the north, then was killed two days after their last phone call, along with roughly twenty members of his family.

Malcolm X's voice opens this episode of *Full Spectrum* — his "Ballot or the Bullet" speech played as evidence that Black voters' loyalty to the Democratic Party proves his own charge that they are "chumps." From there, host Anthony Rogers-Wright and guest Jacqueline Luqman, host of *Darker Than Blue*, trace what they call the party's slide from de facto to de jure racism through the 1965 Moynihan Report, the 1994 Crime Bill, and the rise of the Democratic Leadership Council under Bill Clinton.

That historical arc finds a live example in a recent clip of Democratic strategist James Carville, who dismisses Kamala Harris's 2028 chances and says the path to the nomination runs through making Black voters in South Carolina "hum and sway." Rogers-Wright and Luqman take that line as evidence of what they call the party's contempt for Black material needs. The episode closes on Rogers-Wright's concept of "fourth-way politics," applied to Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez: her 2021 Met Gala appearance in a "tax the rich" dress and her defense of the Biden administration's deportation record in an interview with *Jacobin*.

Ambassador Melenin Lakal, Deputy Representative of the Sahrawi Republic to the African Union, tells Black Agenda Radio host Margaret Kimberley that a 1975 deal Kissinger helped engineer set the foundation for fifty years of Moroccan occupation of Western Sahara. Morocco has since weaponized that position — deploying mass migration into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, Pegasus spyware against Spanish Prime Minister Sánchez, and a drug-trafficking network worth an estimated $23 billion to press European governments into accepting its claims.

Detroit-based journalist and activist Abayomi Azikiwe turns to a closer contest: the Michigan Democratic Senate primary, where Dr. Abdul El-Sayed defeated AIPAC-backed incumbent Haley Stevens despite an estimated $60–70 million spent against him. Azikiwe examines a generational fault line in Detroit — older Black voters broke roughly 60–40 for Stevens while younger voters backed El-Sayed — and connects that divide to the Flint water crisis, deindustrialization, and the broader erosion of Democratic Party legitimacy.

Carlos Mare 139 was painting subway cars in the South Bronx before hip-hop had a name. Now his b-boy sculptures and large-scale paintings, influenced by the Italian Futurists, anchor two simultaneous exhibitions. One just opened on the site of the former Spofford Detention Center in the South Bronx, centered on a Truth and Reconciliation Cypher through dance and words. The other is at the Museum of American Art in Washington, D.C., through the State Department's Arts in Embassies program. He joined host Mazi Mutafa on *Something to Say* alongside Michelle "Noodles" Smith — one of D.C.'s original B-Girls, a 37-year radio veteran, and founder of T-Con, a 10-year-old t-shirt and fashion convention at the Walter E. Washington Convention Center.

Smith started T-Con after customers kept bringing poorly made merch into her store Cookie Ware, and she is currently writing *The Pioneers of Hip-Hop of Washington, D.C.: The Beginning*. The hour opened with 16-year-old Prince George's County poet Chimwekeli Okoro reading an untitled poem about leaving home, followed by additional youth poetry from the monthly open mic Slamtastic.

Dr. Anthony Fauci invoked his Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination more than 120 times before the Senate Homeland Security Committee in July 2026. That committee, chaired by Rand Paul, then voted 8 to 7 along party lines to refer a contempt charge to the Department of Justice. Paulina Vasilev hosts this episode of *Capitalism, Race, and Democracy*.

On the ground in San Francisco, SEIU 1021 mental health chapter president Augusto Guerra describes how his clinic serving Medicaid patients faces closure, accusing union leadership of "direct dealing" that used vulnerable clinics as bargaining chips to protect other workers' jobs. His colleague Cheryl Thornton adds that District 10 — San Francisco's largest and poorest district — has no pharmacies, leaving children with asthma unable to fill prescriptions. The episode then reaches back to 1968, where former Black Panther Party members Clarence Thomas and Judy Juanita explain how Juanita's discovery of a "2% rule" in San Francisco State's admissions office pushed student organizers to raise their open-enrollment demand from 40 to 400 students, building the base that made the strike possible.

After 50 years in classrooms, William Pernickis says the censorship he sees in U.S. public education today is the worst of his entire career. On The Project Censored Show, hosts Mickey Huff and Eleanor Goldfield talk with Pernickis and fellow Human Rights Educators USA co-founder Kristi Redelius-Palmer about building the first pre-K through 12th grade human rights curriculum in the country, developed in Minnesota in 2003, and teaching over 10,000 students — with human rights education required for graduation in one New Jersey school district. Journalist Kevin Gosztola then explains how his newsletter, the Elmwood Park Advocate, drew retaliation from his local library after it reported on uneven weed-code enforcement in his Chicago suburb — a fight that ended with him winning the Illinois Library Association's 2026 Intellectual Freedom Award. Gosztola also covers the House Ways and Means Committee's subpoenaing of Breakthrough News and his film-by-film series on post-9/11 propaganda, beginning with Black Hawk Down, running at weeklymatinee.substack.com.

Taylor Fraser McCollum's family homes sit less than a mile from the site of a proposed $5 billion, 820-megawatt data center campus in Landover. She launched a Change.org petition against it; after the Party for Socialism and Liberation promoted it on Instagram, signatures reached 25,000. David Rabin speaks with McCollum, who credits that pressure with securing Prince George's County's two-year moratorium and now argues for an outright ban on hyperscale data centers, warning that even closed-loop cooling systems discharge wastewater containing biocides, heavy metals, and corrosion inhibitors into the Potomac River — ranked the most endangered river in the United States. Steve Shapiro of Praxis Energy, who has testified before the Montgomery County Council, offers a different path: host communities issue requests for information that set enforceable terms on energy sourcing, property values, and noise before any developer enters negotiations. He points to a Google pilot in New Jersey that installs solar and battery equipment directly in residents' homes as one possible template.

In 1990, Tyrone Colbert received a life-plus-20-year sentence during the crack epidemic while his white co-defendants got five years. He joined *Crossroads* host Roach Brown to talk about his stage play *The Waiting Room*, which centers not on the incarcerated but on the women visiting them: wives, girlfriends, sisters, aunts making one-to-two-hour trips to facilities in Hagerstown and the Eastern Shore. The play draws directly from the life of his wife Ivy, who wrote to Colbert after reading his prison articles in Court of Harlem magazine and visited him for 14 years before Governor Hogan released him in 2022. One scene shows a woman confronted by an officer over her underwire bra.

Now a Justice Ambassador with Prison Fellowship, Colbert also discussed his advocacy trips to Capitol Hill on behalf of returning citizens and his interest in eventually writing a play about Fannie Lou Hamer. *The Waiting Room* runs two performances on September 20th at the Bethesda Writers Center; tickets are at tyvyproductions.com.

Onyeka Igwe noticed something about London's blue plaques: C.L.R. James and Paul Robeson were honored, but the women who worked alongside them — Una Marson, Amy Ashwood Garvey — were not. That absence drove her short film *A Radical Duet*, which imagines a 1947 London encounter between Nigerian activist Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti and a young Caribbean student-dancer based on Sylvia Wynter, the two women attempting to write a revolutionary play together. Igwe discussed the film with co-hosts Nefer Freeman and Craig; it screens August 14–16 at the African Diaspora International Film Festival DC at George Washington University.

The episode also marks the approaching centennial of Fidel Castro, pairing journalist Camila Escalante's report on an ALBA movements gathering at the University of Havana with archival audio of Kwame Ture. Ture argued that Cuba had sent more doctors to Africa than the United States and all of Western Europe combined, and recalled finding Cuban combatants among liberation movements including MPLA and FRELIMO when he first traveled to Africa in the 1960s.

A 4.5-by-6-foot cell at the Alameda County Jail — guards called it the Soul Breaker. In 1964, Huey P. Newton was locked inside one. Historian and retired judge Lisa Pearlman traces that world on *Building Bridges* with host Mimi Rosenberg, discussing her book *Huey P. Newton's Family: Roots of a Revolutionary Suicide* — the Newton family's passage through slavery, Jim Crow, and the Great Migration out of Alabama, Louisiana, and Arkansas to Oakland. She reads a second passage as well, linking Emmett Till's 1955 murder to the political awakening of David Hilliard, future Black Panther Party Chief of Staff.

Professor Emeritus Melvin Newton joins the conversation, explaining that the Black Panther Party's 10-point program was modeled on the Black Muslims' platform and crediting Ralph Ellison's *Invisible Man* with radicalizing his own thinking. D.L. Newton, Huey's nephew and treasurer of the Longshoremen's Union in Oakland, rounds out the program, describing recent work stoppages at the CNA Sugar Factory and at the docks to block ships carrying armaments.

Coach Queen Nai spent a decade married to a narcissistic partner. She has since opened a brick-and-mortar healing center in Woodbridge, Virginia — now in its fifth year — built specifically around narcissistic abuse recovery in LGBTQ+ communities. She tells host Mimi Magic how same-sex relationship abuse gets dismissed as "just a catfight," and why that erasure compounds the harm. Leaving a narcissist, she explains, produces neurological changes visible on brain scans.

Her recovery work draws on selenite wands, inner-child exercises, and nervous system regulation techniques. Queen Nai also announces she is removing tarot card readings from her booking menu in favor of intuitive and prophetic readings. Her book, *She Who Returns to Her*, is available on Amazon.

Scott Kratz of Building Bridges Across the River tells Ambrose Lane Jr. that last year's Back-to-School Festival handed out 750 backpacks in 45 minutes. This year's August 23rd event at the ARC on Mississippi Avenue in Ward 8 is scaling up to 2,000 backpacks, 700 pairs of shoes, 33 barbers, hair braiding, and free eye exams with same-day glasses.

Investigative journalist Eli Clifton, co-author of *Israel's Lobby: America in the Grip of a Foreign Power*, breaks down AIPAC's super PAC spending in the Michigan Democratic Senate primary in an excerpt from the Useful Idiots podcast: $32 million against Abdul El-Sayed, more than the combined $23 million spent to defeat Cori Bush and Jamaal Bowman, with 97% of those donations coming from outside Michigan. The programme closes with a Black history segment covering August 10th through 16th, marking Anna Julia Cooper's birth in 1858, Carol Moseley Braun's birth in 1947, and the 1965 Watts rebellion.

Dr. Theodore Watkins, host of *To Your Health*, once quit sugar and watched his chronic headaches disappear — then traced the cause back to his Saturday-night strawberry milkshake habit. From that starting point he explains how hyper-palatable foods trigger the brain's dopamine and endorphin systems the same way opiates do, with roughly 20% of the U.S. population affected and women addicted at nearly twice the rate of men. Treatment approaches include elimination diets, cognitive behavioral therapy, and fasting.

Co-host Frank Smith brings his own measure of what those changes can mean: he is now 13 years past a 2013 cancer diagnosis that gave him a six-percent survival chance, a margin he attributes to lifestyle change. Watkins widens the lens further, connecting Black Americans' kidney failure rate — four times that of white Americans — to diet-related hypertension and diabetes rather than genetics alone.

Alphonso Coles spent 20 years managing clinics in Ward 7 at D.C. General Hospital. What broke him was finding cigarette machines and 35-cent sodas in a building full of diabetic patients — and watching cardiologists eat badly in the cafeteria. He tells host Seisha Lemira how those observations led him to found Urban Seed, a proposed indoor farming and urban aquaculture operation built around a recirculating aquacultural system. It would grow branzino and vegetables year-round, sell them through an attached bodega, and carry halal and kosher certification alongside a partnership with UDC's urban agriculture program.

Lemira brings the same attention to a single ingredient in her "Story of Food" segment: chayote, the gourd-family vegetable pear standard in Louisiana Creole cooking but rarely appearing on DMV menus. She shares her father's recipe — chayote and tri-color peppers marinated in red wine vinegar, rice wine vinegar, balsamic vinegar, and hoisin sauce. Local tracks by Rent Riot and DSMB R round out the hour.

Among Black women who call themselves progressive, 54% of Gen Z also identify as Democratic Socialists — a number that stops Reverend Mark A. Thompson and Brother Minister Jamil Muhammad cold. Dr. Avis Jones-DeWeaver brings the data: the Annual Black Women's Roundtable Power of the Silent Vote Poll shows a 20-point surge in Black women's motivation to vote compared to two years earlier, and a 17-point increase since 2024 in the share identifying as strongly Democrat. Thompson and Muhammad tie the shift to federal worker layoffs, cuts to SNAP, and attacks on affirmative action, framing each as part of what they call an ongoing assault on Black women's economic security.

The broadcast falls during WPFW's summer pledge drive. Thompson also tells a story about his grandfather, director of admissions at Fisk University, where a young Marion Barry was a student before he came to Washington.

Washington D.C. has the highest rate of kidney disease in the United States, and Dr. Clive Callender — the Howard University transplant surgeon who performed Marion Barry's 2009 kidney transplant — explains on this episode of *To Heal DC* that 12 people die every day nationally from the shortage of organ donors, while Black Americans account for roughly 35% of end-stage kidney disease patients despite being 13.5% of the U.S. population. Dr. Theodore Watkins argues that doctors routinely fail to tell patients they are already in Stage 2 or 3 kidney failure — because a GFR reading the lab slip marks as the reference interval of "greater than 59" actually indicates third-stage failure — and describes reversing late-stage kidney disease in patients through a plant-based diet, activated charcoal, and walking. The second half features two kidney donors: Katea Stitt, who donated to performance poet and professor Sekou Sundiata in 2001 and recounts that six friends (only one a family member) volunteered to be tested together at Westchester Medical Center, and Kim Dickens, who describes the moment Barry wept in a parking lot after encountering a van full of Black men — all amputees, all headed to dialysis — and declared, "Now we have to do something about this."

Exxon and Chevron didn't discover new oil or build anything new, economist Brion Williams of the Groundwork Collaborative tells host Julianne Malveaux — the war in Iran simply repriced the barrels they already had overnight. That windfall went to shareholders, not consumers. An estimated $166 billion collected from Americans through tariffs has similarly never been returned to working families.

Najeeb Mujahid, founder of the Black August Planning Organization, anchors the observance to two fixed points: Jonathan Jackson's armed entry into a Marin County courthouse on August 7, 1970, and the assassination of George Jackson at San Quentin on August 21, 1971. The Black August Organizing Committee in California built the observance afterward around study, physical training, and fasting modeled partly on Ramadan; the Washington, D.C. observance began around 2008 or 2009. Mujahid cautions that a recent resurgence risks diluting what is a commemoration, not a celebration, and directs listeners to blackaugustpo.org for events.

In 1953, the CIA and British intelligence toppled Iranian Prime Minister Mohammad Mosaddegh after he moved to nationalize Iran's oil — then handed the U.S. 50 percent of the profits while ordinary Iranians received nothing. Host Garland Nixon opens *News Views* with that history and argues it is the only honest starting point for understanding current U.S.-Iran tensions. He builds from there into what he calls "imperial overstretch": hypersonic missiles and long-range drones have made the old colonial playbook unworkable, a case he illustrates with Yemen's demonstrated ability to threaten Red Sea shipping. The hour also covers the Belgian colonization of the Congo and France's extraction of uranium from Niger while most Nigerians had no electricity. Nixon draws a closing parallel between the Iranian Revolution's mosque-based organizing and the Black church networks that structured slave revolts in the antebellum South.

Dr. Abdul El-Sayed won the Michigan Democratic primary while being outspent 11 to 1 in what host Jackie and guest Anthony Rogers-Wright of Full Spectrum call the most expensive Senate race in the history of the country. That result becomes the entry point for a wider argument about racism inside the Democratic Party, AIPAC's reach into local elections, and what they describe as a new Red Scare. Central to that argument is a contrast between American resistance to socialist policies and unconditional support for Israel, which they argue already provides universal healthcare and free college tuition.

The conversation ranges back to the Democratic Leadership Council's reaction to Jesse Jackson's 1988 primary campaign, then forward to the Black Panther Party's rule requiring members to study two hours daily, and to the news that Puerto Rico is rationing water while hosting six data centers on the island. This is a pledge-drive edition of *Darker Than Blue*.

shows.t: Resistance Radio with John and Regan
shows.desc:
John Kane, broadcasting from the Cattaraugus territory of the Seneca Nation, asks why Native people were declared citizens in 1924 by an ordinary statute when a constitutional amendment was required to grant citizenship to people of African descent. He points to the "Indians not taxed" language in Section 2 of the 14th Amendment as evidence that the exclusion was deliberate. Hawaiians, he notes, received citizenship through a joint resolution of Congress that carries no force of law. Kane also breaks down why 70% of domestic violence against Native women is committed by non-Native men who cannot be prosecuted in tribal courts, and he criticizes the Deb Haaland-era report on residential schools for calculating redress based on what Congress spent committing the atrocity rather than on the harm caused.

Jacqueline Luqman joins Kane during the fund drive to discuss the citizenship arguments and take calls.

Martina Grifaldo's network had already been tracking ICE movements since 5:30 a.m. when the footage of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo's shooting death arrived at 7 — making her organization, Alianza Latina Internacional, among the first to post it. She tells host Oscar Fernandez how her 350,000-follower Facebook page uses coded language and fire emojis to flag ICE locations without triggering platform censorship. At a press conference included in the episode, Salgado Araujo's son explains that his father ran from the unmarked cars because he thought someone was trying to steal his work tools.

That death landed in a city already on edge. The previous week, 15 groups of construction workers — concrete workers, brick workers, and others — had staged a work stoppage over fear of workplace raids. Grifaldo also announces that a lawsuit against the Houston Police Department was set to be filed the following day, stemming from HPD holding a man for two hours until immigration officers arrived.

shows.t: Community Watch & Comment - Friday / The Local Station Board Show (Last Frid
shows.desc:
A Maryland kid was arrested for holding a bag of Doritos — flagged by an AI surveillance system that, one caller noted, is 8 to 10 times more likely to identify people of color as suspects. On *Community Watch and Comment Friday Edition*, hosts Ron Pinchback and Chip Jones took open phones on artificial intelligence, and the calls kept arriving with more.

Another caller drew a direct line to the nuclear arms race, arguing the U.S. rush to outpace China on AI repeats the same pattern of speed over safety. Proposed "kill switch" legislation would let agencies shut down AI systems that go rogue. Data centers are already driving up residential electricity and water costs, and even the coders building these systems don't fully understand how the decisions are being made.

This episode of Climate Friday, hosted by producer DeJuan Cross, features Sharon Lavine and her daughter Shamaya Lavine-Davey of Rise St. James, the grassroots organization fighting petrochemical expansion in St. James Parish, Louisiana — where Sharon describes founding the group after Louisiana's governor approved a Formosa Plastics facility two miles from her home in 2018. Sharon recounts how Rise St. James uncovered ancestral burial grounds on the proposed plant site, brought evidence including a book of ancestors' names compiled by an archaeologist to the parish council 17 months before Formosa did, and watched the council side with industry anyway; Shamaya then explains that a judge revoked Formosa's air permits in 2022, the decision was overturned on appeal, and Rise St. James is now seeking a Supreme Court appeal while new EPA rules limiting ethylene oxide emissions have put the project's economic viability in doubt. The episode also includes Rev Yearwood's TED Talk arguing that the climate movement suffers from a "crisis of imagination" — that it communicates from "the rage of the privileged" rather than from the communities dying from petrochemical pollution along Cancer Alley's 85-mile stretch between Baton Rouge and New Orleans — and closes with a conversation about the temporary federal pause on LNG permitting and the fossil fuel industry's practice of withdrawing school funding, including a computer lab and dance uniforms at a local high school, after losing a fight to build.

Cliff, co-founder of Blue Montessori on Marion Barry Avenue in Anacostia, teaches 3-to-6-year-olds using go-go drumming and HBCU-style marching. He argues that Montessori's emphasis on self-direction maps directly onto the demands of college and the workplace. His tuition-free school is in its third year.

Baba Ayize's #YouMustLearn turns next to film director Ime Atuk, whose film *Outdoor School* centers on a 12-year-old boy in 1994 Portland, Oregon living under a tree with his mother and sister while guarding a pair of neon Deion Sanders patent leather Nike shoes. After audiences at screenings were repeatedly affected by the film's treatment of domestic violence, Atuk began distributing a resource guide on the subject. He also recounts meeting a 12-year-old boy outside a theater in Ashland, Oregon whose family turned out to be in a situation mirroring the film's story. *Outdoor School* screens August 15th at the George Washington University Student Center as part of the ADIFF DC festival.

Amazon spent $5 million trying to stop Chris Smalls from organizing JFK8 and deliberately churned workers at over 150% annual turnover to keep wages at entry level and block collective identity from forming. Renee Bowser of *Unionism Drives Community* walks through Smalls' book *When the Revolution Comes: A Fight for the Future of the Working Class*, tracing how the Amazon Labor Union prevailed anyway at the Staten Island warehouse. That same company, in 2025, was required to pay $3.95 million to the District of Columbia after the Office of the Attorney General found it had diverted customer tips meant for Amazon Flex delivery drivers to offset their base wages.

A caller working for a Washington, D.C. landscape company raises the legal bar on agricultural workers forming unions in D.C., Virginia, and Maryland. That question carries the conversation into Biden-era Department of Labor regulations that may extend some organizing protections to those workers.

Jeffrey Herbsman called 911 saying "I think I may be a danger to others" and appeared on body camera audio saying "I killed her" — yet it was Michael Jackson Bolanos, a young Black Detroit man, who stood trial for the 2023 murder of Samantha Wohl, a Jewish community leader and founder of the Muslim Jewish Forum of Detroit. Host Jon Jeter of *Short Money: Dissecting Racial Capitalism* interviews Bolanos's defense attorney, Poorna Krishnamoorthi, who describes how prosecutors offered Herbsman immunity to testify only after she threatened to play his recorded confession for the jury. The jury acquitted Bolanos of murder.

The judge sentenced him to 18 months to 15 years in prison anyway, overriding a probation recommendation, for lying to police about checking car door handles. Krishnamoorthi and Jeter examine Wayne County prosecutor Kym Worthy's decision to charge Bolanos and place the case alongside other examples of disparate criminal-justice outcomes for Black defendants.

A 10-year-old Matt Damon lived next door to Howard Zinn in Boston, heard him typing *A People's History of the United States* through the wall, then went to school and argued Columbus was a monster — citing eyewitness Bartolomé de las Casas. On *Labor Heritage Power Hour*, host Chris Garlock interviews sports writer Dave Zirin about *The People's Historian: The Outsized Life of Howard Zinn*, six years in the making and Zirin's first non-sports book. They cover Zinn's union basketball team captaincy in the 1930s, his three produced plays including *Emma* and *Marx in Soho*, and how corporate broadcasters repeatedly passed on Matt Damon's attempts to adapt *A People's History* before it became *The People Speak* on the History Channel, with James Earl Jones, Chuck D, and Lupe Fiasco. The labor arts news segment reports Graham Nash and Jesse Wells canceling concerts at Richmond's Lewis Ginter Botanical Garden over a labor dispute, special effects workers across the Star Wars franchise organizing with IATSE, and the opening of *Woody Guthrie's American Song* in Washington, D.C.

Venezuelan oil revenue now flows straight into U.S. Treasuries, with Marco Rubio controlling its distribution — Code Pink co-founder Medea Benjamin tells host Marcy Winograd that the Venezuelan foreign minister had to walk back even mild criticism of a U.S. action after Trump objected. Dima Khatib, managing director of Al Jazeera's multilingual digital service, reports that Israeli military personnel arrived in Caracas in full uniform under a humanitarian label, delivering a national reconstruction plan following a June 24 earthquake and reversing nearly two decades of severed ties. A clip of Representative Ro Khanna describes his 90-minute detention in the West Bank by the IDF, which he says sided with armed settlers against him. Code Pink digital organizer Mikayla Heiser reports that over 18,000 Dallas residents have been taken by ICE and that Dallas Love Field Airport is being used to charter deportation flights. She also walks through how to start a local Code Pink chapter and join the organization's biweekly calling parties targeting institutions such as the American Medical Association over the imprisonment of Palestinian hospital director Dr. Hussam Abu Safia.

Carly Chardonnay Webb of OutSports opens with a blunt claim: the right wing has already lost the culture war — through Black quarterbacks, Jackie Robinson, and the WNBA's embrace of its queer fan base. The attacks on trans athletes, she argues, are less about sports than about erasing transgender Americans from public life entirely. She details Washington State's Ballot Initiative 638, which would require SRY gene testing of schoolchildren and includes a provision opening the door to genital inspection. That same morning, Connecticut Children's Hospital ended gender-affirming care and agreed to a $500,000 settlement with anti-trans parent groups.

Co-host Chuck Modiano joins from a Zoom court appearance stemming from his arrest at a protest outside the Delaney Hall ICE detention facility, where detainees had gone on hunger strike over maggots in the food. He and Dave Zirin turn to the Michigan Democratic primaries, including Abdul El-Sayed's victory despite being outspent roughly 10 to 1, and deliver a pointed critique of Bernie Sanders for failing to shield Cori Bush and Palestinian solidarity legislators when it mattered.

Tracy Childs McGee looked at the NEA's 24-book list for the U.S. 250th anniversary and noticed something: no Black women authors. That absence prompted her and a committee of 10 to build the Power Read 25 Initiative, a counter-list of 25 biographies of Black women. McGee walks host E. Ethelbert Miller through specific titles — among them Dana A. Williams's *Toni at Random*, covering Toni Morrison's years as an editor before her fame as a novelist, and Alexis Gumbs's biography of Audre Lorde.

McGee is also at work on her own Zora Neale Hurston biography, tentatively titled *Becoming Cosmic Zora*, centered on Hurston's time in Baltimore. She recounts how Robert Hemingway, author of a 1977 literary biography of Hurston, opened his research files to Valerie Boyd, whose *Wrapped in Rainbows* was published in 2003.

Viles Dorsainville, executive director of the Haitian Support Center in Springfield, Ohio, has watched TPS holders get summoned to ICE offices in Cincinnati and Westerville, fitted with ankle monitors, and offered $2,600 — money he says he has never seen anyone actually receive. Getting to those appointments is itself a problem: Springfield has no public transportation connecting it to either city, and TPS termination has stripped many holders of the ability to drive legally, leaving hundreds of community members dependent on others just to show up. Dorsainville, himself a plaintiff in a Northern California TPS case, tells host Eugenia Charles what that looks like on the ground.

The Haitian Support Center he now leads grew out of a specific moment of loss — it was founded in the aftermath of the 2023 school-bus accident that killed 11-year-old Aiden Clark. Dorsainville also raises two pieces of pending legislation: S.4814, which would extend TPS by three years, and S.2106, both of which listeners can bring to their representatives.

Liv Grace couldn't join the pandemic protests — immunocompromised family members were home — so she wrote "Hear Me Roar" instead, building it around a recitation of dozens of victims of police brutality. "I might not be able to breathe, but you gonna hear me roar." That track opens a "Pride, Purpose, Power Black August mashup" from the Freedom Futures Collective's *New World Order*, songs chosen, as the hosts put it, for "the streets, the study, and the spirit."

The hour moves through tracks by Suckatash (formerly Holding Access), Dynamism, and artists from the Afro Surrealist Research Bureau's seven-part *Black Noise for Black August* mixtape series, with the hosts drawing a continuous line from the 1803 Igbo Landing story — told in one interlude — to Tupac, James Brown, and Nat Turner.

Three police cars pulled David Black over mid-interview — his car in park — and handed him a ticket for being on his phone. Black, a DC native who spent 26 years in prison for a 1997 murder he says he didn't commit, was on the inaugural episode of *All Eyes on DC* to discuss a pending motion to vacate his conviction. The motion cites witness intimidation, recanted statements, and prosecutorial suppression of evidence. He also described repeated failed attempts, while incarcerated, to reach organizations including Roc Nation for help.

The conversation then turned to what community infrastructure looks like from the outside of a cell. Brother Johannes of Pan-African Community Action laid out the group's People's Transit Solidarity Program — launching August 8th at Anacostia Metro Station with free SmarTrip card distribution — as part of a strategy for community control over public infrastructure in Southeast DC. Host Sam P.K. Collins closed by invoking Mumia Abu-Jamal and Ida B. Wells, naming the show a platform for Black journalism that refuses to be "watered down.

Rukaiya Shamseddine drove through roughly 60 destroyed villages in South Lebanon — Arzoun, Ksaibe, At-Sheet — and recorded what she found: flattened neighborhoods, a bombed UNESCO-protected castle, demolished mosques, churches, and Roman-era ruins. Her field report airs on Zain Al-Amin's *Shay Nana Show* alongside an interview with Laith Marouf, founder of Radio Free Palestine. Marouf reads the Israeli strike on Al-Mansouri as a political message timed to undercut a Hezbollah speech by Secretary General Sheikh Naim al-Qassem. He also argues that HTS threats against Lebanon are being used as a "scarecrow" to build momentum for the Lebanese government's negotiations with Israel.

The hour opens elsewhere: Al-Amin on Abdul El-Sayed's narrow Michigan Senate primary win — called by NBC but disputed by the New York Times as too close to call — framing it alongside the "Mamdani tsunami" as evidence that candidates who focused on affordability and rejected corporate money beat the Democratic establishment.

Dr. Janaína Oliveira has a blunt verdict on Brazil's all-digital election system: it's the best in the world. The film curator, scholar, and activist joins *AfricaNow!* host Mwiza Munthali from Washington to survey the country ahead of its October 4th general elections. Four years of Bolsonaro's presidency, she argues, gutted public education and health — and the co-conspirators behind the January 2023 coup attempt ended up jailed alongside ordinary participants. Oliveira also takes on Brazil's high rates of feminicide and the Lula government's shift to state-led prevention campaigns. Current polls favor Lula over Jair Bolsonaro's son Flávio, even as a bank corruption scheme implicating the Bolsonaro family continues to unfold.

Oakland 8th-grade English teacher Gabriel Kahn did the math on CalSTRS's Israeli bond holdings: 6 thousandths of 1 percent of the portfolio, "an Uber from San Francisco to Oakland on a Saturday." He was one of the California teachers rallying outside a CalSTRS board meeting in Burlingame on July 23rd, demanding the pension fund divest from Israeli bonds and Palantir — even as CalSTRS bought more Israeli bonds after 2023. Felipe Luciano, co-founder of the Last Poets and first elected chairman of the Young Lords Party, remembers his friend Denise Oliver-Vélez, WPFW's founding program director, including the internal Young Lords criticism session that demoted him and elevated her to the Central Committee as its only woman member. University of Memphis historian Bryan Kuwoba traces how Caribbean-born Black Marxist Hubert Harrison was written out of history — by the Socialist Party, the Garvey movement, and the Harlem Renaissance framework alike — each reacting to his criticisms of them, a pattern Kuwoba examines in his book on Harrison.

Dr. Franklin Malone, president and CEO of 100 Fathers Incorporated, tells *Wake Up and Stay Awake* that the root problem in DC is not violence but fatherlessness. His organization recently held a ceremony at Howard University — the Restorers of the Covenant of Peace — giving posthumous awards to two deceased Council of Elders members. One honoree, Ray Savoy, brought 100 Fathers into DC schools including Ballou, Phelps, Woodson, Anacostia, and Friendship Collegiate, and taught young men golf at Langston Golf Course.

The hour, hosted by Dr. E. Fay Williams and airing during a station fundraising drive, also turns to Howard University itself. Dr. Robert Cosby, Assistant Dean for Administration at the Howard University School of Social Work, explains the school's dual master's programs — an on-campus "Flagship" and an online "Starship" — as it marks its 90th year. He currently teaches a doctoral course tracing social welfare history from 1619 forward, drawing on Nikole Hannah-Jones's work.

Forensic pathologist Dr. Nicole Jackson — who has performed over 2,000 autopsies and served as a medical examiner in Chicago and Seattle — tells host Verna Avery Brown that Mississippi illegally retained 18-year-old Nolan Wells's brain and neck structure, including the trachea, which should have been returned to the family's second pathologist, Dr. Roger Mitchell. Civil rights law professor Justin Hansford, executive director of the Thurgood Marshall Civil Rights Center at Howard University, draws a direct parallel to the 2014 Mike Brown case in Ferguson. A leak about Wells's alleged drinking, timed after release of a controversial Sea Tow phone-call audio, mirrors, Hansford argues, the character-assassination playbook used before that grand jury declined to indict.

The episode also turns to the longer history behind such patterns, with an archival clip from WPFW programmer Ambrose I. Lane Sr.'s series *Never Again for White Men Only*, tracing racist laws passed as early as 1690 in what became South Carolina.

Felipe Luciano — Afro-Puerto Rican poet, co-founder of the Young Lords and the Last Poets — recalls the night he was demoted after being drugged with angel dust at the apartment of a woman he later concluded was a police informant. He remembers Denise Oliver-Vélez, who died July 15th, as the person who held him accountable without condemning him as a person. Oliver-Vélez had been the first and only woman on the Young Lords' Central Committee and WPFW's founding program director.

The episode opens with audio from a July 23rd rally outside a CalSTRS board meeting in Burlingame, California, where Oakland teacher Gabriel Khan, speaking as an executive board member of the Oakland Education Association, said Israeli bonds represent six one-thousandths of one percent of the pension portfolio — and that CalSTRS bought more of them after 2023. Historian Bryan Cuoba then discusses his book *Hubert Harrison: Forbidden Genius of Black Radicalism*. Harrison, born to plantation workers in Saint Croix in 1883, founded the Colored Socialist Club in Harlem and edited the Garvey movement's *Negro World*, then was written out of socialist, Garveyist, and Harlem Renaissance histories for criticizing each of them. Hosted by Thomas O'Rourke on *Capitalism, Race, and Democracy*.

Jacqueline Luqman opens by noting that managing stress is hard enough "not worried about multiple genocides" — and that sets the register for the hour. Luqman, chair of the coordinating committee of the Black Alliance for Peace and a kidney-transplant recipient, joins host Anthony Rogers-Wright on this August pledge drive edition of *Full Spectrum*, Tuesday, August 4, 2026. Much of the conversation is shaped by the recently deceased historian Dr. Johanna Fernández, whose book on the Young Lords traces their role in the original Rainbow Coalition alongside Chairman Fred Hampton and the Black Panther Party. That history frames a sharp charge against today's Congressional Black Caucus: that the CBC PAC backed a candidate with $35 million in AIPAC money over Dr. Abdul El-Sayed in a Michigan primary running that same night, abandoning the redistributionist politics of the caucus's founders.

A clip from John Oliver's segment on predictive policing and license-plate readers draws Luqman's argument that Democratic city governments actively want racially biased surveillance technology to control working-class Black and Latinx youth. Resistance to that technology, she contends, has looked no different under Democrats than Republicans.

Dr. Charisse Burden-Stelly, author of *Black Scare, Red Scare: Theorizing Capitalist Racism in the United States*, says the Cuba document Marco Rubio authored reads like AI-generated text and functions as a pretext for a U.S. ground invasion. She draws a direct line from the Palmer Raids and McCarthyism to the RICO and conspiracy charges now being leveled against groups named in the report, including Black Alliance for Peace and Code Pink.

Kshama Sawant — former Seattle City Council member, now running as a socialist in Washington State's 9th Congressional District against 29-year incumbent Adam Smith — explains how her office won Seattle's minimum wage of $21.30 an hour, currently the highest in the nation. The method: treat Democratic colleagues as class enemies, not allies. She argues the same approach could force a floor vote on Medicare for All in Congress. Margaret Kimberley hosts.

A D.C.-born community organizer tells Mazi Mutafa that ancestral divination guided his decision to move his family to Benin Republic when Trump first took office. That choice came after years of trauma-relief and housing work at the D.C. Housing Authority, post-Katrina New Orleans, and rural Florida — work that included redeveloping the old Magnolia Project, now called Harmony Oaks. His wife Mina discusses her book *The Great Moment: 11 Powerful Secrets to Becoming an Authentic Radical Risk Giver*, which emerged from watching heart-centered CEOs, activists, and change agents "crumbling on the inside" while focused outward.

Gerald Watson, co-founder of Shaolin Jazz and Can I Kick It, traces his path from streetwear and lifestyle magazines *DC Pulse* and *Frank 151* to live film screenings where DJ Two Tone Jones builds a real-time soundtrack embedded scene by scene into movies like *Black Panther*. An outdoor screening is set for Skyland Town Center in Southeast D.C. on August 8th. A League of Women Voters of D.C. representative rounds out the program by outlining the Youth Voices for D.C. Statehood Showcase — open to ages 11–18 — scheduled for September 12th at the Festival Center in Adams Morgan.

An Oakland teacher standing outside CalSTRS's Burlingame board meeting puts the divestment demand in precise terms: the pension fund's Israeli government bonds and Palantir holdings add up to six-thousandths of one percent of the portfolio — roughly 67 cents on a million dollars — yet CalSTRS bought more Israeli bonds after 2023. Felipe Luciano, co-founder of the Young Lords and the Last Poets, remembers Denise Oliver-Vélez as someone who could move between street organizers, welfare mothers, and theoretical discussions of Albizu Campos and Marcus Garvey without shifting gears. He recalls the internal party session that demoted him and elevated her to the Central Committee, and reflects on her tenure as WPFW's first program director.

The history behind that kind of organizing runs deep. University of Memphis historian Bryan Kuwoba traces Hubert Harrison's founding of the Colored Socialist Club in Harlem to recruit Black workers the Socialist Party ignored. Harrison edited the Garvey movement's *Negro World* while simultaneously pushing the movement toward class consciousness. Kuwoba's book *Hubert Harrison: Forbidden Genius of Black Radicalism* examines how nearly every institution Harrison criticized then wrote him out of history.

Nadine Saech spent six months unable to place her article anywhere. The piece, "State Soldiers and Systematic Sadism: The Israeli Military's Normalization of Sexual Violence," documents state-sanctioned sexual torture in detention facilities while exposing what she calls "purple washing" — the Israeli Hasbara tactic of using women's empowerment narratives, including sexualized images of female IDF soldiers, to obscure it. A New York Times op-ed eventually broke the silence.

Nora Barrows-Friedman, associate editor at The Electronic Intifada, covers the ground that silence leaves untouched: Hamas's announcement that it would step down from governing Gaza, biometric-screened militarized "humanitarian" camps being constructed in the ruins of Rafah, and the United Nations Human Rights Office's count of at least six settler attacks per day in the occupied West Bank. Both guests speak with host Eleanor Goldfield on Project Censored.

Roach Brown says Dr. Frances Cress Welsing saved him from the electric chair — a fact, he notes, that most people who know her work have never heard. Brown did 14 years in prison and started his radio career at Lorton Reformatory with Petey Greene in 1973. He hosts this edition of *Crossroads Today* live from Ben's Chili Bowl, with David Rabin presenting.

His guest, Jay Jefferson, spent nine years as a correctional officer at Lorton from 1989 to 1998 and has written *Lorton Penitentiary: Rules Are Meant to Be Broken*. Jefferson describes arranging with a trusted inmate to protect a frightened fellow officer on his days off, and having a prisoner named Buddy Love back him in a confrontation over a bag of cigarettes — the same man he later recruited to speak to at-risk youth after Jefferson moved to the Metropolitan Police Department. Jefferson also notes that Welsing testified as the first Black psychiatrist at St. Elizabeths Hospital.

Walt Pavlov runs a newsletter called Prisonology. A returning citizen who tracks federal prison law, he told Crossroads host Roach Brown exactly how an Attorney General override of Bureau of Prisons designation decisions could be used to punish inmates for political reasons — pointing to Ghislaine Maxwell's transfer from a low-security facility to a camp as an early sign. Brown is broadcasting live from Ben's Chili Bowl on U Street for this conversation about what happened when Lorton closed and roughly 3,500 to 4,500 DC prisoners got scattered across the federal system. Pavlov also walks through the prison-census loophole that credits incarcerated DC residents to rural Southern and Western communities, and the Bureau of Prisons' drop from 230,000 to 150,000 inmates over roughly 14 years.

That drop in numbers has not kept people out of trouble with the system. Gwen Levi of Baltimore calls in: she was released under the CARES Act, took a class without reporting it, and was sent back to prison.

Mumia Abu-Jamal opens the August 4, 2026 edition of *Voices With Vision* by tracing Black August through three points: 1967 FBI memos ordering the disruption of Black liberation groups, the 1971 assassination of George Jackson at San Quentin, and the 1978 police raid on MOVE in Philadelphia, where the MOVE 9 were each sentenced to up to 100 years. Co-hosts Netfa Freeman and Brother Craig frame his recorded commentary.
