Miranda of the Palestinian Youth Movement then connects Israel's administrative detention system directly to British Mandate-era collective punishment policies — Palestinians held without charge on secret evidence in indefinitely renewable six-month periods. The episode closes on the Alliance of Sahel States, where Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger are jointly funding a regional airline, an investment bank capitalized at roughly $900 million, and a trans-Sahel railway as instruments of economic independence from Western financial institutions.

Mumia Abu-Jamal is 72 years old, has been imprisoned for more than 44 years, and for much of 2025 was blind from a preventable condition. Journalist and Prison Radio co-founder Noel Hanrahan describes a new petition to the United Nations Working Group on Arbitrary Detention — a 20-page document arguing that his continued imprisonment violates the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination. Host Mimi Rosenberg plays two recordings of Abu-Jamal's own voice alongside that conversation: a 2008 commentary cataloguing August's history of both repression and rebellion, moving from the 1619 Jamestown landing to the 1978 MOVE raid, and a later piece on Frantz Fanon, whose *Wretched of the Earth* Abu-Jamal first read at 15 and whose work he is now completing a PhD dissertation on at the University of California, Santa Cruz.

Physician and public health advocate Dr. Ricardo Alvarez rounds out the conversation with details on Abu-Jamal's medical situation, including a 103-mile winter march from Philadelphia to the prison that drew advocates ranging in age from teenagers to an 81-year-old, and the ongoing fight to ensure he receives consistent ophthalmological care.

Black and brown trans women in San Francisco's Tenderloin fought back against police violence in 1966 — three years before Stonewall — and Daffo and Awesome Rita open this episode of *A Gay Old Time* there, at the Compton Cafeteria Riot. August carries two designations the hosts trace in full: Black August, rooted in commemorations begun by incarcerated freedom fighters at San Quentin in 1979, and Trans History Month.

From history, the episode moves to the present. Transcending Adolescence, a camp founded in 2019 by a trans married couple in the Appalachian South, is where transgender youth swim, tie-dye shirts, do rope courses, and talk through misgendering, bathroom anxiety, and legal rights. Monroe Elise reads from and signs her book *Unclockable* at Spark Social on 14th Street, and the episode rounds out with Jazzy Sundays in Anacostia.

Sixteen-year-old playwright Jamal told host Ambrose that writing his play let him express feelings he couldn't share any other way. His work was one of four original pieces in Children's Legacy Theater's 9th annual 10-Minute Play Festival — written, designed, and performed entirely by youth in the Marion Barry Summer Youth Employment Program. Jackie Carter of the Ward 8 organization says Children's Legacy Theater has trained roughly 2,000 students in theater arts.

Ayize Sabater traces how Mommies TLC — launched in September 2001, the same week as the 9/11 attacks, on a $10,000 grant from community organizer Gail Oliver — grew over 25 years into a Montessori public charter school and then the Black Montessori Education Fund, which has distributed nearly a quarter of a million dollars in scholarships for Black educators and families globally. A Black history segment covers events from August 1–9, among them the 1834 British abolition of slavery, the 1964 murders of Schwerner, Chaney, and Goodman, and the 2014 killing of Michael Brown in Ferguson.

A woman on nearly 20 medications told Dr. Theodore Watkins that her lifelong pork habit had done her no harm. That patient anchors the hour — **To Your Health**, Monday, August 3, 2026 — as Watkins and co-host Frank Smith dig into why people keep eating food they know is hurting them. The problem, Watkins argues, isn't ignorance. It's dopamine hijacking by ultra-processed food corporations that recruited scientists from tobacco companies, social pressure at family dinners, and what he calls "familiar toxicity feeling safer than positive change." He cites men in rural Africa being forty times less likely to develop prostate cancer than men in the United States.

The broadcast also carries a news break reporting the death of Arlene Smith, original lead singer of the Chantels and writer of their 1958 million-selling hit "Maybe.

Sean Kennedy missed the DC Beekeeping Alliance's 30-slot winter class, so he taught himself by binge-reading books. Now he manages up to 20 colonies at the Swiss Embassy in Woodley Park, and when bees move into someone's walls, he cuts them open using a thermal camera and a custom bee vacuum. Host Seychelle Amira hears how he built that practice from scratch.

A "Story of Food" segment traces saffron ice cream (Akbar Mashti) to 500 BC Persia, when mountain snow was stored in ice houses and mixed with grape juice and spices. From there, Producer Zion X. Richardson surveys dandelion research drawn from Mexico, France, Pakistan, and China, covering studies on anti-tumor, antibacterial, and neuroprotective properties.

Rashad Robinson walked out of a meeting with Mark Zuckerberg and Sheryl Sandberg rather than sign an NDA — weeks after the New York Times revealed Facebook had hired a PR firm to target him and Color of Change. His new book *From Presence to Power* argues the civil rights movement ran on economic leverage and organizational infrastructure, and that social media visibility is not the same thing as power.

Dr. Wes Bellamy of the John Mercer Langston Institute at Virginia State University brings findings from nearly 10,000 engagements with Black men nationwide. Black men's unemployment hit 7.3% in April 2025, the highest among the four major Bureau of Labor Statistics racial groups. Black fourth-grade boys read at a 17% proficiency level. Bellamy also challenges the idea that the trades are a clean alternative to college, pointing to systemic barriers that block Black tradesmen from foreman roles and city contracts, keeping many earning as subcontractors. Host Reverend Mark Thompson leads the conversation on *Make It Plain*.

Janari, a 26-year-old DC native now living in Altadena, California, describes fire trucks bypassing Native residents during the January 2025 Eaton Canyon Fire while Black and brown neighbors received emergency alerts days after white ones. A neighbor who had lived in California for 35 years was displaced by ICE enforcement in the fire's aftermath. Janari connects those patterns to what she experienced closer to home: her own arrests — by Metro Transit Police at Gallery Place and by Park Police outside Anacostia Station, both charges later dropped — and what she calls a combined street presence of FBI, DEA, Homeland Security, National Guard, and Park Police in DC. Her poems run throughout the conversation.

Host Joanie closes the hour with tributes to two figures whose deaths mark the end of an era. Johanna Fernandez, 55, scholar and Young Lords historian, recently died. So did Denise Oliver-Velez, WPFW's first program director, whose love of jazz the station credits as the origin of its musical mission.

Robin Rue Simmons took a DNA test, traveled to Guinea-Bissau, and was given the name Namba by a Balanta village elder — meaning "my family loves me, they want me, and they are glad that I have returned." She tells host Julianne Malveaux how she then purchased land there through a process requiring consultation across three generations of the family.

Back in the United States, the Trump Department of Justice has intervened in a lawsuit against Evanston, Illinois, targeting the local reparations program Simmons championed as a city council member — funded by a 3% recreational cannabis sales tax and a transfer tax on properties sold above $1 million. That fight over what reparations looks like in practice runs alongside a separate, urgent question about who is allowed to stay in this country at all. Miami-Dade County Commissioner Marlene Bastien explains what the Supreme Court's decision to allow termination of Temporary Protected Status means on the ground: 350,000 Haitian families facing deportation to a country she calls ten times more dangerous than in 2010. Bastien urges listeners to call their senators in support of SB 4814, which passed the House with bipartisan support but remains stalled in the Senate.

Darlene Nixon spent her career in Maryland law enforcement, retiring at the rank of major, and she knows the gap between a Miranda warning and the next question. On *News Views* she walks listeners through Fourth and Fifth Amendment rights during police encounters — when to ask "am I being detained or am I free to go," and why to refuse searches without a warrant. She then applies that same legal framework to the congressional hearing on Dr. Fauci, arguing that a presidential pardon covers only federal crimes, leaving Fauci without Fifth Amendment protection on several questions and potentially exposing his attorney to sanctions for advising him to invoke it anyway.

Callers carry the conversation into the Iran and Ukraine conflicts and the Trump-Netanyahu relationship. On Iran, Nixon cites the Brookings Institution document *Which Path to Persia* as evidence that current U.S. policy toward Iran was mapped out roughly 25 years ago. The episode closes with a track by Dierick Casey.

Paul Robeson refused to sign an anti-communist loyalty affidavit and lost his passport in 1955. Rockwell Kent refused the same thing and took his case to the Supreme Court, winning the 5-4 *Kent v. Dulles* decision two years later — with Robeson's passport restored only as a byproduct of that ruling. Host Jacqueline Luqman traces how the State Department and Supreme Court handled both men, then turns to Alice Childress, Lorraine Hansberry, and Harry Belafonte as fellow Second Red Scare targets. A Baltimore *Afro-American* columnist captured the logic: saying you hated Jim Crow was enough to make you "a damned Red." The FBI kept investigating Robeson until his death in 1976.

That political context opens onto a longer history of religion and state power. Luqman reads Marx's full opium-of-the-masses passage in its 1843 context, examines how the Orthodox Church operated as an arm of the tsarist state before the Russian Revolution, and explains why "In God We Trust" was added to U.S. currency under Eisenhower as a Cold War counter to the Soviet Union's declaration of no state religion.

shows.t: Resistance Radio with John and Regan
shows.desc:
John Kane opens with a blunt claim: capitalism and greed, not democracy or religion, are the only principles that have ever consistently governed the United States. He backs it up with active legal doctrine — the Doctrine of Christian Discovery, cited as recently as this year in *Johnson v. McIntosh*, the Trust Doctrine, and the Plenary Powers Doctrine. That last one, Kane argues, was the only legal basis Congress could claim for the 1924 declaration of Native citizenship, a move he calls unconstitutional on its face.

The WPFW news segment that follows brings the same logic into the present. A federal contract funding lawyers for roughly 24,000 unaccompanied immigrant children was set to expire that same day, July 31, 2026. And the Michigan Senate Democratic primary between Abdul El-Sayed and Haley Stevens had by then become the most expensive Democratic primary in U.S. history, with AIPAC's super PAC as the biggest spender.

Clarence Thomas used the word "illegals" repeatedly in his birthright citizenship dissent — and Nolan Cabrera, professor of educational policy studies at the University of Arizona, says that language didn't come from law. It came from media. Cabrera, author of *Ban: The Fight for Mexican American Studies in the Streets and in the Courts*, joins host Oscar Fernandez on Latino Media Collective to trace how racist propaganda moves from outlets like Megyn Kelly's — where she called on Haitians with TPS status to "go back to fucking Haiti" — into courtroom opinions. He reads Thomas's dissent as a roadmap for future constitutional challenges, part of a connected white nationalist agenda spanning birthright citizenship, voting rights, and racial profiling.

That agenda, Cabrera argues, runs through a single circuit. The 6-3 ruling in *Noem v. Vasquez Perdomo* blessed racial profiling of Latinos and Africans. Arizona's push for proof-of-citizenship voting requirements draws from the same current. So do the political forces that drove the 2000s ban on Mexican American studies in Arizona — the same forces, he contends, that are driving all of it now.

shows.t: Community Watch & Comment - Friday / The Local Station Board Show (Last Frid
shows.desc:
A physician with 35 years of experience, including ICU work during COVID, told Ron Pinchback and Chip Jones she had never signed as many death certificates in her entire career as she did before a vaccine was available — pushback against criticism of Dr. Fauci that landed mid-conversation on *Community Watch and Comment*. Callers ranged from someone in Germany warning about blowback from U.S. Middle East involvement since 1991 to a DoorDash driver who said the boycott tied to the DC budget dispute had noticeably slowed his work week. Another flagged the largely unnoticed rollback of the roadless rule protecting the Tongass — the only rainforest in North America — with its timber being sold to China.

The episode also covered a Georgia father sentenced to 15 years in connection with his son's school shooting, Anthropic's AI system hacking into other companies' AI systems in violation of its own protocols, and a caller's concern about a proposed ICE headquarters on the St. Elizabeths campus in Ward 8.

Liz Halstad, managing director and COO of Hip Hop Caucus, tells co-host Brittany that close election results in Mississippi are being deliberately silenced — what Brittany calls a "silencing of the data." The conversation marks the 18th anniversary of the Respect My Vote campaign, launched in 2008 at the 930 Club near Howard University, and Halstad outlines what continuous voter engagement looks like in practice.

Rev Yearwood and Brittany trace Black August from its origins with incarcerated organizers at San Quentin State Prison in 1979 through the Haitian Revolution and Hurricane Katrina. Rev Yearwood also describes walking 5 miles a day — 2.5 miles to a coffee shop and back — as a way of managing grief since his mother's death on May Day. The episode closes on heat safety and the climate justice stakes of extreme summer temperatures reaching Southern California with unfamiliar humidity.

Curtis Valentine's great-grandfather co-founded a Rosenwald School; his book *Real Men Teach* traces that lineage back to John Chavis, a free Black man who taught white students in the early 1800s whose student went on to become a U.S. Senator from North Carolina. Valentine, founding president of the Male Educator Network and Policy Institute, joins host Daman Harris on *You Must Learn* at WPFW, with testimony from former students of Black male educators including U.S. Senator Raphael Warnock and Governor Deval Patrick, and a discussion of figures such as Charles Ogletree. 

Baba Clifton of Mommy's TLC announces a pre-celebration at 2616 Georgia Avenue Northwest on August 1st, marking 25 years and over 16,000 children served through the out-of-school-time program. Dr. Sekou Africa of Bowie State University describes building a pipeline for Black male educators from 8th grade through master's degree level, and explains how symptoms he mistook for a stroke and a heart attack shaped his new initiative, the Black Male Educator Classroom.

Lynn Reinhardt, former General Counsel of the AFL-CIO and senior counselor to the Secretary of Labor in the Biden administration, has a pointed answer to the claim that project labor agreements drive up construction costs: labor is roughly 20–25% of total project costs, and efficiency gains offset higher wages. Now a senior fellow at the Economic Policy Institute, Reinhardt joins host Renee Bowser on *Unionism Drives Community* to explain how PLAs actually function on publicly subsidized projects like the RFK Stadium redevelopment, and why they are legally distinct from pre-hire agreements. The cost advantage non-union contractors hold on public bids — up to 30%, she argues — comes not from paying lower wages outright but from misclassifying workers as independent contractors.

Union hiring halls, which are legally required to refer qualified non-members, enter the conversation alongside what the Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act provides for apprenticeship transportation and childcare subsidies. Bowser points to Ward 7 and Ward 8 residents, where unemployment runs into double digits, as a population still underconnected to building-trades apprenticeship pipelines.

Bunchy Carter crossed town to teach the Brown Berets how to run a feeding program. That alliance — Panthers and Berets jointly picketing a grocery chain that was deliberately destroying food rather than letting the Panthers collect it — is the historical thread Jon Jeter pulls through this episode of *Short Money: Dissecting Racial Capitalism*. His guest is Al Osorio, longtime Bay Area activist and capitán of the Oakland Brown Berets, who argues Black-Brown coalition building remains possible today.

The two work through the leaked Los Angeles City Council tape in which council president Nury Martinez called a 2-year-old Black child a "changuito" and said he needed a beatdown, reading it as a "petition to be white." That framing carries them to the moment when Latino supporters of councilmember Kevin de León heard the recording and switched sides, joining Black Lives Matter protesters in the street.

Karsi Blanton accepted an award at Folk Alliance without a guitar and told the room she'd gone from $80,000 in debt at her last attendance to over $200,000 in debt a decade later. That speech anchors the final segment of this *Labor Heritage Power Hour*, hosted by Chris Garlock and Elise Bryant.

Before that, physician-songwriter Mindy Murray tells the Labor John podcast how her father's childhood farm labor near Morrisville, Pennsylvania drove her to write "Striking at Kings" — a song about the 1938 King Farm strike, where workers earned as little as 17 cents an hour. Labor journalist Kim Kelly sits down with J. Albert Mann to discuss her young-readers book *Fight to Win*, moving from Lucy Parsons to a trans autoworker named Joni Christian, and making the case that workers have organized under worse conditions than today's.

Two Iranian Americans walked into a Pete Hegseth hearing holding photos of the 168 girls killed in the Manab school bombing — and were arrested. Marcy Winograd and Code Pink co-founder Medea Benjamin use that moment to open a wider accounting of the U.S. war on Iran, including the gap between Hegseth's stated war cost of $39.5 billion and Moody's estimate of $132 billion once energy costs are included. They then work through Marco Rubio's 100-page State Department report, "Cuba: Capital of 21st Century Communism," which names Code Pink, the DSA, the National Lawyers Guild, the People's Forum, Haitian Women for Haitian Refugees, and Equality for Flatbush as part of a Cuba-directed conspiracy — a framing both guests call a pretext for military intervention. The episode also covers the House-passed NDAA provision establishing a Pentagon coordinator for permanent U.S.-Israeli co-development of weapons and AI. It closes on two primary upsets: Milad Kyros, a 29-year-old barista, defeated 15-term Denver Congresswoman Diana DeGette, and Clara Valdez won New York's 7th Congressional District — both backed by the DSA.

Media coverage blamed Nolan Wells for his own death by citing his drinking. Aton Thomas and Chuck Modiano of *The Collision* argue that playbook is the same one deployed after Michael Brown Jr.'s death, and mirrors how rape cases shift focus to what a victim was wearing. On the sports media side, Modiano calls ESPN's pressure on analyst Monica McNutt over her Caitlin Clark critiques part of "the Trumpification of sports media," naming Ryan Clark, Cam Newton, Bomani Jones, Jemele Hill, Max Kellerman, and Dan Le Batard as others pushed out.

Guests Deanne and Jay Thompson, co-hosts of the *Why Do I Give a F* podcast, bring the conversation to Netanyahu's scheduled visit to New York and the Democratic Party's continued support for Israel. Deanne describes unpacking what she calls Zionism indoctrination as parallel to unpacking whiteness, and the discussion draws a distinction between Judaism and Zionism.

Keith Leonard spent 3.5 years editing the *Cambridge History of African American Poetry* and watched it shrink from 40 chapters to 32. He will tell you himself there's no chapter on Islam's influence on Black poetry — not the Black Arts Movement, not hip-hop's Five Percenters. E. Ethelbert Miller isn't letting that go unexamined.

On *On the Margin*, Miller pushes Leonard on whether a Cave Canem-to-MFA-to-Copper Canyon pipeline is quietly homogenizing the canon, citing Amiri Baraka's 2013 *Poetry Magazine* critique of Charles Raul's *Angles of Ascent* as evidence the stakes are real. He also names two poets he considers unjustly absent from the scholarly record: Amos T. Bolton and Brenda Marie Osby.

At a July 21st congressional hearing, Ambassador Michael Kozak could not confirm the State Department was consulted before DHS Secretary Noem terminated Temporary Protected Status for over 350,000 Haitians. The termination took legal effect July 27th, after the Supreme Court's June 25th ruling returned the case to Judge Ana Reyes. Host Eugenia Charles plays that audio, which features questioning by Representatives Gabe Amo and Gregory Meeks. She then turns to House Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast's description of the Kenya-led security mission as "an ineffective boondoggle," countering that the U.S. drafted the resolution creating it, brokered Kenya's participation through IMF and World Bank access, and still owes Kenya unpaid funds.

The program also covers a congressional delegation's July 27th visit to Haiti and a newly published electoral calendar scheduling a first-round presidential vote for December 13, 2026. Listeners are given a phone number to call their senators in support of Senate Bill S.4814, which would extend TPS for three years.

Black Americans are 40% more likely than white Americans to have asthma — and Mary Black of the Black Hive at the Movement for Black Lives traces that disparity directly to why Hurricane Katrina communities were left to rebuild without resources. Beth Yerga, a Black Hive founding member and educator, lays out three foundations of community preparedness: neighbor relationships, sustained mutual aid networks, and political education linking climate change to environmental racism. Yerga describes recruiting students into climate organizing through the George Floyd protests and is working to certify every student ages 13–19 in her school in Community Emergency Response Team training.

Hosts Majé, Ahmad, Tre'logy, and Liv Grace of the Freedom Futures Collective carry the conversation forward alongside a Pride Purpose Power Top 5 Countdown of independent artists and a Mic Drop Mix from Southampton, England DJ Nadia Zaki.

Francesca Albanese, the U.N. special rapporteur on the occupied Palestinian territory, calls Netanyahu's seventh visit to Washington since Trump returned to office "bullying in a diplomatic suit." Barred from entering the United States under U.S. sanctions, she tells *Democracy Now!* host Amy Goodman and returning producer Anjali Kamat that Italy, France, and Greece each violated their obligations as Rome Statute parties by opening their airspace to an ICC-wanted fugitive.

Dr. Deborah Howery, the former chief medical officer at the CDC who resigned in protest last year, explains how gutting FoodNet's mandatory pathogen tracking — dropping cyclospora and five others including Listeria — left the agency unable to respond to an outbreak that has now sickened nearly 11,000 people across 41 states. Then Neha Bura, national president of the All India Students Association and a 23-day hunger striker, describes India's Cockroach Movement: over 600 students detained in Bihar alone, pellet guns fired on protesters in Delhi, and an AK-47 fired by police in Bihar — all after the education minister's resignation and government assurances of no reprisals.

Shirkuh — the general who cleared the path for Saladin — died of tonsillitis after a single month as wazir. Host Zain Al-Amin and political philosopher Roy Casagrande use that detail as a doorway into the 1099 Crusader conquest of Jerusalem, examining how Saladin's calculated mercy toward the city's inhabitants was designed to strip the Crusaders of their fanatical edge. From there the conversation moves through the Dreyfus Affair, Theodor Herzl, and the Balfour Declaration, drawing direct parallels between Crusader settlement tactics — Arab labor building the forts meant to keep Arabs out — and the founding of the State of Israel.

The news segment covers Israeli strikes on a mosque sheltering displaced Palestinians in Gaza and U.S.-Saudi joint airstrikes on Iranian-backed militias in Iraq.

Dr. Ayize Sabater opened an African-centered school in Atlanta four months after graduating from Morehouse — September 1992 — then ran a vegetarian restaurant chain, Delights of the Garden, on Georgia Avenue across from Howard University. Now founder of Mommy's TLC and the Black Montessori Education Fund, he tells host Mwiza Munthali how his organization has distributed nearly a quarter of a million dollars in mini grants to Black people entering Montessori education, reaching families and schools across the U.S., the Caribbean, and countries including The Gambia, Senegal, Nigeria, and Kenya. He argues that Montessori's century-old model was deliberately sidelined in favor of a Prussian factory system built for conformity rather than critical thinking.

The episode also carries reporting from Ituri, DRC, where Congolese journalist Akili Mali Chomachoma and Stella Ramazani of the Basanja Coalition, joined by Maurice Carney of Friends of the Congo, describe an Ebola outbreak whose official death toll was approaching 1,000 — but whose real count, they say, runs three to five times higher. A displacement camp of roughly 25,000 people near Bunia recorded 57 suspected deaths before a single case was officially confirmed.

Jarvis C. McInnis calls it the "affordances of Tuskegee" — what the institution produced beyond Booker T. Washington's own limiting vision. His book *Afterlives of the Plantation* tracks how Afro-Cuban journalist Rafael Serra y Montalvo, Haitian intellectual Jean Price-Mars, and a young Marcus Garvey each selectively adapted a model built on a degraded former cotton plantation founded in 1881. McInnis also recovers two figures largely written out of that history: Margaret Murray Washington — twice president of the National Association of Colored Women's Clubs and founder of the International Council of Women of the Darker Races of the World — as an early architect of international women's studies, and Clara Sheppard, a Tuskegee French teacher who traveled to Paris and became a key translator for *La Revue du Monde Noir*, the bilingual journal central to the Negritude movement.

This broadcast is host David Whetstone's final episode of *We the People*, a program he had hosted since October 2016.

Danielle Smith's granddaughter stood before Representatives Clyburn, Jasmine Crockett, and Melanie Campbell at the Congressional Black Caucus — one example of how Smith's Baltimore chapter of Black Women for Positive Change pushes young people directly in front of elected officials. The chapter's Month of Nonviolence program has run poetry cyphers, peace circles, and an essay contest where participants wrote on changing community violence culture and competed for donated laptops.

Dr. Franklin Malone of 100 Fathers brings a complementary perspective. Named the number-one family support organization in the DMV by the *Washington Informer*, 100 Fathers holds an annual Healing and Restoring the Soul of Our Community conference at Howard University. Malone announces the August 2nd Restorers of the Covenant of Peace Awards ceremony at the Howard University School of Social Work, honoring community members including parents who lost children to gun violence and returned to schools to work against it. Host Faye Williams leads the conversation on Wake Up, Stay Woke.

Pope Leo's May 2026 apology for slavery runs to a single point on page 176 of an encyclical primarily about artificial intelligence — issued on Africa Day, then buried. Attorney Enola Aird, co-convener of the Global Circle for Reparations and Healing, tells host Fahima Sekh that Catholic doctrine itself demands more: complete confession, contrition, restitution, penance, amendment, and the rescinding of the 15th-century papal bulls that authorized the Portuguese and others to "search out, invade, and subject to perpetual slavery" the peoples of Africa. Aird and Sekh also take up the UN General Assembly resolution introduced by Ghana's President John Mahama declaring the transatlantic trafficking of African people the greatest crime against humanity.

That conversation opens onto the June 2026 High-Level Consultative Conference on Reparations in Accra, whose outcome document — shaped in part by Dr. Cheryl Grills — acknowledges that "a healing-centered framework is essential to the reparations process." The same thread runs through the documentary *Centering Healing Across Global Africa*, available at gcrh.org, and through local reparations efforts from Georgetown University to Palm Springs, California.

A 4-year-old, moved by a lesson about violist Robin Faye Massey's earthquake fundraising, argued her parents into opening a lemonade stand to send money to the Japanese Embassy after the tsunami. That same instinct — teaching children that their actions reach beyond themselves — runs through the conversation guest host Daman Harris has with Baba Ayize Sabater and Carl Science McFadden about Mommy's TLC, which grew from a $10,000 seed grant and 12 students into a million-dollar out-of-school-time program now operating across multiple D.C. and Maryland sites.

The program then turns to who is doing the teaching. Dr. Richter Craig, founder and CEO of the National Association of Black Male Educators, joins to discuss the fact that Black men make up only 1.2% of the public education workforce. He outlines a panel on Black male educator mental health — featuring the heads of the Surge Institute and the Center for Black Educator Development, moderated by the CEO of the National Black Justice Collective — set for August 12th at Old Whaling Church in Edgartown, Massachusetts. Craig also describes Statesman College Preparatory Academy for Boys in Southeast D.C., where 7th graders travel to Paris, London, and Madrid, and 8th graders to Cape Town and Johannesburg, at no cost to students.

Representative James Clyburn traveled to Michigan to campaign for Haley Stevens against Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, and Anthony Rogers-Wright opens *Full Spectrum with Anthony Rogers-Wright* calling that out by name. His "Burn Notice" segment targets the Congressional Black Caucus for backing pro-Zionist candidates over progressive ones — AIPAC and affiliated groups spent $30 million on that single race, which Rogers-Wright describes as the largest amount the Zionist lobby has ever spent on one contest.

Recorded at COP30 in Belém, Brazil, his conversation with David Cobb lands the same day the UN denied Afro-descendants standalone constituency status within the UNFCCC. Rogers-Wright and Cobb work through the Black Alliance for Peace's framework of climate liberation over climate justice, and the Battle of Blair Mountain as a model of multiracial class solidarity. Rogers-Wright traces his own entry into this work to Harlem's West Side Little League, where Black and brown friends had to stop after two or three innings because their asthma was too severe to keep playing.

A Wits University study puts foreigners at just 3.4–3.5 percent of formal jobs in South Africa, yet the country's 35–40 percent unemployment rate keeps getting blamed on migrants. Clinton Ndzala, a Nairobi-based political writer, traces that scapegoating to a labor system reaching back to the 1901 founding of the Witwatersrand Native Workers Association, which pulled workers from Mozambique, Malawi, and Zambia into Johannesburg's gold mines. The ANC's embrace of liberal economic policies in the 1990s, compounded by the legacy of Bantu education, he argues, set the conditions for the first major xenophobic violence in 2008.

That history of structured displacement has its parallels elsewhere. Attorney Brian Concannon of the Institute for Justice and Democracy in Haiti breaks down the Supreme Court's June 25 ruling ending Temporary Protected Status for more than 350,000 Haitians, contending it signals to lower courts that 14th Amendment protections against racist federal discrimination no longer hold. A bill led by Representative Ayanna Pressley passed the House in April to extend TPS three years, but still needs 63 Senate co-sponsors to reach a vote. Margaret Kimberley hosts throughout for Black Agenda Report.

Rapper and educator Bomani Armah built his new album *Watermelon Man 2: The Big Slice* around Kwanzaa principles and a four-part biographical suite tracing Malcolm X from Malcolm Little through El-Hajj Malik El-Shabazz. Host Marlon Mutafa broadcasts *Something to Say* from Puerto Rico for a two-hour listening party that goes track by track through the record, including an ode to the DMV that name-checks Sherman Circle, Largo, and Sankofa Video and Books on Georgia Avenue.

From there the program turns to Aize, founder of Mommy's TLC, who describes how an out-of-school-time program that started with a $10,000 grant and 12 children in Columbia Heights now runs a budget of more than $1 million across multiple sites in D.C. and Maryland — 25 years later. Poetry readings come from Arlington, Virginia's 2022 Youth Poet Laureate Kashvi and Nigerian-born writer Chimwekele Okoro.

A striker on tape describes a scab driver plowing through the crowd at the C&H Sugar refinery in Crockett, California, then fleeing — the flashpoint behind a July 21st walkout by Bay Area ILWU Local 10 longshoremen who shut down West Coast ports to honor the picket line there. The Fanjul family's company had bused in replacement workers. A Filipino community organizer explains that the sugar aboard the ship *Tia Herald* originates in Negros Occidental in the Philippines, where armed forces under Marcos Jr. massacred 19 people in April, among them Bay Area activist Lal Frijoles. Greg Mitre, president of the ILWU Southern California Pensioners, argues that automation has already eliminated 400 to 500 jobs at the Maersk terminal alone, and that pairing AI with automation will leave no one left to consume or sustain the economy.

ATU Local 1208 president Charles Torrence Jr. joins from Jackson, Mississippi, where his 60-member transit local was three weeks into a strike against contractor MV Transportation over wages, seniority rights, and MV's proposal to cut two fixed routes and Saturday service. Paulina Vassilian hosts.

Flock Safety's license plate readers don't just record where your car has been — they log its color, make, bumper stickers, and dents into a searchable national database. Ed from Deflock tells Project Censored co-hosts Eleanor Goldfield and Mickey Huff how that data has been used by police officers stalking ex-girlfriends, by immigration enforcement, and to monitor abortion activity. California and Illinois passed laws barring ICE access; Ed documents how both have been routinely broken. More than 80 ALPR contracts have been canceled through community organizing, including in Austin and Denver.

That organizing impulse carries into the question of AI. Climate communicator Heidi Lim of AI Resist List outlines nine pillars of resistance to large-scale generative AI, among them Nightshade, a tool that poisons training data, and a map tracking over $1 billion in tech-company funding of newsrooms. She also describes Te Hiku Media, a Māori-owned organization that built a small language model trained on community-consented data to preserve the Māori language without Silicon Valley infrastructure.

Abby Rozner found her 36 interview subjects — elders using psilocybin and other psychedelics to make peace with mortality, heal trauma, and build community — simply by attending integration circles run by local psychedelic societies. Her book, *Psychedelics and the Counterculture of Aging*, grew from those conversations. She tells host David Rabin how ibogaine, a sacred medicine from the Bwiti people of Gabon, traveled a chain from Rick Perry to Joe Rogan to Trump himself, and raises the question of who profits when indigenous intellectual property enters pharmaceutical development. The second half moves to Mosaic Theater's 2025-26 season, where Artistic Director Reginald Douglas walks through three productions. Among them: *Somewhere Over the Border*, playwright Bryan Quijada's retelling of his Salvadoran mother's immigration story as *The Wizard of Oz*, set to cumbia, mariachi, hip-hop, and rock, and the world premiere of *7th Street Echo*, a go-go music play set in Congress Heights, developed with the Go-Go Museum in Anacostia.

Daniel Ortega's July 19th statement on elections was taken entirely out of context, says journalist John Perry. Ortega was objecting to U.S. State Department-funded candidates, not to elections themselves — and when Nicaragua's government tried to correct the record, no corporate outlet ran the story. Perry, who has lived in Nicaragua for 23 years, walks co-hosts Brother Craig and Netfa Freeman through U.S. intervention from the Marines' early-20th-century occupation to the Reagan-era Contra war, which he says was funded by drug money and arms sales to Iran. He describes the 2018 coup attempt in concrete terms: stones shipped in, homemade mortars distributed, 22 police officers killed, and his own wife held at gunpoint at a roadblock in Masaya.

The episode also carries a recorded address by political prisoner Mumia Abu-Jamal to the 2026 Galaxy Community Conference, in which he cites Robin D.G. Kelley's *Hammer and Hoe* and the repression of Alabama agricultural workers and miners in the 1930s. "The state does not want people to awaken from their slumber," Abu-Jamal tells the conference.

Vernon Eugene Hawkins told his family he would never run for elected office: "That's not my role." He died July 2, 2025, and his daughter Laverne Hawkins Jones, along with colleagues Saleem Hilton and Norm Nixon, join host Joni on *To Heal DC* to remember the Washington DC organizer. Hawkins ran voter registration drives across 12 states and worked as a behind-the-scenes force alongside Mayor Marion Barry. In the 1980s he directed the Commission on Social Services' HIV/AIDS response, training 1,000 staff members and coordinating with health commissioner Reed Tuckson. He also built Unifest, a street festival on Martin Luther King Avenue in Anacostia that ran from the early 1980s into the 2000s, with five stages of entertainment alongside health and social services outreach. The activists he mentored called themselves the Vernonites.

Nixon announces that a scholarship fund in Hawkins's name at Union Temple Baptist Church distributed $16,000 the previous day, including grants directed specifically to HBCU attendees.

A ship that could have replaced the MV Barima has sat idle for years — and is now reportedly used by Guyana's First Lady to host galas. Parliamentarian and maritime attorney Amanza Walton told host Julianne Malveaux the ferry disaster, which left roughly 77 dead and 50 still unaccounted for inside the sunken vessel, was entirely preventable: two procurement cycles failed to finish the stellings needed to dock replacement ships sourced from India and Greece. Walton also revealed that Guyana's government disbanded its ferry inspectorate unit in 2021, and that the National Assembly's speaker has banned parliamentarians from using the word "corruption" on the floor. Then Katie Sanson of the National Women's Law Center explains that the EEOC has proposed eliminating the EEO-1 data collection requirement — which has tracked workforce composition by race, sex, and job category since the 1960s — citing a priority drawn directly from the labor chapter of Project 2025. The public comment period runs through August 24th at regulations.gov.
